cite: Macintyre, A Spy Among Friends, 2015; Boyle, The Climate of Treason, 1979; Oxford DNB (Clive, 2004)

n: Diplomat Donald Maclean reported Anglo-US atomic policy to Moscow
rank: Washington embassy First Secretary; head of Foreign Office American Department
d: Donald Maclean, a British diplomat recruited through the Cambridge spy ring, passed Foreign Office secrets to Soviet intelligence from inside the British embassy in Washington (1944–48) and later as head of the Foreign Office's American Department. In Washington he served as secretary of the Combined Policy Committee, the body coordinating American, British and Canadian atomic energy policy, and became Moscow's main source on it, including how much plutonium the Americans had. He reportedly passed a record of the December 1950 Attlee–Truman summit. Venona decrypts identified a source called 'Homer'; facing exposure, he fled to Moscow with Guy Burgess on 25 May 1951.
cite: Cecil, A Divided Life, 1988; Holzman, Donald and Melinda Maclean, 2014; Andrew & Mitrokhin, The Mitrokhin Archive

n: John Cairncross passed Cabinet Office and Bletchley Park secrets to Moscow
rank: Private secretary to Lord Hankey; Bletchley Park; MI6
d: John Cairncross, a British civil servant recruited in 1937, worked for Soviet intelligence from posts in the Foreign Office, the Treasury, the Cabinet Office (as private secretary to minister Lord Hankey), the Bletchley Park code-breaking centre (1942–43) and MI6. Russian archives indicate he supplied 5,832 documents between 1941 and 1945. Through Hankey's office, which sat on Britain's early atomic committees, he gave Moscow early evidence that Britain was considering an atomic bomb. From Bletchley he smuggled out decrypted German messages that gave advance warning of the German offensive at Kursk in 1943. He confessed to MI5 in 1964 but was never prosecuted; in 1990 KGB defector Oleg Gordievsky confirmed him as the 'fifth man' of the Cambridge ring.
cite: Andrew & Gordievsky, The Times, 1990; Smith, The Last Cambridge Spy, 2019; Independent obituary (Bower), 1995

n: MI5 officer Anthony Blunt passed wartime secrets to the NKVD
rank: MI5 officer; Surveyor of the King's Pictures
d: Anthony Blunt, an art historian recruited by Soviet intelligence around 1937, joined Britain's domestic security service, MI5, in 1940 and passed it secrets to the NKVD throughout the war. He handed over Ultra intelligence from decrypted German Enigma traffic on the Eastern Front, details of German spy rings in the Soviet Union and German war plans the British had chosen to withhold. After 1945 he became Surveyor of the King's Pictures, kept contact with Soviet agents and passed on gossip from MI5 colleagues until 1951. He confessed on 23 April 1964 in return for immunity, which was kept secret until Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher named him in the Commons on 15 November 1979. He was then stripped of his knighthood.
cite: Hansard, 15 Nov 1979; Carter, Anthony Blunt: His Lives, 2001; Oxford DNB

n: MI6 officer George Blake betrayed Western agents and the Berlin tunnel
d: George Blake, an officer of Britain's foreign intelligence service, MI6, volunteered to work for the Soviet MGB (the KGB's predecessor) while held prisoner during the Korean War and then served Moscow from inside MI6. He told his Soviet contacts about Operation Gold, a tunnel dug into East Berlin to tap Soviet military telephone lines, and the similar Operation Silver in Vienna. From 1955, as a case officer in Berlin recruiting Soviet officers, he exposed agents; Britain says hundreds of Western agents in Eastern Europe were compromised, some executed. Unmasked by a Polish defector, he was sentenced in May 1961 to 42 years, escaped from Wormwood Scrubs on 22 October 1966 and reached Moscow.
cite: Guardian obituary (Norton-Taylor), 2020; BBC News, 2020; Hermiston, The Greatest Traitor, 2013

n: Melita Norwood passed Britain's atomic research files to Moscow for 35 years
rank: Secretary at the British Non-Ferrous Metals Research Association
d: Melita Norwood, a secretary at the British Non-Ferrous Metals Research Association from 1932, was a Soviet agent from 1937 until she retired in 1972. Her post as secretary to a department head gave her access to material from Tube Alloys, Britain's wartime atomic weapons project, which the association worked on, and she passed it to Soviet intelligence. She was exposed in September 1999 by The Mitrokhin Archive, based on notes from KGB files. She said she acted 'not to make money, but to help prevent the defeat of a new system'. British authorities decided not to prosecute her, then aged 87.
cite: Andrew & Mitrokhin, The Mitrokhin Archive, 1999; BBC News, 1999; Guardian obituary, 2005

n: Moldovan president Dodon charged with treason over Russian party money
rank: President of Moldova (2016–2020); Socialist Party leader
d: Igor Dodon, president of Moldova from December 2016 to December 2020 and leader of the pro-Russian Socialist Party (PSRM), is accused of keeping his party running on money from Russia. In June 2019 videos showed him telling the oligarch Vladimir Plahotniuc that the party received monthly funding from the Russian Federation. In March 2020 three MPs presented documents they said showed Russian money reaching PSRM MPs through a Bahamas account, with Dodon as main beneficiary. He was arrested on 24 May 2022 and charged with passive corruption, illegal party financing by a criminal organisation, illicit enrichment and high treason. The US Treasury says he conspired with Russia to interfere in Moldova's elections. His trial was ordered restarted in November 2025.
cite: Wikipedia 'Igor Dodon' (citing Moldovan prosecutors, RFE/RL, US Treasury); Ziarul de Gardă

n: Romania's top court annuls presidential vote after Russian-backed campaign
d: Romanian intelligence documents, declassified by President Klaus Iohannis on 4 December 2024, said that the first-round winner of the presidential election, Călin Georgescu (22.94%), rose through a campaign funded and coordinated by a 'state actor', which Romanian authorities identified as Russia. One TikTok account, reportedly registered to Bogdan Peșchir, paid about €381,000 to accounts promoting Georgescu, and more than 25,000 accounts were involved. On 6 December 2024 the Constitutional Court annulled the election. In March 2025 the electoral bureau barred Georgescu from the rerun, and in September 2025 he and 21 others were charged with plotting a coup.
cite: Romanian Supreme Council of National Defence (CSAT) documents, 4 Dec 2024; BBC News, 4 Dec 2024; Guardian, 6 Dec 2024; Reuters, 9 Mar 2025

n: Montenegro coup plot: GRU officers and pro-Russian MPs, later acquitted
d: Prosecutors in Montenegro alleged that two officers of Russia's military intelligence (GRU), Eduard Shishmakov and Vladimir Popov, worked with leaders of the pro-Russian Democratic Front party to seize parliament on election day, 16 October 2016, kill Prime Minister Milo Đukanović and install a government that would halt Montenegro's entry into NATO. On 9 May 2019 a court convicted 13 people: the GRU officers in absentia (15 and 12 years) and Democratic Front MPs Andrija Mandić and Milan Knežević (five years each). The appeals court annulled the verdict in February 2021 for procedural violations; a retrial acquitted all defendants in July 2024, upheld in February 2026. Montenegro joined NATO in 2017.
cite: Reuters, 9 May 2019; BalkanInsight, 9 May 2019 and 12 Jul 2024; RFE/RL, 5 Feb 2021; RTCG, 20 Feb 2026

n: Greece expels Russian diplomats for trying to bribe state officials
d: In July 2018 Greece expelled two Russian diplomats and barred two others, citing threats to national security. The Greek Foreign Ministry later said Russia had attempted to bribe state officials, undermine Greek foreign policy and interfere in Greece's internal affairs. The expulsions came weeks after Greece signed the Prespa agreement with North Macedonia, which opened the way for that country to join NATO and which Russia opposed; some Greek politicians accused Russia of trying to block the deal. Russia expelled Greek diplomats in August 2018 and Greece recalled its ambassador.
cite: Reuters, 11 Jul 2018; BBC News, 11 Jul 2018; Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements, 18 Jul and 10 Aug 2018

n: US sanctions Serbia's spy chief Vulin for aiding Russia's activities
rank: Director of Serbia's Security Intelligence Agency (BIA)
d: Aleksandar Vulin, Serbia's defence minister (2017–2020), interior minister (2020–2022) and then director of the Security Intelligence Agency (BIA), the country's main intelligence service, was sanctioned by the US Treasury on 11 July 2023. The Treasury said he carried out 'corrupt and destabilizing acts that have also facilitated Russia's malign activities in the region', and accused him of supporting a drug-trafficking network and illegal arms shipments involving Serbian arms dealer Slobodan Tešić and the Belarusian state firm Beltechexport. Vulin resigned from the BIA on 3 November 2023 under Western pressure but became deputy prime minister in May 2024.
cite: US Treasury press release jy1606, 11 Jul 2023; AP, 11 Jul and 4 Nov 2023

n: Gazprom's Nord Stream 2 funded a German state's 'climate' foundation
d: The state government of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern in north-east Germany, led by Minister-President Manuela Schwesig, set up a public 'Climate and Environmental Protection Foundation' whose charter stated the goal of completing the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline from Russia. The money came from Nord Stream 2 AG, a subsidiary of Russia's state gas company Gazprom, and Reuters reported that the foundation set out to help the project get around US sanctions on firms working on the pipeline. A state body thus served as a channel for a Russian state company. In March 2024 media reported that Schwesig's office removed passages from a supposedly independent report saying closing the foundation was feasible and desirable.
cite: Reuters explainer (Escritt & Marsh), 11 Feb 2022; Business Insider Deutschland, 7 Mar 2024

n: Russian 'illegals' cultivated a Clinton campaign co-chair and US policy circles
d: Russia's foreign intelligence service, the SVR, placed long-term 'illegals' (agents living under false identities without diplomatic cover) in the United States with orders to build ties to academics, industrialists and policymakers and report on US policy. One, Cynthia Murphy (real name Lidiya Guriyeva), cultivated Alan Patricof, a venture capitalist who had co-chaired Hillary Clinton's 2008 presidential campaign; her handlers told her to 'build up relations little by little'. The FBI arrested ten agents on 27 June 2010. None was charged with obtaining classified material. On 9 July 2010 all ten pleaded guilty to acting as unregistered agents and were swapped in Vienna for four prisoners held by Russia, including Sergei Skripal.
cite: US Department of Justice, 28 Jun 2010; FBI, 'Operation Ghost Stories', 31 Oct 2011; NYT, 28 Jun 2010

n: GRU officer with false identity nearly took a job at the ICC
rank: Position at the International Criminal Court
d: Sergey Cherkasov, an alleged officer of Russia's military intelligence (GRU), spent years in Brazil building the false identity of a Brazilian, Victor Muller Ferreira, and in April 2022 flew to the Netherlands to take up a position at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague. The ICC was then investigating war crimes in Ukraine. The Dutch intelligence service AIVD judged the threat potentially very high; he was refused entry at Schiphol airport and sent back to Brazil, where he was convicted of using forged documents. His sentence was cut from 15 years to five years and two months, and in January 2024 Brazil added a money-laundering charge.
cite: Guardian, 16 Jun 2022; BBC News, 16 Jun 2022; CNN, 28 Jul 2023; Deutsche Welle, 30 Jan 2024

n: Polish judge who ruled on security clearances fled to Belarus
d: Tomasz Szmydt, a judge at the Voivodeship Administrative Court in Warsaw, sat in the department that ruled on whether members of the military and intelligence services could access classified information, and reportedly on access to NATO and EU top-secret material. On 1 May 2024 he left Poland and went to Belarus, Russia's close ally, where he sought asylum and appeared at a press conference by the state news agency BelTA. On 9 May the Supreme Administrative Court lifted his immunity at prosecutors' request amid espionage charges. Polish officials, including his former superior Łukasz Piebiak, said he had worked for Russia; this has not been proven.
cite: Gazeta Wyborcza, 6–9 May 2024; TVP World, 9 May 2024; BelTA, 6 May 2024

n: CIA translator Larry Wu-tai Chin spied for China for over 30 years
rank: CIA Foreign Broadcast Information Service analyst
d: Larry Wu-tai Chin, recruited by Chinese intelligence in 1944, worked as a Chinese-language translator and analyst at the CIA's Foreign Broadcast Information Service from 1952 to 1981 while spying for China. He passed CIA intelligence reports on China and East Asia, profiles of CIA employees and information that helped Chinese counter-intelligence find agents in China. In 1970 he passed CIA documents on President Nixon's plans to open relations with China, which Mao reportedly used in negotiations. A senior Chinese intelligence official, Yu Qiangsheng, defected in 1985 and exposed him. He was arrested on 23 November 1985, convicted in February 1986 and found dead in his cell on 21 February 1986.
cite: Los Angeles Times, 8 and 21 Feb 1986; Hoffman, The Spy Within, 2008; Washington Post, 6 Dec 1985

n: FBI's top China informant Katrina Leung also worked for Beijing's MSS
d: Katrina Leung, a Los Angeles businesswoman whom FBI agent James J. Smith recruited as an informant code-named 'Parlor Maid' in 1982, was also recruited by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) in 1984, according to the FBI. Smith, her handler, had a long affair with her and brought classified material to their meetings. In 1991 another agent recognised her voice on a recording of a call with an MSS official, and the FBI learned she had disclosed a classified operation. Prosecutors said she contaminated about 20 years of FBI intelligence on China. Arrested in April 2003, she had the main charges dismissed for prosecutorial misconduct and in December 2005 pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI and filing a false tax return.
cite: CNN, 2003; Wise, Tiger Trap, 2011; DOJ Office of the Inspector General review, 2006

n: Chinese military intelligence chief allegedly gave $300,000 for US Democrats
d: Donor Johnny Chung testified to a House committee in May 1999 that General Ji Shengde, then head of China's military intelligence, told him 'I will give you 300,000 U.S. dollars' for the Democrats, and that $35,000 of his donations came via the general through Liu Chaoying, an aerospace executive. In 1997 the Washington Post reported that a Justice Department investigation found evidence that Chinese agents had tried to steer foreign money to the Democratic National Committee before the 1996 election, using the Chinese embassy to coordinate. China denied it. Several fundraisers, including Chung, John Huang and Charlie Trie, pleaded guilty or were convicted of campaign-finance crimes, and the party returned donations.
cite: Washington Post, 13 Feb 1997; NYT, 12 May 1999; Senate Governmental Affairs Committee final report, 10 Mar 1998

n: Ex-CIA officer Jerry Chun Shing Lee took MSS cash as CIA's China agents vanished
d: Jerry Chun Shing Lee, a CIA officer with top-secret clearance from 1994 to 2007, was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) in Shenzhen in April 2010, when two MSS officers gave him $100,000 in cash and promised to 'take care of him for life'. He deposited hundreds of thousands of dollars in cash in Hong Kong bank accounts from 2010 to 2013. In the same period the CIA lost 18 to 20 of its informants in China, who were killed or imprisoned. Arrested by the FBI in January 2018, he was charged with conspiracy to commit espionage, pleaded guilty in May 2019 and was sentenced in November 2019 to 19 years.
cite: South China Morning Post, 16 May 2018; US Department of Justice, Nov 2019

n: China's MSS paid an American to apply for jobs at the State Dept and CIA
rank: Applicant to the Foreign Service and CIA clandestine service
d: Officers of the Shanghai State Security Bureau, part of China's Ministry of State Security, recruited an American student, Glenn Duffie Shriver, around 2004 and paid him to get inside US government agencies. They paid him $10,000 and $20,000 to sit the Foreign Service exam in 2005 and 2006, which he failed, and $40,000 when he applied in 2007 to the CIA's National Clandestine Service, which runs its spies abroad. He hid the contacts during CIA vetting in 2010; the CIA already knew, and the FBI arrested him in June 2010. He pleaded guilty in October 2010 to conspiracy under the Espionage Act and on 21 January 2011 was sentenced to four years.
cite: US Department of Justice, 21 Jan 2011; Reuters, 22 Oct 2010; Washingtonian (Wise), 7 Jun 2012

n: Ex-CIA officer Kevin Mallory sold defence secrets to Chinese intelligence
d: Kevin Mallory, a former US Army soldier, State Department security agent, CIA officer and contractor who had held top-secret clearance, was approached in 2017 by an officer of China's Ministry of State Security posing as a headhunter. He then gave his Chinese contacts US defence secrets, including top-secret documents. A jury convicted him on 8 June 2018 of conspiracy to transmit national defence information to a foreign government, and in May 2019 he was sentenced to 20 years. He had left government service and was working as a consultant when the approach came.
cite: US Department of Justice, 17 May 2019; Wikipedia 'List of Chinese spy cases in the United States'

n: State Department's Candace Claiborne traded documents for Chinese agents' gifts
d: Candace Claiborne, a US State Department employee with top-secret clearance, hid her contacts with agents of the People's Republic of China and accepted gifts and benefits from them in return for internal State Department documents. The State Department runs US foreign policy and embassies, so its internal papers show American positions and plans on China. Claiborne was charged in 2017 and pleaded guilty in April 2019. On 9 July 2019 she was sentenced to 40 months in prison, three years' supervised release and a $40,000 fine.
cite: US Department of Justice, 9 Jul 2019; Wikipedia 'List of Chinese spy cases in the United States'

n: US Navy sailor on USS Essex sold ship details to a Chinese intelligence officer
rank: Machinist's mate, amphibious assault ship USS Essex
d: Jinchao 'Patrick' Wei, a US Navy machinist's mate with security clearance on the amphibious assault ship USS Essex, based in San Diego, passed photos, videos and documents about Navy ships to a Chinese intelligence officer in 2022. He was charged in August 2023, convicted in August 2025 and sentenced to more than 16 years. In a parallel case, another Navy servicemember, Wenheng Zhao, sent sensitive military information, including on a radar system in Okinawa, in return for bribes, and in January 2024 was sentenced to 27 months.
cite: US Department of Justice, Aug 2023 and 2025; Wikipedia 'List of Chinese spy cases in the United States'

n: MSS agent Ji Chaoqun joined the US Army Reserve to spot recruits
d: Ji Chaoqun, a Chinese citizen in Chicago, worked under a senior officer of the Jiangsu State Security Department, a provincial branch of China's Ministry of State Security, and enlisted in the US Army Reserve through a programme for foreign nationals with needed skills (MAVNI). He was tasked with gathering biographical details on eight people, including engineers and scientists working for US defence contractors, whom Chinese intelligence might recruit. Arrested on 25 September 2018, he was convicted in September 2022 of acting as an MSS agent and lying about his contacts on a military form, and in January 2023 was sentenced to eight years. He was released in a November 2024 prisoner exchange.
cite: Chicago Tribune, 26 Sep 2022; US Department of Justice, Jan 2023

n: Ex-CIA officer Alexander Ma gave Chinese handlers secrets, then joined FBI
rank: Former CIA officer; FBI contract linguist
d: Alexander Yuk Ching Ma, a CIA officer from 1982 to 1989, gave classified material to Chinese intelligence handlers in return for cash and gifts, and later took a job as a contract linguist for the FBI, which hired him while it monitored him. He was arrested in 2020 and pleaded guilty on 24 May 2024, under a deal expected to bring about ten years in prison. The case showed a former CIA officer passing secrets to China decades after leaving the agency.
cite: US Department of Justice, 24 May 2024; Wikipedia 'List of Chinese spy cases in the United States'

n: Engineer Chi Mak sent US Navy technology from a defence contractor to China
d: Chi Mak, an engineer at Power Paragon, a California unit of the defence contractor L-3 Communications, passed US defence technology to China while working on Navy projects, including submarine propulsion data. The Washington Post described him as a Chinese 'sleeper' agent placed in the United States for two decades. He was convicted in 2007 of conspiring to export sensitive defence technology to China, and on 24 March 2008 was sentenced to 24 years and four months.
cite: Washington Post (Warrick & Johnson), 2008; BBC News, 2008; AP/NBC, 2007

n: Chinese agents paid aide in Taiwan's Presidential Office for documents
d: Wang Jen-ping, an aide in Taiwan's Presidential Office, the staff that serves Taiwan's head of state, was found in 2009 to have sold nearly 100 confidential documents to China since 2007. The People's Republic of China claims Taiwan as its territory, so documents from the presidency give Beijing a view of Taiwan's policy towards it. The case was one of a series of discoveries of Chinese agents inside Taiwan's presidency, military and intelligence services in 2009 and 2010, including a double agent in the Military Intelligence Bureau.
cite: Wikipedia 'Chinese intelligence activity abroad' (citing Taipei Times, 2009)

n: Taiwan army general Lo Hsien-che spied for China; life sentence
rank: Major general, head of army electronic communications department
d: Lo Hsien-che, a major general who headed the Taiwanese army's electronic communications and information department, spied for China after being recruited around 2004 while he was military attaché in Thailand. Reports say a woman with an Australian passport drew him in, and local media cited payments of possibly US$1 million. Investigators found classified documents on military electronic warfare and strategy; concern centred on the Po Sheng command-and-control system, though the defence ministry said his access to it was limited. His office and home were raided on 27 January 2011, and on 26 April 2012 a military court sentenced him to life imprisonment.
cite: BBC News, 9 Feb 2011; Central News Agency, 26 Apr 2012; South China Morning Post, 9 and 11 Feb 2011

n: Retired Taiwan admiral and ex-MP charged over PLA, United Front recruiting
who: PLA and United Front Work Department
d: Hsia Fu-hsiang, a retired Taiwanese rear admiral, and Lo Chih-ming, a former member of Taiwan's legislature, were charged in 2023 after being recruited by China's People's Liberation Army and the United Front Work Department, the Chinese Communist Party body that cultivates people and groups outside the party to serve its aims. Prosecutors say they worked to recruit serving Taiwanese military officers. In the same year an active officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Hsieh, was detained for leaking secrets and suspected of building a network inside the armed forces.
cite: Wikipedia 'Chinese intelligence activity abroad' (citing Taiwanese prosecutors and Focus Taiwan, 2023)

n: Taiwan military intelligence officer was a double agent for China
d: Lo Chi-cheng, an officer of Taiwan's Military Intelligence Bureau, the agency that runs Taiwan's spies on the mainland, was found in 2010 to have been working as a double agent for China since 2007. A double agent pretends to work for one service while reporting to another, so Chinese intelligence could learn about Taiwan's operations against it. In 2015 a Chinese officer, Zhen Xiaojiang, was convicted in Taiwan of recruiting Taiwanese officers, among them Major-General Hsu Nai-chuan; Zhen was deported in 2018.
cite: Wikipedia 'Chinese intelligence activity abroad' (citing Taipei Times and Focus Taiwan)

n: CEFC China Energy envoy offered Chad's president a $2m bribe for oil rights
d: Patrick Ho, a former Hong Kong home affairs secretary who ran a lobbying body funded by the Shanghai-based CEFC China Energy, worked with former Senegalese foreign minister Cheikh Gadio to offer Chad's President Idriss Déby a US$2 million bribe, disguised as a donation, to win oil rights for CEFC. CEFC promoted Xi Jinping's Belt and Road Initiative. Ho was arrested in New York in November 2017 and convicted on 5 December 2018 of seven counts of bribery and money laundering under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act; Gadio testified against him. In March 2019 Ho was sentenced to three years and fined US$400,000. CEFC's chairman Ye Jianming denied authorising him.
cite: US Department of Justice, 5 Dec 2018; NYT, 5 Dec 2018; Hong Kong Free Press, 26 Mar 2019

n: CEFC wired $500,000 to Uganda's foreign minister, the former UN Assembly head
rank: Foreign Minister of Uganda; President Museveni
d: Patrick Ho, working for the Chinese conglomerate CEFC China Energy, arranged in May 2016 for US$500,000 to be wired to an account provided by Uganda's foreign minister Sam Kutesa, who had served from 2014 to 2015 as President of the UN General Assembly (2014–15). Ho also urged CEFC's chairman to give President Yoweri Museveni US$500,000 in cash as a 'campaign donation' after his re-election. US prosecutors said the payments were meant to get both men to use their power to steer business to CEFC. A New York jury convicted Ho on 5 December 2018. The record contains no statement from Kutesa answering the allegation; he remained foreign minister until May 2021.
cite: US Department of Justice, 5 Dec 2018; Wikipedia 'Sam Kutesa'

n: Think-tank head Gal Luft charged with paying a Trump adviser for China
d: Gal Luft, co-director of a Washington think tank, was charged in an indictment unsealed by the US Justice Department on 10 July 2023 with acting as an unregistered agent of Chinese entities. Prosecutors say that, at their request, he recruited and paid an unnamed adviser to then President-elect Donald Trump to promote pro-China positions. The indictment also charges arms trafficking, breaking Iran sanctions and lying to federal agents. Cypriot police arrested Luft in February 2023; he vanished while on bail in March 2023. In September 2024 prosecutors said he had been re-arrested and would be extradited.
cite: US Department of Justice (SDNY), 10 Jul 2023; Washington Post, 15 Jul 2023; Reuters, 9 Sep 2024

n: Ecuador charges ex-president Moreno with bribery over Chinese-built dam
d: Ecuador's Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant, one of the country's largest, was built from 2009 to 2018 by Sinohydro, a contracting arm of China's state-owned PowerChina, with a $1.7 billion loan from China's Export-Import Bank. On 6 March 2023 a judge approved bribery charges against former president Lenín Moreno, vice-president during the build, and others over the contract. In a separate case, the 'INA Papers', prosecutors allege $76 million in kickbacks moved through an offshore company in Belize founded by Moreno's brother. Moreno, living in Paraguay, denies it. The plant later showed 7,648 cracks; in April 2026 PowerChina agreed $400 million in compensation.
cite: Reuters, 23 Feb and 6 Mar 2023; NYT, 24 Dec 2018; Reuters, 10 Apr 2026

n: ZTE broadband deal: Philippine election chief accused of seeking kickbacks
rank: Election commission chair; cabinet; presidential spouse
d: ZTE, a Chinese telecoms company controlled through state-owned shareholders, signed a US$329 million contract on 20 April 2007 to build the Philippines' government broadband network. In Senate hearings from September 2007, economic planning secretary Romulo Neri testified that election commission chairman Benjamin Abalos offered him 200 million pesos to approve it; a witness said ZTE advanced US$1 million to Abalos, and another linked President Gloria Arroyo's husband to the kickbacks. Arroyo cancelled the deal in October 2007. The Ombudsman indicted Arroyo, her husband and Abalos for graft in 2011, but the anti-graft court dismissed the case against Arroyo in 2016.
cite: GMA News, 18 Sep 2007; Reuters, Sep 2007; Rappler, 7 Mar 2012; CNN Philippines, 16 Sep 2016

n: Chinese state port builder accused of funding Rajapaksa's 2015 campaign
d: China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a Chinese state-owned contractor that built Sri Lanka's Hambantota port with Chinese state loans, is accused of funding President Mahinda Rajapaksa's January 2015 re-election campaign. A leaked US embassy cable said Sri Lanka had to accept CHEC as builder to obtain the loan. Sri Lankan newspapers reported in 2015 and 2016 that police investigators were examining the payments, and in 2018 State Minister Eran Wickramaratne called for an inquiry after further reports. CHEC denied funding the campaign. In July 2017, unable to service its debts, Sri Lanka leased Hambantota for 99 years to a Chinese state firm.
cite: NYT, 25 Jun 2018; Sunday Observer, 1 Jul 2018; BBC News, 29 Jul 2017

n: Canada's top-security lab scientist worked to benefit China, CSIS found
who: Chinese state and military research bodies
d: Xiangguo Qiu, who headed a vaccine and antiviral section at Canada's National Microbiology Laboratory in Winnipeg, Canada's highest-security pathogen laboratory, worked with Chinese state institutions while employed there. About four months before she and her husband Keding Cheng were escorted out by police in July 2019, she shipped Ebola and Henipavirus samples to the Wuhan Institute of Virology. She was co-inventor on Chinese government patents and co-wrote papers with a PLA major-general. They were dismissed in January 2021. Documents released in February 2024 included a CSIS (Canadian intelligence) report saying her work with China's government benefited China and that she 'repeatedly lied'. Neither has been charged.
cite: CBC News, Feb 2024; Globe and Mail, 2021 and 2024; National Post, 2021

n: Oil men Sinclair and Doheny bribed US Interior Secretary Albert Fall
org_label: Harry Sinclair's and Edward Doheny's oil companies
d: Two oil executives, Harry Sinclair and Edward Doheny, paid the US Secretary of the Interior, Albert Fall, who then handed them navy oil reserves. Fall leased Teapot Dome in Wyoming to Sinclair's Mammoth Oil in 1922 and Elk Hills in California to Doheny's company, without competitive bidding. Doheny had given him a $100,000 interest-free loan in 1921, and gifts from the two men came to about $404,000. A Senate inquiry led by Senator Thomas Walsh uncovered the loan. In 1927 the Supreme Court ruled that the leases had been corruptly obtained and returned both reserves to the navy. Fall was convicted in 1929 of taking bribes from Doheny, the first US cabinet member to go to prison.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Teapot Dome scandal'; HISTORY.com, 'Cabinet member guilty in Teapot Dome scandal'

n: Lockheed paid ¥500m to PM Tanaka's office to sell jets to ANA
d: The US aircraft maker Lockheed paid about ¥2.4 billion in Japan to win an order from All Nippon Airways (ANA) for its L-1011 TriStar airliner, and about ¥500 million of it went to the office of Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka. The fixer Yoshio Kodama received ¥1.7 billion and ANA officials ¥160 million. ANA announced the purchase of 21 TriStars in October 1972. The payments came out in February 1976, when Lockheed's vice-chairman told a US Senate subcommittee led by Frank Church that about $3 million had gone to Tanaka's office. Tanaka was arrested in July 1976. In October 1983 a Tokyo court found him guilty of foreign-exchange violations and sentenced him to four years, but he stayed free on appeal until his death in 1993.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lockheed bribery scandals'; Britannica, 'Tanaka Kakuei'; Christian Science Monitor, 18 Nov 1981

n: Lockheed paid Dutch Prince Bernhard $1.1m over a fighter-jet choice
rank: Prince consort with senior military posts
d: Lockheed paid Prince Bernhard, husband of Queen Juliana of the Netherlands, a $1.1 million bribe in the early 1960s to help its F-104 Starfighter beat France's Dassault Mirage 5 in the Dutch fighter purchase. Bernhard held senior military and public posts and sat on more than 300 corporate boards and committees. The payment surfaced in December 1975, during US Senate hearings into Lockheed's foreign bribes, which were found to total $22 million. Prime Minister Joop den Uyl ordered an inquiry, and the queen threatened to abdicate if her husband was prosecuted. He was spared trial but had to give up several public positions and was barred from wearing military uniform. Interviews published after his death in 2004 showed he admitted taking the money.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lockheed bribery scandals'; Time, 'The Prince Errant Loses His Epaulets' (1976); Expatica, 'Prince Bernhard admitted taking Lockheed bribe'

n: Lockheed bribes for Hercules planes led to Italian defence minister's jailing
d: Lockheed was accused of paying Christian Democrat and Socialist politicians in Italy to favour the Italian Air Force's purchase of its C-130 Hercules transport planes. The magazine L'Espresso named former ministers Luigi Gui and Mario Tanassi, former Prime Minister Mariano Rumor and President Giovanni Leone. Leone resigned on 15 June 1978 under the pressure of the allegations. In 1979 the Constitutional Court, which then tried cases against ministers, convicted Tanassi, defence minister in 1970–1974, of bribery and sentenced him to four months in prison. He was the first former Italian minister to serve a prison sentence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lockheed bribery scandals'; Wikipedia, 'Mario Tanassi'; Corte costituzionale, sentenza penale Lockheed (1979)

n: Recruit gave cheap shares to Japan's PM and Diet members before flotation
rank: Prime Minister, cabinet and Diet members
d: Recruit, a Japanese recruitment-advertising and publishing company led by Hiromasa Ezoe, offered shares in its property subsidiary Recruit Cosmos to senior politicians and business leaders shortly before the shares went public in 1986. The share price then rose sharply, and recipients made about ¥66 million each on average. Seventeen members of the Diet, Japan's parliament, were involved, and another thirty were later found to have received favours from Recruit. They included Prime Minister Noboru Takeshita, former Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone and Chief Cabinet Secretary Takao Fujinami, as well as opposition party leaders. The scandal broke in 1988 and forced Takeshita's cabinet to resign; his term ended on 3 June 1989.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Recruit scandal'; Wikipedia, 'Noboru Takeshita'

n: Flick paid DM25m to West German parties while seeking a tax break
d: The Flick industrial group gave money to all the main parties in West Germany's parliament, about 25 million Deutsche Mark between 1969 and 1989, which its manager Eberhard von Brauchitsch called 'cultivation of the political landscape'. Cash-book entries listed payments to CSU leader Franz Josef Strauss and CDU leader Helmut Kohl. In 1976 Flick applied for a tax exemption on its sale of Daimler shares worth 1.9 billion DM to Deutsche Bank; economics minister Hans Friderichs approved it, and his successor Otto Graf Lambsdorff did too. The payments came to light in 1981 and Der Spiegel published them. Lambsdorff resigned in 1984. In 1987 both ministers were fined for tax evasion only, as a payment for the decision could not be proven.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Flick affair'

n: Siemens paid over $100m to Argentine officials for a $1bn ID-card deal
d: The German engineering company Siemens paid more than $100 million in bribes to Argentine government officials, including two former presidents and cabinet ministers, to win and keep a $1 billion contract to produce national identity cards for every Argentine citizen. The scheme ran from about 1996 to 2007. Siemens won the contract in 1998, but it was suspended and then cancelled after a change of government. In December 2008 Siemens and its Argentine subsidiary pleaded guilty in the US to foreign-bribery offences over the contract, as part of a $1.6 billion settlement with the US and Germany covering about $1.3 billion in bribes worldwide. In December 2011 US authorities charged eight former Siemens executives over the Argentine payments.
cite: US SEC press release 2011-263, 13 Dec 2011; MercoPress, 13 Dec 2011; Wikipedia, 'Siemens'

n: KBR consortium paid $180m to Nigerian officials for gas plant contracts
rank: executive branch, NNPC and Nigeria LNG officials
d: A joint venture led by KBR, the engineering firm then owned by Halliburton, paid about $180 million in bribes to Nigerian officials between 1994 and 2004 to win four contracts to build the Bonny Island liquefied natural gas plant, business worth more than $6 billion. The money went through consultants: one received over $130 million to pay high-level executive branch officials, and another over $50 million for lower-level officials, including staff of the state oil company NNPC and the government-controlled Nigeria LNG. KBR pleaded guilty in the US on 11 February 2009, and with Halliburton paid $579 million in combined penalties. KBR's former chief executive Albert 'Jack' Stanley had pleaded guilty in 2008.
cite: A&O Shearman FCPA database, 'US v. Kellogg Brown & Root' and 'SEC v. Halliburton and KBR'; Government Executive, Feb 2009

n: Unaoil paid Iraqi oil ministry officials $17m for $1.7bn of contracts
rank: Ministry of Oil and South Oil Company officials
d: Unaoil, a Monaco-based firm that acted as a fixer for foreign oil-service companies, paid more than $17 million in bribes to officials at Iraq's Ministry of Oil and the state-owned South Oil Company to secure about $1.7 billion in contracts after the 2003 occupation. The contracts, for oil pipelines and offshore mooring buoys in the Gulf, were part of the ministry's plan to rebuild Iraq's oil export capacity. The UK Serious Fraud Office prosecuted. In July 2020 a jury convicted Ziad Akle, Unaoil's Iraq territory manager, and Stephen Whiteley, sentenced to five and three years. Unaoil's Iraq partner Basil Al Jarah, who had pleaded guilty in 2019, was jailed for three years and four months in October 2020.
cite: UK Serious Fraud Office, 8 Oct 2020 and July 2020 releases; OCCRP, July 2020

n: Elf Aquitaine's secret funds paid French parties and African contacts
d: Executives of the French state oil company Elf Aquitaine used secret company funds to buy political favour in France and Africa, along with spending on themselves. Elf acted as an unofficial arm of French policy in Africa, and its Africa specialist André Tarallo was close to Gabon's President Omar Bongo. Former chairman Loïk Le Floch-Prigent admitted secretly funding political parties and named Jacques Chirac's RPR as the main beneficiary. The scandal came to light in 1994 and was investigated by magistrate Eva Joly. On 12 November 2003 a Paris court sentenced Le Floch-Prigent and his deputy Alfred Sirven to five years in jail each and Tarallo to four, in a $350 million embezzlement case with 37 defendants.
cite: Al Jazeera, 12 Nov 2003; Transparency International, 'The Elf trial: a victory over impunity'; Wikipedia, 'Elf Aquitaine'

n: Gürtel: Correa's firms paid Spain's ruling party for regional contracts
rank: People's Party and PP-run regional governments
d: A network of businesses led by Francisco Correa paid kickbacks to officials of Spain's People's Party (PP) in return for public contracts from PP-run local and regional governments, including in Valencia and the Community of Madrid. On 24 May 2018 Spain's National Court (Audiencia Nacional) convicted 29 of 37 defendants: Correa received 51 years and former PP treasurer Luis Bárcenas 33 years and a €44 million fine. The court found that the PP itself had taken part in the kickback scheme since 1989. A week later, on 1 June 2018, Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy was removed by a parliamentary vote of no confidence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Gürtel case'

n: Mani pulite: companies' kickbacks to Italy's ruling parties for contracts
d: Italian and foreign companies paid kickbacks, known as tangenti, to Italy's governing parties to win public works contracts; the bribes were estimated at $4 billion a year in the 1980s. Milan prosecutors uncovered the system in the 'Mani pulite' (clean hands) inquiry, which began with the arrest of Socialist official Mario Chiesa on 17 February 1992. At one point more than half the members of the Italian Parliament were under indictment, and over 400 councils were dissolved. Socialist leader Bettino Craxi admitted his party had received $93 million in illegal funds; he was convicted twice and fled to Tunisia in 1994. The Christian Democrats and Socialists, who had governed for decades, dissolved.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mani pulite'

n: Lobbyist Abramoff bought favours from Congressman Ney and officials
d: Jack Abramoff, a Washington lobbyist who charged Native American tribes with casinos an estimated $85 million, gave trips, meals, event tickets and campaign money to officials in return for official favours. Representative Bob Ney, chair of the House Administration Committee, put statements into the Congressional Record to help Abramoff's SunCruz casino deal and pursued legislation to reopen a casino for the Tigua tribe. Abramoff pleaded guilty to conspiracy, fraud and tax evasion on 3 January 2006 and was sentenced to four years in 2008. Ney pleaded guilty in October 2006 and got 30 months. Former deputy interior secretary Steven Griles and more than a dozen congressional aides and officials were also convicted or pleaded guilty.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jack Abramoff Indian lobbying scandal'; Wikipedia, 'Bob Ney'; Fox News/AP, 'People caught up in the Abramoff corruption probe'

n: Defence contractors paid Congressman Cunningham $2.4m for earmarks
d: Two defence contractors, Mitchell Wade of MZM and Brent Wilkes of ADCS, gave US Congressman Randy 'Duke' Cunningham about $2.4 million in cash and benefits to steer Pentagon money to their companies. Cunningham sat on the House Defence Appropriations Subcommittee, which sets military spending, and slipped earmarks, spending lines reserved for a named purpose, into bills that led to contracts for Wilkes's firms. Wade provided a yacht and other perks tied to about $150 million in contracts, and Wilkes received nearly $90 million in defence work. Cunningham pleaded guilty and was sentenced to seven years for bribery and tax evasion. Wade pleaded guilty in February 2006, and Wilkes was sentenced to 12 years in 2008.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Cunningham scandal'; NPR, 4 June 2013; NBC News, 'Defense contractor gets 12 years in bribery case' (Feb 2008)

n: Air Force buyer Druyun took a Boeing job while handling Boeing deals
rank: Air Force principal deputy for acquisition
d: Boeing hired Darleen Druyun, the US Air Force's senior civilian acquisition official, who had been handling Boeing business, including a plan to lease 100 Boeing KC-767 refuelling tankers. Acquisition is the office that buys the Air Force's aircraft and weapons. Druyun joined Boeing in 2003 at $250,000 a year with a $50,000 signing bonus. She pleaded guilty to a felony in 2004 and was sentenced in October 2004 to nine months in prison. Boeing fired its chief financial officer Michael Sears, who was sentenced to four months in February 2005, and Boeing paid $615 million in fines. The tanker plan, revised in 2003 to 20 leased and 80 bought planes, was put under investigation.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Darleen Druyun'; Government Executive, Oct 2004

n: Keating Five: S&L owner's senators pressed US bank regulators
d: Charles Keating, chairman of Lincoln Savings and Loan, gave about $1.3 million in political contributions to five US senators, who then pressed federal regulators on his behalf. In April 1987 Senators Alan Cranston, Dennis DeConcini, John Glenn, John McCain and Donald Riegle met Edwin Gray, chair of the Federal Home Loan Bank Board, which supervised savings banks, and later San Francisco regulators, seeking a lenient outcome in the investigation of Lincoln. The regulators backed off. Lincoln collapsed in 1989, costing the federal government $3.4 billion and leaving about 23,000 bondholders with worthless investments. In 1991 the Senate Ethics Committee reprimanded Cranston and criticised the other four.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Keating Five'

n: Oil firms' gifts and favours inside the US drilling regulator MMS
d: Oil and gas companies got close enough to officials of the Minerals Management Service (MMS), the US agency that leased offshore drilling areas, collected oil royalties and inspected rigs, that staff took gifts, holidays and favours from them. In September 2008 the Interior Department's inspector general, Earl Devaney, reported that more than a dozen MMS officials had engaged in unethical and criminal conduct, including drug use and sex with energy company representatives, in 'a culture of ethical failure'. A May 2010 report found that Gulf region inspectors had let industry officials fill in inspection reports themselves. After the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, Interior Secretary Ken Salazar ordered MMS split into three agencies in May 2010.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Minerals Management Service' (citing Interior Inspector General reports, Sept 2008 and May 2010)

n: Bofors paid kickbacks in India's 1986 howitzer deal
d: The Swedish arms maker Bofors paid kickbacks to win a contract signed on 24 March 1986 to supply India's army with 410 155mm field howitzers. Swedish Radio reported the payments on 16 April 1987, based on a leak from Swedish police investigator Sten Lindström, and Chitra Subramaniam of The Hindu then obtained over 350 documents. Payments to Indian politicians and defence officials were put at about ₹640 million. India's Central Bureau of Investigation named the Italian middleman Ottavio Quattrocchi, arms agent Win Chadha and the late Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in a 1999 charge sheet. The Delhi High Court quashed the charges against Gandhi in 2004 and no one was finally convicted. The scandal contributed to Congress's defeat in the 1989 election.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bofors scandal'

n: Kazakhgate: US adviser charged with paying Nazarbayev for oil deals
d: James Giffen, an American businessman who advised Kazakhstan's President Nursultan Nazarbayev, was charged by US prosecutors in 2003 with paying bribes to Nazarbayev and former Prime Minister Nurlan Balgimbayev to win oil contracts, including in the Tengiz field, for Western companies in the 1990s. Prosecutors alleged he moved $20 million through Swiss bank accounts. A former Mobil executive, J. Bryan Williams, was charged with tax evasion over kickbacks from Mobil's Kazakh business. In August 2010 Giffen pleaded guilty only to a tax misdemeanour and his company Mercator pleaded guilty to a foreign-bribery offence; the other charges were dropped and in November 2010 the judge gave him no prison term or fine.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kazakhgate'

n: Denis O'Brien paid Irish minister Lowry, who delivered a mobile licence
d: An official tribunal found that Irish businessman Denis O'Brien made payments to Michael Lowry, the minister responsible for communications, who 'not only influenced, but delivered the result' of the 1995 competition for Ireland's second mobile phone licence to O'Brien's consortium, Esat Digifone. The licence was awarded in May 1996. The Moriarty Tribunal's final report in March 2011 found two payments from O'Brien to Lowry, in 1996 and 1999, and support for a £420,000 loan, which it treated as a benefit. It said Lowry bypassed his cabinet colleagues and gave O'Brien valuable information, a 'cynical and venal abuse of office'. O'Brien rejected the findings, and the tribunal judge later admitted some mistakes.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Moriarty Tribunal' (final report, March 2011)

n: Harrods owner Al-Fayed paid British MPs to table questions
d: Mohamed Al-Fayed, owner of the London department store Harrods, paid Conservative MPs to ask questions in the House of Commons on his behalf. The Guardian reported in October 1994 that the lobbyist Ian Greer had paid MPs Neil Hamilton and Tim Smith about £2,000 each to table questions for Al-Fayed. Smith admitted taking payments from Al-Fayed directly and resigned his government post. In July 1997 the parliamentary standards commissioner, Sir Gordon Downey, called the evidence of cash payments to Hamilton 'compelling', and a Commons committee found Smith had taken £18,000 to £25,000. The affair led Prime Minister John Major to set up the Committee on Standards in Public Life. Hamilton lost his seat in 1997.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Cash-for-questions affair'

n: Holyland developers bribed Jerusalem's mayors, including Ehud Olmert
d: Developers of Holyland, a large housing project in Jerusalem, bribed city officials to get planning approvals, including two mayors: Ehud Olmert, who later became Israel's prime minister, and his successor Uri Lupolianski. On 31 March 2014 a Tel Aviv court convicted 10 of 13 defendants. Olmert was convicted of receiving NIS 560,000 in bribes, acquitted of two other bribery charges, and given a prison term and a NIS 1 million fine. Developer Hillel Charney was convicted of bribing Olmert, his aide Shula Zaken and Lupolianski, and was sentenced to three and a half years. Lupolianski was convicted of accepting bribes totalling more than NIS 2 million.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Holyland Case'

n: Tycoon Truong My Lan secretly controlled Saigon Commercial Bank
rank: owner and lender of Saigon Commercial Bank
d: Truong My Lan, chair of the Vietnamese property group Van Thinh Phat, secretly controlled Saigon Joint Stock Commercial Bank (SCB) from 2012 to 2022 through more than two dozen middlemen who held its shares for her. She owned over 90 percent of the bank, and 93 percent of its loans reportedly went to her company and to shell companies. Prosecutors said she used 916 fake loan applications to take more than 304 trillion dong (US$12.5 billion) from the bank between February 2018 and October 2022, and the case caused a run on SCB. On 11 April 2024 a court sentenced her to death for embezzlement, in a first trial of 85 defendants.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Truong My Lan'

n: Viet A paid officials $35m to sell overpriced Covid tests to the state
d: Viet A Technology, a Vietnamese company, admitted bribing officials with more than US$35 million in total so that they would buy its Covid-19 test kits. Between September and December 2021 it imported rapid tests from China at about US$0.96 each, marketed them as Vietnamese-made and sold them to local officials for about US$20.75. The scandal became public in December 2021. By June 2022 dozens of officials had been arrested and charged, including Health Minister Nguyen Thanh Long and Hanoi's mayor Chu Ngoc Anh, both of whom were expelled from the Communist Party and dismissed. In January 2023 the National Assembly removed two deputy prime ministers and President Nguyen Xuan Phuc resigned.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Viet A scandal'

n: e-KTP contractors paid Indonesia's House Speaker Setya Novanto
rank: Speaker of the House of Representatives
d: Members of the business consortium that won Indonesia's tender for electronic identity cards, known as e-KTP, paid Setya Novanto, Speaker of the House of Representatives, while the project's budget and tender went through parliament. Prosecutors said he received Rp 300 billion and a $135,000 wristwatch. The Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) named him a suspect in July 2017 in a Rp 2.3 trillion corruption case, and he resigned as Speaker after his arrest. On 24 April 2018 the Jakarta Corruption Court sentenced him to 15 years in prison, finding corruption in the budgeting and tender processes from 2011 to 2013, and barred him from public office for five years after his sentence ends.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Setya Novanto'

n: Napoles' fake NGOs drew Philippine lawmakers' pork-barrel funds
d: Businesswoman Janet Lim-Napoles was accused of arranging for members of the Philippine Congress to send money from their Priority Development Assistance Fund, known as 'pork barrel', to fake foundations run by her JLN Group, which carried out no projects. The Philippine Daily Inquirer exposed the scheme in July 2013, and losses were estimated at about ₱10 billion. Plunder charges were filed against Napoles and Senators Juan Ponce Enrile, Jinggoy Estrada and Ramon 'Bong' Revilla. In November 2013 the Supreme Court declared the fund unconstitutional. In 2024 Napoles was convicted on seven counts of corruption of public officials, while Estrada and Enrile were eventually acquitted.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Priority Development Assistance Fund scam'

n: Gold trader Zarrab accused of bribing Turkish ministers and Halkbank's chief
d: Reza Zarrab, an Iranian-born gold trader, was accused by Turkish prosecutors in December 2013 of paying bribes to cabinet ministers and to the general manager of the state-owned Halkbank to run a scheme that moved gold and money to Iran through the bank, around international sanctions. Police reported finding US$4.5 million in shoeboxes at the home of Halkbank's Süleyman Aslan, and the indictment alleged that Economy Minister Zafer Çağlayan received $52 million. Çağlayan resigned on 25 December 2013. Zarrab was freed after 70 days, and in January 2015 parliament declined to lift the ministers' immunity, ending the case. Zarrab later took a plea deal in the US and testified against a Halkbank deputy chief executive.
cite: Wikipedia, '2013 corruption scandal in Turkey'; Wikipedia, 'Reza Zarrab'

n: Loans-for-shares: bankers who funded Yeltsin took Russia's top firms
d: In 1995 a group of Russian commercial bankers got President Boris Yeltsin's government to hand them shares in the country's largest state companies in return for loans, under a scheme proposed by Vladimir Potanin of Oneximbank and endorsed by deputy prime minister Anatoly Chubais. The government was short of money, including for Yeltsin's 1996 re-election campaign. The auctions were rigged and run by politically connected insiders. Potanin acquired Norilsk Nickel at a bargain price, and Mikhail Khodorkovsky's Menatep took a 78 percent stake in the oil company Yukos, worth about $5 billion, for $310 million. The scheme created the businessmen known as oligarchs, some of whom then financed Yeltsin's re-election and took government posts.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Loans for shares'

n: Banker Potanin became Russia's First Deputy PM after loans-for-shares
d: Vladimir Potanin, president of Oneximbank and the proposer of the 1995 loans-for-shares scheme, which gave politically connected banks shares in Russia's biggest state companies in return for loans, served as Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister from 14 August 1996 to 17 March 1997, under Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and President Boris Yeltsin. Through the scheme Potanin and Mikhail Prokhorov came to own 54 percent of Norilsk Nickel, the nickel and palladium producer. His appointment came weeks after Yeltsin's re-election, which the bankers had helped fund. After leaving government he returned to business and remained Norilsk Nickel's main owner.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Vladimir Potanin'; Wikipedia, 'Loans for shares'

n: Tycoon Berezovsky, Yeltsin's campaign funder, entered the Security Council
rank: Deputy Secretary of the Security Council
d: Boris Berezovsky, a businessman who had controlled the main state television channel ORT since December 1994, helped organise the 'Davos Pact' of tycoons who bankrolled President Boris Yeltsin's 1996 re-election campaign. On 30 October 1996 Yeltsin appointed him Deputy Secretary of Russia's Security Council, the body that advises the president on defence and security, a post he held until November 1997. From April 1998 to March 1999 he was Executive Secretary of the Commonwealth of Independent States, the grouping of former Soviet republics. He and Badri Patarkatsishvili also helped Roman Abramovich take control of the oil company Sibneft in the 1995–1997 loans-for-shares auctions.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Boris Berezovsky (businessman)'

n: Gorilla file: Penta partner recorded discussing kickbacks with ministers
d: A leaked file called 'Gorila', said to be drawn from a 2005–2006 wiretap by the Slovak Information Service of a Bratislava flat, reportedly records officials, politicians and executives of Penta Group, one of Slovakia's two biggest investment companies, discussing kickbacks for privatisation and procurement contracts. Penta partner Jaroslav Haščák allegedly spoke there with Deputy Prime Minister Jirko Malchárek, and Robert Fico and others are also named. The file appeared online on 21 December 2011. Penta called it fiction, its accuracy has not been officially confirmed and no convictions followed, but in January 2012 a court confirmed it had authorised the wiretaps, and 'Protest Gorila' rallies shaped the 2012 election.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Gorilla scandal'

n: Agusta and Dassault bribe forced NATO chief Willy Claes to resign
d: The Italian helicopter maker Agusta and the French aircraft maker Dassault were linked to a bribe of over 50 million Belgian francs accepted while Willy Claes was Belgium's economy minister, during negotiations on defence contracts with the two companies. The bribe came to light during the investigation into the murder of former deputy prime minister André Cools. Claes had become Secretary General of NATO in 1994 and resigned on 20 October 1995. The Court of Cassation, which tries ministers, convicted him; he received a three-year suspended sentence, a fine and a five-year ban on standing for office, and the European Court of Human Rights upheld the sentence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Willy Claes'

n: Construction firms paid kickbacks to Laval and Montreal city halls
d: Construction and engineering firms in Quebec formed a bid-rigging cartel and paid city politicians to win public works contracts. At the Charbonneau Commission, a public inquiry set up in 2011, a former construction boss testified that for years 3 percent of the value of his Montreal contracts went to the mayor's party and 1 percent to a city official. Montreal mayor Gérald Tremblay resigned in November 2012, and interim mayor Michael Applebaum was convicted on eight corruption-related charges in 2017. Gilles Vaillancourt, mayor of Laval from 1989 to 2012, pleaded guilty in December 2016 to fraud, breach of trust and conspiracy over city construction contracts from 1996 to 2010, and was jailed for six years.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Charbonneau Commission'; Wikipedia, 'Gilles Vaillancourt'

n: Brazil's meatpackers paid farm ministry inspectors to pass unfit meat
d: Brazilian meatpacking companies, chiefly JBS and BRF, were accused by the Federal Police in March 2017 of paying officials of the Ministry of Agriculture's inspection service to approve unfit meat. In 'Operation Weak Flesh' (Carne Fraca), police said ministry employees moved inspectors around to keep the scheme going; one inspector's refusal to be transferred started the inquiry. Police said part of the bribes went to the PMDB and PP parties, and the companies under investigation had given about R$393 million to politicians in the 2014 elections. Thirty-three officials were suspended, the European Union asked for an emergency meeting with Brazil, and BRF's former president was arrested in 2018.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Operation Weak Flesh'

n: Karachi affair: submarine deal commissions funded Balladur's campaign
d: Commissions paid on France's 1994 sale of Agosta 90B submarines to Pakistan, a contract worth about €826 million, were partly used to finance the 1995 presidential campaign of Prime Minister Édouard Balladur, according to reported French court findings. Commissions of 6.25 percent, about €50 million, were reportedly paid to lobbying firms and officials in both countries; the businessman Ziad Takieddine received millions. Pakistan's Benazir Bhutto government had chosen the French boats over cheaper British ones. In 2002 a bomb in Karachi killed eleven French engineers working on the submarines; Pakistani investigators blamed militant groups, while some European reports linked the attack to the cancellation of the commissions, which Pakistan rejected.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Karachi affair'

n: US says Peevski used bribes to control key Bulgarian institutions
rank: State Agency for National Security head (2013); key institutions
d: Delyan Peevski, a Bulgarian MP and media owner, was sanctioned by the US Treasury in June 2021 under the Global Magnitsky Act, a US law that targets corruption, for 'regularly' using influence peddling and bribes to shield himself from scrutiny and to exert control over key Bulgarian institutions and sectors. His family's New Bulgarian Media Group reportedly owned six of the 12 largest newspapers by 2013. On 14 June 2013 parliament elected him head of the State Agency for National Security (DANS), the counter-intelligence agency; thousands protested and he stepped down the next day. The protests contributed to Prime Minister Plamen Oresharski's resignation. The UK sanctioned Peevski in February 2023.
cite: US Treasury designation, June 2021; UK FCDO sanctions, Feb 2023; Wikipedia, 'Delyan Peevski'

n: Fishing firm Corpesca paid Chilean senator Orpis over the fishing law
d: The fishing company Corpesca paid Jaime Orpis, a senator of Chile's UDI party, 230 million pesos in exchange, prosecutors said, for favourable votes on fishing quota legislation. The 2012 fisheries law, promoted by minister Pablo Longueira, allocated a large share of Chile's national fishing quota to companies controlled by a few families on an indefinite basis. The citizens' group Fundación Ciudadano Inteligente filed a bribery complaint in 2015. Orpis lost his parliamentary immunity in January 2016 and left the UDI. In April 2021 a court sentenced him to prison for bribery and fraud against the Treasury, and an appeals court upheld the sentence in January 2022.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Corpesca case'; Wikipedia, 'Jaime Orpis'; Radio Universidad de Chile, 16 Apr 2021; Radio Cooperativa, 6 Jan 2022

n: Sri Lanka central bank bond sale favoured governor's son-in-law's firm
d: In February 2015 Sri Lanka's central bank, under Governor Arjuna Mahendran, advertised Rs 1 billion of 30-year bonds but accepted about Rs 10 billion, and Perpetual Treasuries, a bond dealer owned by Mahendran's son-in-law Arjun Aloysius, received about Rs 5 billion at 12.5 percent. A presidential commission reported in December 2017 that Mahendran was directly responsible for losses of LKR 11,145 million. In March 2018 a Colombo court issued an arrest warrant alleging he had passed confidential central bank information to Perpetual Treasuries; Aloysius had been arrested in February. Mahendran denied wrongdoing and stayed in Singapore, which declined to extradite him, and in 2022 a special court dismissed the charges.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Arjuna Mahendran'

n: Coal lobbyist Andrew Wheeler became head of the US EPA
d: Andrew Wheeler, who lobbied for the coal producer Murray Energy from 2009 to 2017, moved into the leadership of the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which regulates pollution from coal mining and coal-fired power plants. Murray was his best-paying client and lobbied against Obama-era climate rules for power plants; in March 2017 Wheeler arranged a meeting between Robert Murray and Energy Secretary Rick Perry at which Murray pressed for rollbacks. Wheeler was confirmed as EPA deputy administrator in April 2018, became acting head when Scott Pruitt resigned in July 2018, and was confirmed as administrator in February 2019. In April 2020 the EPA weakened mercury regulation by narrowing the health benefits counted in rule-making.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Andrew R. Wheeler'

n: Oil and water lobbyist David Bernhardt became US Interior Secretary
org_label: Westlands Water District and oil-industry clients
d: David Bernhardt, a lawyer and lobbyist whose clients included the Westlands Water District, a large California farm-water supplier, the oil-sector firms Halliburton, Cobalt International Energy and Samson Resources, and the Independent Petroleum Association of America (IPAA), moved into the leadership of the US Interior Department, which manages federal land, water and drilling leases. He became deputy secretary in August 2017, acting secretary in January 2019 and secretary in April 2019. He had said he would not involve himself in former clients' matters unless authorised. During his tenure Interior substantially increased fossil fuel sales on public land and cut regulation, and in 2019 Politico reported IPAA leaders celebrating their ties to him.
cite: Wikipedia, 'David Bernhardt'

n: Monsanto's lawyer and executive Michael Taylor held top US food posts
d: Michael Taylor moved several times between US food regulators and the side of the biotech company Monsanto. From 1981 to 1991 he worked at the law firm King & Spalding, which represented Monsanto. As the Food and Drug Administration's deputy commissioner for policy from 1991 to 1994 he oversaw biotechnology policy, including 1992 guidance on genetically modified foods and guidance that milk from cows treated with bovine growth hormone, a Monsanto product, need not be labelled. He was Monsanto's vice-president for public policy from 1998 to 2000, and the FDA's deputy commissioner for foods from January 2010 to 2016. US government reviewers found he had complied with his recusal agreement on the hormone approval.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Michael R. Taylor'

n: Ex-Verizon lawyer Ajit Pai chaired the FCC and repealed net neutrality
rank: Chairman of the Federal Communications Commission
d: Ajit Pai, associate general counsel at the telecoms company Verizon from 2001 to 2003, chaired the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the US regulator of telephone, broadband and broadcasting companies, from January 2017 to January 2021. On 14 December 2017 the FCC under his leadership voted to stop regulating internet service providers under Title II of the Communications Act, ending the 'net neutrality' rules that barred providers such as Verizon from blocking or slowing traffic or selling priority. Broadband companies had fought the rules since they were adopted in 2015. The decision changed how internet access is regulated across the United States.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ajit Pai'

n: Eli Lilly's US president Alex Azar became Health Secretary
rank: Secretary of Health and Human Services
d: Alex Azar, president of Lilly USA, the largest division of the drug maker Eli Lilly, from 2012 to January 2017, became US Secretary of Health and Human Services, the department that includes the Food and Drug Administration and the Medicare programme, which pays for many Americans' medicines. The Senate confirmed him on 24 January 2018 by 55 votes to 43. During his time at Lilly the price of its top-selling insulin roughly tripled, and Lilly was one of three companies accused in a class-action lawsuit over insulin pricing. Senator Ron Wyden, who voted against him, said Azar had 'never, not one time, signed off on a decrease in the price of a drug.'
cite: Wikipedia, 'Alex Azar'

n: Raytheon's head of lobbying Mark Esper became US Defense Secretary
d: Mark Esper, hired in July 2010 as vice-president of government relations, the lobbying arm, at the weapons maker Raytheon, moved from that job into the posts that buy Raytheon's products. He was confirmed as Secretary of the Army on 15 November 2017 by 89 votes to 6. After serving as acting Secretary of Defense from June 2019, he was confirmed as the 27th US Secretary of Defense on 23 July 2019 by 90 votes to 8. The Defense Department is the main customer for Raytheon's missiles and other military systems.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mark Esper'

n: Alcatel accused of paying Costa Rica's president for a phone contract
d: Prosecutors in Costa Rica alleged that the French telecoms company Alcatel paid more than US$800,000 to Miguel Ángel Rodríguez while he was president, in return for help winning a government contract to supply 400,000 mobile phone lines. Rodríguez had been elected Secretary General of the Organization of American States (OAS) in 2004 and stepped down in October 2004, about a month into the job, after a former political associate accused him. In April 2011 a Costa Rican court sentenced him to five years in prison, but in December 2012 an appeals court acquitted him, citing problems with the main witness, who had immunity and changed his account several times. Rodríguez denied wrongdoing throughout.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Miguel Ángel Rodríguez'

n: Businessmen paid Politburo member Bo Xilai and his family
org_label: Businessmen Xu Ming and Tang Xiaolin
rank: Politburo member and Chongqing party chief
d: Two Chinese businessmen, Xu Ming and Tang Xiaolin, gave Bo Xilai and his family money and benefits worth about 21.79 million yuan (US$3.56 million), prosecutors said. Bo had been Minister of Commerce from 2004 to 2007 and was Communist Party secretary of Chongqing and a member of the Politburo, the party's top leadership body, from 2007 to 2012. At trial Xu said he gave Bo's wife Gu Kailai $3.23 million in 2000 to buy a villa in Nice, and paid for their son's travel and credit card bills. On 22 September 2013 a court in Jinan found Bo guilty on all counts, including bribery, and sentenced him to life imprisonment.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bo Xilai'

n: Drug firms bribed the head of China's drug regulator, Zheng Xiaoyu
rank: head of the State Food and Drug Administration
d: Eight pharmaceutical companies paid Zheng Xiaoyu, head of China's drug regulator, more than 6.49 million yuan (about US$850,000) in bribes, and in return he personally approved unproven and unsafe medicines. Zheng led the State Drug Administration from 1998 and its successor, the State Food and Drug Administration, from 2003 to 2005. Over eight years he ordered approval of more than 150,000 new medicines, most of them from the companies that had paid him. One unsafe drug killed 14 people, and his approvals were linked to cough syrup that killed more than 800 people in Panama. He was convicted of bribery and dereliction of duty, sentenced to death on 29 May 2007 and executed on 10 July 2007.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Zheng Xiaoyu'

n: Railway minister Liu Zhijun took bribes while building China's fast rail
d: Liu Zhijun, China's Minister of Railways from 2003 until his dismissal in February 2011, took more than 64 million yuan in bribes, according to the charges brought in April 2013, while overseeing the fast expansion of the country's high-speed rail network. Ding Shumiao, a Shanxi business magnate whose Boyou investment group gained greatly from high-speed rail construction, was linked to his fall. State media said the ministry had illegitimate business ties with large companies and used illegal subcontracting. In July 2013 Liu was convicted and sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve, a sentence commuted to life imprisonment in December 2015.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Liu Zhijun'

n: Hanbo Steel bribed politicians and bankers for loans in South Korea
rank: Home Minister, presidential aides and state-influenced bank chiefs
d: Hanbo, a small South Korean steelmaker that began building a huge plant in 1992, got bank loans by bribing politicians and bankers, who pressed banks to lend to it. Hanbo went into receivership on 28 January 1997 with losses estimated at US$6 billion. In June 1997 a court found that it had received illegal preferential treatment from President Kim Young-sam's government, mainly through these loans. Founder Chung Tae-soo was sentenced to 15 years. Those convicted included former Home Minister Kim Woo-suk, presidential aides, lawmakers and two former presidents of Korea First Bank, and the president's son Kim Hyun-chul was sentenced to three years in a related case. The collapse added to the country's economic troubles that year.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Hanbo scandal'

n: Samsung paid legal fees for ex-president Lee Myung-bak's family firm
d: South Korean courts convicted former President Lee Myung-bak of taking bribes from Samsung, the country's largest business group, in the form of nearly $6 million in legal fees paid for DAS, a car-parts maker owned by Lee's brother, according to prosecutors. They said the money was meant to win a presidential pardon for Samsung chairman Lee Kun-hee, who had been convicted of tax evasion and stock fraud. On 5 October 2018 Lee was convicted of bribery, embezzlement and abuse of power and sentenced to 15 years; an appeals court raised it to 17 years and the Supreme Court upheld that on 29 October 2020. President Yoon Suk-yeol pardoned him in December 2022. Samsung and Lee denied the charges.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lee Myung-bak'

n: Businesses paid Taiwan's President Chen Shui-bian and his wife
d: Taiwanese business owners paid former President Chen Shui-bian and his wife Wu Shu-chen in connection with government decisions, including millions from the owners of a company after the government bought its land at Longtan for a science park. Chen was president from 2000 to 2008. On 11 September 2009 the Taipei District Court sentenced him to life in prison and a NT$200 million fine for embezzlement, bribery and money laundering involving about US$15 million during his presidency, and found that the couple had amassed NT$800 million. In June 2010 the High Court reduced the sentence to 20 years. He was the first Taiwanese president imprisoned; his supporters called the case political.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Chen Shui-bian'

n: Sagawa Kyubin payments reached LDP vice-president Shin Kanemaru
rank: Vice President of the Liberal Democratic Party
d: Shin Kanemaru, vice-president of Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and a former deputy prime minister, was indicted in the 1992 Sagawa Kyubin scandal over payments from the parcel delivery company and from construction companies seeking political influence. Kanemaru, a senior figure in Noboru Takeshita's faction, resigned and was arrested on 13 March 1993 on charges of evading taxes on those payments. Investigators reported finding at least $51 million in bearer bonds and hundreds of pounds of gold at his home. He died in March 1996.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Shin Kanemaru'

n: Goldenberg: Pattni's firm drew Kenyan public money for fake gold exports
rank: Finance Minister and Central Bank of Kenya
d: Goldenberg International, a company run by businessman Kamlesh Pattni, was given a monopoly on gold exports in November 1990 and paid compensation from Kenyan public funds worth about 35 percent above its foreign-currency earnings, though its exports may have been minimal or nonexistent. Finance minister George Saitoti authorised an extra 15 percent over the objections of Treasury advisers. David Munyakei, a Central Bank of Kenya clerk, exposed the scheme in 1993 and was fired. The cost was estimated at more than 10 percent of Kenya's annual GDP. The Bosire Commission reported in February 2006, tracing KSh 158.3 billion in Goldenberg-linked transactions and recommending charges against Saitoti, but a court ruled that year that he could not be charged.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Goldenberg scandal'

n: Anglo Leasing: phantom firms got Kenyan security contracts via ministers
org_label: Anglo Leasing Finance and related phantom firms
d: Phantom companies, beginning with the British firm Anglo Leasing Finance, were given heavily overpriced Kenyan government security contracts that were never delivered, with ministers named as involved. In the first case a French firm quoted about €6 million to replace Kenya's passport printing system, but the contract went to Anglo Leasing at about €30 million. In January 2006 John Githongo, the government's former anti-corruption chief, released a report naming ministers Kiraitu Murungi, David Mwiraria and Chris Murungaru and Vice-President Moody Awori, and said President Mwai Kibaki was complicit; all denied wrongdoing. Mwiraria and Murungi resigned in February 2006. No one was punished, and a UK Serious Fraud Office probe was halted.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Leasing scandal'

n: SNC-Lavalin paid C$47.7m to Libyan officials linked to Saadi Gaddafi
rank: officials linked to the ruling Gaddafi family
d: The Canadian engineering company SNC-Lavalin paid about C$47.7 million in bribes between 2001 and 2011 to Libyan officials linked to Saadi Gaddafi, a son of Libya's ruler Muammar Gaddafi, and defrauded Libyan organisations of about C$130 million. The money went through two companies whose sole beneficial owner was Riadh Ben Aissa, a former SNC-Lavalin executive. The prosecution in Canada led to the 2019 political crisis in which Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's office pressed the attorney general to offer the company a deferred prosecution agreement. In December 2019 SNC-Lavalin Construction pleaded guilty to fraud and was fined C$280 million.
cite: Wikipedia, 'SNC-Lavalin affair'

n: BAE paid £115m in commissions to win South Africa's arms deal
d: BAE Systems, the British arms maker, paid about £115 million in commissions to advisers to help win contracts in South Africa's 1999 arms package, valued at R29.992 billion at signing, the UK Serious Fraud Office found. One adviser, Fana Hlongwane, received over R100 million from BAE, which the SFO said was for corrupt ends, and South Africa's Scorpions investigators found 'at the very least a reasonable suspicion' that he used money to reward officials who evaluated the bids. BAE denied paying bribes. The government's Seriti Commission found no corruption in 2016, but in August 2019 the High Court set its findings aside for failing to pursue relevant evidence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'South African Arms Deal'

n: Angolagate: arms dealers' money reached French political figures
rank: senator and former minister; president's son
d: Arms dealers Pierre Falcone and Arcadi Gaydamak, who sold $633 million of weapons to Angola's government by late 1994, paid French political figures to promote their interests, a Paris court found in 2009. Jean-Christophe Mitterrand, son of former president François Mitterrand, was found guilty of receiving $2 million and given a suspended sentence, and former interior minister Charles Pasqua was convicted of taking money from the two men. In all 36 people were convicted, and Falcone and Gaydamak got six years. On 29 April 2011 the Paris Court of Appeal overturned the convictions of Pasqua and his aide Jean-Charles Marchiani and dropped charges against the dealers, accepting that they had acted under an Angolan state mandate.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Angolagate'

n: Ex-deputy mayor gave Kansai Electric bosses ¥320m for contracts
d: Eiji Moriyama, a former deputy mayor of Takahama, the town that hosts one of Kansai Electric Power's nuclear plants, gave cash and gifts worth about ¥320 million to executives of the utility, which awarded contracts to local firms including Yoshida Kaihatsu, a company linked to him. Kansai Electric, known as Kanden, supplies electricity to the Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe region and runs nuclear plants in Fukui Prefecture. Investigations found more than 380 cases of gifts.
