The scandal broke in 2019; chairman Makoto Yagi resigned that year and president Shigeki Iwane in 2020.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kansai Electric Power Company'

n: S. Alam Group took control of Islami Bank and other Bangladeshi banks
rank: board and management of Islami Bank Bangladesh
d: S. Alam Group, a Bangladeshi conglomerate founded by Mohammed Saiful Alam, took over Islami Bank Bangladesh in 2017 under the Awami League government, installing a new chairman and remaking the bank's board, management and hiring. It also came to control First Security Islami Bank, Union Bank and Global Islami Bank, and bought half of Social Islami Bank through 19 subsidiaries, beyond the 5 percent limit in banking law. Media reported that the group took Tk 300 billion in loans from Islami Bank, which the bank denied, and Islami Bank needed Tk 80 billion of emergency central bank money in January 2023. After the government fell in August 2024 the interim government opened investigations; the group denies wrongdoing.
cite: Wikipedia, 'S. Alam Group'

n: Penta group funded Chilean UDI politicians through fake invoices
d: Grupo Penta, a Chilean holding company, used fake invoices, with help from employees of the tax service (SII), to pass money to the campaigns of politicians, mainly from the right-wing UDI party. Penta's directors Carlos Alberto Délano and Carlos Eugenio Lavín were charged in March 2015; they were fined, spent a few days in prison and were ordered to attend ethics classes. Former UDI president Jovino Novoa received a three-year suspended sentence in December 2015 for tax crimes, and SII employees Iván Álvarez and Sergio Díaz were given prison terms, fines and asset forfeitures. Several Penta employees and relatives were convicted of tax evasion, bribery and money laundering.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Penta case'

n: US charges Firtash's group with $18.5m bribe to Indian officials
d: A US grand jury in Chicago indicted Dmytro Firtash, a Ukrainian businessman who heads Group DF, and five others in 2014 on bribery, racketeering and money-laundering charges over an alleged $18.5 million bribe to Indian officials to obtain titanium mining licences. Firtash, co-owner of the gas trader RosUkrEnergo, was influential under Ukrainian presidents Viktor Yushchenko and Viktor Yanukovych and reportedly helped finance Yanukovych's 2010 campaign. Arrested in Vienna in 2014, he fought extradition to the US for years, and in November 2024 a Vienna court ruled extradition not permissible. He denies the charges. In June 2021 Ukraine's security council sanctioned him.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Dmytro Firtash'

n: Radia tapes: lobbyist for Tata and Reliance and India's cabinet posts
org_label: Niira Radia (lobbyist for Tata and Reliance)
d: Niira Radia, a corporate lobbyist whose clients included India's Tata Group and Reliance Industries, was recorded by the income tax department over six months in 2009, while the new cabinet was being formed after the general election. Transcripts published in 2010 suggested she had influence over how ministerial posts were allocated, including the telecom ministry held by A. Raja. The recordings became a foundation of the 2G spectrum case, in which the government was accused of selling mobile radio spectrum cheaply to ineligible companies; the national auditor put the potential loss at ₹1,760 billion. In February 2012 the Supreme Court cancelled 122 licences. Raja resigned and was later acquitted, and Radia left lobbying in 2011.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Niira Radia'

n: Juárez Cartel had Mexico's drug czar, General Gutiérrez Rebollo
rank: Head of the National Institute to Combat Drugs (INCD)
d: The Juárez Cartel of Amado Carrillo Fuentes had Mexico's top anti-drug official working for it. General Jesús Gutiérrez Rebollo was named head of the National Institute to Combat Drugs (INCD), the federal anti-narcotics agency, in December 1996; weeks later the US drug czar Barry McCaffrey praised his 'impeccable integrity'. On 6 February 1997 the defence minister had him arrested and said he had protected Carrillo Fuentes for several years. Investigators acted on a tip that he lived in an expensive apartment supplied by a Carrillo associate. He was sentenced to more than 31 years for weapons offences, and in 2007 a court added 40 years. He died in custody in December 2013.
cite: Transnational Institute, 'Mexico: The Narco General Case' (1997); Wikipedia, Jesús Gutiérrez Rebollo

n: General Navarro Lara offered Tijuana's anti-drug chief $1m a month
d: An army general tried to buy Mexico's top counter-narcotics official in Tijuana on behalf of a drug cartel. On 17 March 1997, a month after the arrest of the national drug czar, Mexico jailed Brigadier General Alfredo Navarro Lara on charges of drug corruption, bribery and criminal association. Prosecutors said he had offered the Tijuana anti-drug official $1 million a month to protect one of the country's largest trafficking groups, and threatened to kill him and his family if he refused. Prosecutors separately linked the general to the Tijuana mafia of the Arellano Félix brothers. He was the second general jailed in the same high-security prison in a month.
cite: Spokesman-Review / AP, 'Mexico busts general for drug bribe' (18 Mar 1997)

n: Generals Acosta Chaparro and Quirós convicted of working for Carrillo
d: Two senior Mexican army generals helped the drug lord Amado Carrillo Fuentes, leader of the Juárez Cartel, move drugs. In 2002 a military court found Generals Arturo Acosta Chaparro and Francisco Quirós Hermosillo guilty of drug smuggling and related charges; Quirós was also convicted of taking the trafficker's bribes. Quirós received 16 years and Acosta 15. Both also faced separate charges over the deaths of more than 130 people during the 1970s 'dirty war' against leftist rebels. Acosta Chaparro was later cleared of the drug charges and was shot dead in Mexico City in 2012.
cite: VOA (2 Nov 2002); Al Jazeera (21 Apr 2012); Fox News/AP on Acosta Chaparro's killing

n: Beltrán Leyva cartel paid officials inside Mexico's organised-crime unit
d: The Beltrán Leyva cartel bought officials inside SIEDO, the elite unit of Mexico's federal attorney general's office that prosecutes drug trafficking and organised crime. In October 2008 the government admitted that at least 35 SIEDO officials and agents, including a senior intelligence director, had leaked operations, raids and evidence to the cartel for up to four years, for $150,000 to $450,000 a month each. The inquiry began on tips from an informant who walked into the Mexican embassy in Washington. Noé Ramírez Mandujano, SIEDO's head from 2006 to August 2008, was accused of taking $450,000 a month to tip off traffickers. Several later cases collapsed, and Ramírez called the operation a farce.
cite: Los Angeles Times via Spokesman-Review, 'Drug gang breaches top agency' (28 Oct 2008); Wikipedia, Noé Ramírez Mandujano; Reforma interview via vLex

n: Ex-deputy defence secretary charged with aiding Beltrán Leyva cartel
rank: Former Deputy Secretary of National Defence and generals
d: Mexican prosecutors charged a former deputy defence secretary and four other senior officers with selling military intelligence to the Beltrán Leyva cartel. In August 2012 a federal judge ordered Tomás Ángeles Dauahare, former army under-secretary and military attaché in Washington, to stand trial with Brigadier Generals Roberto Dawe González and Rubén Pérez Ramírez, retired General Ricardo Escorcia Vargas and a retired lieutenant colonel who had run Sinaloa's state police. They were accused of taking cartel bribes in 2007 and 2008 in return for information on military operations and protection for cocaine shipments. The officers denied the charges, one said he was coerced, and the defence attacked shifting witness accounts.
cite: Justice in Mexico, 'Six current and former military officials formally charged with aiding Beltrán Leyva Cartel' (9 Aug 2012)

n: El Chapo bribed Puente Grande prison staff to walk out in 2001
rank: Puente Grande maximum-security prison staff and director
d: Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán of the Sinaloa Cartel bought the staff of the maximum-security prison holding him. On 19 January 2001 a guard opened his electronic cell door at Puente Grande, Jalisco, and a maintenance worker wheeled him out in a laundry cart that bribed guards did not search. Officials later said 78 people were implicated and that the escape cost him about $2.5 million; the prison's director was jailed for aiding it, and Jalisco police were reportedly paid to give him 24 hours to leave the state.
cite: Wikipedia, Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán (citing contemporary reporting)

n: Thirteen officials held over El Chapo's 2015 Altiplano tunnel escape
rank: Federal prison system and Altiplano prison command
d: Officials of Mexico's federal prison system were charged over Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán's second escape. On 11 July 2015 the Sinaloa Cartel leader left the Altiplano maximum-security prison through a tunnel dug into his cell. By September judges had ordered 13 public officials held for trial: a former national coordinator of federal prisons, a former director general, the Altiplano prison's director and commander, and nine monitors from the control room that watched his cell. It was his second escape from a maximum-security prison in 14 years.
cite: Fox News/AP, 'Number of Mexican prison officials held in connection to Chapo Guzmán escape rises to 13' (25 Sep 2015); Wikipedia, Joaquín Guzmán

n: 'El Mayo' Zambada admits paying Mexican police and army commanders
d: Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada, co-founder of the Sinaloa Cartel, admitted in a US court that his organisation bought Mexico's security forces. Pleading guilty in Brooklyn on 25 August 2025 to running a continuing criminal enterprise from 1989 to 2024 and to racketeering, he said people working for him paid bribes to Mexican police and military commanders so the cartel could operate freely. Mexican press accounts of the hearing reported he also named corrupt politicians. His cartel moved at least 1.5 million kilograms of cocaine between 1980 and 2024. The plea is the cartel's own leader confirming the protection system that Mexican and US cases had described for decades.
cite: NPR (26 Aug 2025); Al Jazeera (25 Aug 2025); Zeta Tijuana (25 Aug 2025)

n: Congressman Julio César Godoy accused of serving La Familia Michoacana
d: A man charged with working for the La Familia Michoacana cartel got into Mexico's federal Congress. Julio César Godoy Toscano, half-brother of Michoacán's governor, was elected a federal deputy for the PRD party in 2009, and that July was charged with ties to La Familia and money laundering. He evaded arrest, then on 23 September 2010 slipped past police checkpoints into the Chamber of Deputies to be sworn in, gaining parliamentary immunity. In October recordings surfaced of him talking with the cartel leader Servando 'La Tuta' Gómez; he left the PRD, and on 14 December 2010 Congress voted 384 to 2 to strip his immunity. He remains a fugitive.
cite: Wikipedia, Julio César Godoy Toscano (citing El Universal, Proceso and others)

n: Michoacán's interim governor Jesús Reyna met Knights Templar leaders
rank: Interim Governor and Secretary of Government of Michoacán
d: The Knights Templar Cartel, which grew out of La Familia Michoacana, reached the top of Michoacán's state government. Jesús Reyna García of the PRI was the state's secretary of government and served six months as interim governor in 2013. In April 2014 federal prosecutors detained him; Attorney General Jesús Murillo Karam said the investigation confirmed he had met cartel leaders, and a 2012 state security document described three meetings with the leader Servando 'La Tuta' Gómez. In May 2014 he was sent to the Altiplano prison on organised-crime charges. That August the governor's son, Rodrigo Vallejo, was arrested after a video showed him meeting Gómez.
cite: Al Jazeera/AFP (8 Apr 2014); InSight Crime (May 2014); Wikipedia, Fausto Vallejo

n: Allende police rounded up victims for Los Zetas, rights commission finds
rank: Allende and northern Coahuila municipal police
d: Los Zetas, a cartel founded by army deserters, used the municipal police of Allende, a town in northern Coahuila, as its own force. From 18 to 20 March 2011 Zetas gunmen and local police rounded up families sharing a surname, apparently to punish a suspected betrayal. In 2018 Mexico's National Human Rights Commission found the police complicit in at least 38 abductions and killings, carried out 'with the authorization, support or acquiescence' of local police. A 2017 Colegio de México study led by Sergio Aguayo said numerous mayors' offices and police departments in the region operated at the Zetas' direction, and put the dead and missing above 100.
cite: AP via Fox News, 'Mexico rights agency: police were complicit in 2011 killings' (19 Mar 2018); ProPublica (21 Nov 2017)

n: Zetas witnesses say they paid Coahuila's governor for control of the state
rank: Governor of Coahuila and state attorney general
d: Former members of Los Zetas testified in US courts that the cartel paid Coahuila's state government to let it operate. At a 2016 trial in San Antonio, Texas, the convicted trafficker Rodrigo Uribe Tapia said he helped deliver $2 million in bribes for then-Governor Humberto Moreira; a 2017 University of Texas law school review of the testimony recorded two $2 million payments routed through Moreira's secretary and the state attorney general Jesús Torres Charles 'for control over Coahuila'. Another ex-Zeta said cash was loaded at a ranch in 2012 as campaign money for Governor Rubén Moreira. Both Moreiras and the state government denied the claims, and no court has ruled on them.
cite: Borderland Beat (July 2016); El Financiero, 'Los Zetas pagaron a gobernadores de Coahuila y Veracruz' (7 Nov 2017)

n: US testimony says Zetas gave $12m to Veracruz governor's campaign
d: Testimony in US trials of Los Zetas members said the cartel financed a governor's election in Veracruz. A 2017 review by University of Texas law students of statements from more than 20 Zetas tried in Austin, San Antonio and Del Río reported that in 2004 the Zeta commander Efraín Torres gave $12 million, through the businessman Francisco Colorado Cessa, to support Fidel Herrera's campaign for governor. The same testimony described Zetas using Colorado's oil-services company ADT Petroservicios, a Pemex contractor, to launder money. Herrera, governor from 2004 to 2010, denied cartel links; the testimony was never tested against him in court, and he died in 2025.
cite: El Financiero (7 Nov 2017); Wikipedia, Fidel Herrera Beltrán

n: Operación Enjambre: 19 mayors among 85 officials held for crime ties
org_label: La Familia Michoacana, CJNG, Sinaloa Cartel and local gangs
rank: Mayors, councillors and municipal police chiefs
d: Mexico's federal security ministry is prosecuting municipal governments that it says criminal groups had taken over. Operación Enjambre ('Swarm') began on 22 November 2024 in the State of Mexico, targeting officials accused of running extortion, kidnapping and murder alongside groups such as La Familia Michoacana. By July 2026 more than 85 public servants had been detained, among them at least 19 serving or former mayors, plus councillors and police commanders, in at least 28 municipalities across nine states. Excélsior calculated that the municipalities affected hold more than 2.2 million people, most of them in the State of Mexico.
cite: Excélsior, 'Operación Enjambre rompe el control criminal sobre 2 millones de habitantes' (19 Jul 2026); UnoTV

n: Federal Security Directorate agents served the Guadalajara Cartel
rank: Federal Security Directorate (DFS), national intelligence police
d: The Guadalajara Cartel, Mexico's first large trafficking organisation, worked with officers of the Federal Security Directorate (DFS), the national political police and intelligence agency. On 7 February 1985 several DFS officers took part in kidnapping the US drug agent Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena and pilot Alfredo Zavala in Guadalajara; both were tortured and killed. The journalist Manuel Buendía, murdered in 1984, had been investigating ties between DFS director José Antonio Zorrilla and the cartel. The government formally dissolved the DFS on 29 November 1985. The Camarena case strained US–Mexico relations for decades.
cite: Wikipedia, Dirección Federal de Seguridad; Wikipedia, Guadalajara Cartel

n: Police chief took $300,000 to let Caro Quintero fly out of Guadalajara
d: The Guadalajara Cartel bought the federal police commander leading the hunt for its own leader. After the kidnapping of US drug agent Enrique Camarena in February 1985, Rafael Caro Quintero was found at Guadalajara airport, but Armando Pavón Reyes, the Federal Judicial Police commander, reportedly took a $300,000 bribe and let him leave on a private jet on 9 March 1985. Caro Quintero was arrested in Costa Rica on 4 April. Pavón Reyes was fired, charged with bribery and complicity in the Camarena murder, and convicted of bribery in 1986, according to the Associated Press.
cite: Wikipedia, Rafael Caro Quintero and Guadalajara Cartel (citing AP 1986)

n: Félix Gallardo, ex-federal agent, used Sinaloa governor's connections
rank: Governor of Sinaloa's household and state officials
d: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, who built the Guadalajara Cartel, began inside the state. He had been a Mexican Federal Judicial Police agent and worked as a family bodyguard for Sinaloa governor Leopoldo Sánchez Celis, becoming godfather to the governor's son. The governor's connections helped him build his trafficking organisation, and he brokered corruption of state officials. US officials said he later stayed as a guest at the house of Sinaloa governor Antonio Toledo Corro, who denied it. Félix Gallardo was arrested on 8 April 1989 and has been imprisoned since, moving to house arrest in 2022.
cite: Wikipedia, Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo (citing Los Angeles Times and others)

n: Mexico City police chief Durazo took cocaine-trade kickbacks
d: Cocaine traffickers paid the chief of police of Mexico's capital. Arturo Durazo Moreno, a childhood friend of President José López Portillo, ran Mexico City's police from 1976 to 1982 and reported directly to the president. A US grand jury had indicted him on narcotics charges about eleven months before he took the post. On a salary under $1,000 a month he acquired two large homes, vintage cars and property abroad, attributed to police bribes and payments from the cocaine trade. The FBI arrested him in Puerto Rico in 1984; after extradition in 1986 he was convicted of corruption, extortion and cocaine-trade kickbacks and sentenced to 16 years.
cite: Wikipedia, Arturo Durazo Moreno (citing New York Times, Los Angeles Times)

n: Three Tamaulipas ex-governors held in Mexico over Gulf Cartel ties
d: Mexico's federal prosecutors investigated whether the Gulf Cartel and its former armed wing Los Zetas had the governors of Tamaulipas, the border state where the cartel was based. On 30 January 2012 the Attorney General ordered three former governors, Manuel Cavazos Lerma (1993–1999), Tomás Yarrington (1999–2004) and Eugenio Hernández Flores (2005–2010), and their families not to leave the country while they were investigated for possible cooperation with cartels. The PAN politician Santiago Creel said the PRI in Tamaulipas had protected the Gulf Cartel for years. In May 2015 the US indicted Hernández for laundering about $30 million; a Mexican judge refused to extradite him.
cite: Wikipedia, Gulf Cartel (citing Excélsior, 30 Jan 2012); Wikipedia, Eugenio Hernández Flores

n: Batista gave Meyer Lansky's mafia Cuba's casinos for kickbacks
rank: President Fulgencio Batista; government gambling adviser
d: The American Mafia, through its financier Meyer Lansky, reached the head of Cuba's government. In the late 1940s Fulgencio Batista agreed to give Lansky and the Mafia control of Cuba's casinos and racetracks in return for kickbacks. After seizing power in a 1952 coup, Batista made Lansky an adviser on gambling reform. In 1955 the law was changed so any hotel worth $1 million could host a casino, and the state matched large hotel investments. Lansky put most of the roughly $14 million into the Havana Riviera, opened in 1957. The arrangement ended with the 1959 revolution, when casinos were looted and then nationalised.
cite: Wikipedia, Meyer Lansky (citing Lacey, 'Little Man'; English, 'Havana Nocturne')

n: Pablo Escobar elected to Colombia's Congress with parliamentary immunity
d: Pablo Escobar, leader of the Medellín Cartel, got himself into Colombia's Congress. In the March 1982 election he won a seat as an alternate (substitute) member of the Chamber of Representatives for Medellín on a Liberal list, which automatically gave him parliamentary immunity and a diplomatic passport. Justice Minister Rodrigo Lara Bonilla accused him of crime from the first days of Congress, and the Liberal leader Luis Carlos Galán expelled him from his movement. Escobar's term ended in October 1983 and he announced his retirement from politics in January 1984. Lara Bonilla was murdered on 30 April 1984 and Galán in August 1989, both by the cartel.
cite: Wikipedia, Pablo Escobar; Wikipedia, 1982 Colombian parliamentary election; Wikipedia, Medellín Cartel

n: Drug lords suspected of swaying the 1991 assembly that banned extradition
d: Colombia's drug lords were suspected of influencing the assembly that wrote the country's 1991 constitution. The Medellín Cartel had fought extradition to the United States with bribery, threats and killings of judges and ministers. The Constituent Assembly wrote a ban on extraditing Colombian citizens into the new constitution, approved in 1991, and Pablo Escobar surrendered that year under a deal that let him be held in La Catedral, a prison he built himself. Suspicions that traffickers paid or pressed assembly members were widely reported but not proven.
cite: Wikipedia, Pablo Escobar; Wikipedia, Medellín Cartel

n: Uribe's intelligence chief Noguera put the DAS at paramilitaries' service
d: The AUC, Colombia's paramilitary and drug-trafficking federation, had the head of the national intelligence agency working for it. Jorge Noguera, a regional campaign manager for Álvaro Uribe, ran the Administrative Department of Security (DAS) from August 2002 to October 2005. A former DAS IT chief testified that Noguera made DAS resources available to the AUC's Northern Bloc under 'Jorge 40', including information used to kill trade unionists. On 14 September 2011 the Supreme Court convicted him of conspiracy, conspiracy to murder, destroying public documents and leaking secret information, and sentenced him to 25 years.
cite: Wikipedia, Jorge Noguera Cotes; Colombia Reports (Sept 2011); CTV/AP (14 Sep 2011)

n: Former DAS chief Maza Márquez jailed for role in Galán assassination
d: Colombia's Supreme Court found that the director of the national intelligence agency took part in the cartel-ordered killing of a presidential frontrunner. General Miguel Maza Márquez ran the Administrative Department of Security (DAS) from 1985 to 1991. The Liberal presidential candidate Luis Carlos Galán was assassinated in August 1989 on the orders of the Medellín Cartel's leader. In November 2016 the Supreme Court sentenced Maza Márquez to 30 years for participating in the assassination. The Medellín Cartel had also tried to kill him, including with the December 1989 DAS building bombing.
cite: Wikipedia, Miguel Maza Márquez (citing BBC Mundo, Nov 2016)

n: Ex-justice minister Santofimio convicted as co-author of Galán murder
rank: Former Minister of Justice and senator
d: A former Colombian justice minister and senator was convicted of helping the Medellín Cartel kill a presidential candidate. Alberto Santofimio Botero had been justice minister in 1974–75, a senator and twice a presidential candidate. In October 2007 he was sentenced to 24 years as a co-author of the August 1989 assassination of Luis Carlos Galán, on testimony from the Escobar hitman Jhon Jairo 'Popeye' Velásquez. A court overturned the verdict in 2008, but on 31 August 2011 the Supreme Court reinstated the 24-year sentence. He was paroled in March 2020. In 2018 he was placed under investigation over the 1984 killing of Justice Minister Rodrigo Lara Bonilla.
cite: Wikipedia, Alberto Santofimio

n: Medellín's chief prosecutor shielded 'Don Mario' drug gang
d: The drug gang of Daniel Rendón Herrera, alias 'Don Mario', a former paramilitary commander, had Medellín's chief prosecutor protecting it. Guillermo León Valencia Cossio, brother of the then Minister of Interior and Justice Fabio Valencia Cossio, was arrested on 25 September 2008. The Supreme Court found he had ordered a police commander to leave Don Mario's second-in-command off an investigation chart of the gang, and convicted him of conspiracy, suppression of documents and illicit enrichment, with a 15-year sentence. In October 2010 the US listed him as a Specially Designated Narcotics Trafficker. His sentence was later extended as more criminal ties emerged.
cite: Colombia Reports, 'Former chief prosecutor sentenced to 15 years'; El Colombiano (25 Sep 2008)

n: Cali Cartel had insiders in the police Search Bloc and phone company
rank: Search Bloc police unit; Bogotá–Cali telephone exchange
d: The Cali Cartel, which preferred bribery to violence, placed people inside the bodies hunting it. It recruited Jorge Salcedo, a Colombian military member, to run its intelligence and build a hidden radio network across Cali. A 1995 raid showed its counter-intelligence unit had been monitoring calls in and out of Bogotá and Cali, including those of the US Embassy and the Ministry of Defence, with help from an insider at the phone company. A high-ranking member of the Search Bloc, the police unit formed to catch the cartel's leaders, hid Miguel Rodríguez Orejuela in his car during a 1995 raid. Six of the seven leaders were arrested that year.
cite: Wikipedia, Cali Cartel (citing Time, 1991; Chepesiuk, 'The Bullet or the Bribe')

n: President Petro's son says traffickers' money entered the 2022 campaign
org_label: Samuel Santander Lopesierra and Gabriel Hilsaca
d: Money from a convicted drug trafficker reached the campaign of Colombia's president, according to the president's own son. Nicolás Petro, a former regional legislator on the Caribbean coast, was arrested on 29 July 2023 and charged. Prosecutors said about $270,000 had been delivered to him by Samuel Santander Lopesierra, known as the 'Marlboro Man', who was convicted of drug trafficking in the US, and by Gabriel Hilsaca, and that part went to Gustavo Petro's 2022 campaign. Nicolás Petro told prosecutors the campaign received money of dubious origin, then pleaded not guilty. The president said he would not interfere.
cite: WLRN/AP (4 Aug 2023); El Tiempo; Vanguardia (3 Aug 2023)

n: Ñeñepolítica: wiretaps of a trafficker discuss buying votes for Duque
d: Wiretaps of a drug trafficker suggested he moved money to buy votes for Iván Duque in Colombia's 2018 presidential election. José Guillermo 'Ñeñe' Hernández, said by Colombian and US authorities to be a partner of the trafficker Marcos Figueroa, was recorded during a Barranquilla murder investigation. In audio published in March 2020 he spoke of vote-buying money for the second round and of enlisting businessmen. He was a main guest at Duque's inauguration and was killed in Brazil in May 2019. The prosecutor's office and Congress's accusations committee closed their inquiries, and no court found that Duque or Álvaro Uribe took part.
cite: Colombia Reports (4 Mar 2020); El Tiempo (Fiscalía archive decision); El Universal Cartagena (15 Dec 2021)

n: Norte del Valle Cartel bribed police and legislators to block extradition
d: The Norte del Valle Cartel, a cocaine group based in Colombia's Valle del Cauca, tried to buy the state's protection against extradition. A 2004 US racketeering indictment said its leaders 'bribed and corrupted Colombian law enforcement and Colombian legislators' to block extraditions, and ran their own wiretaps on rivals and on Colombian and US police. The cartel's lawyer Gabriel Puerta Parra, arrested in October 2004, reportedly influenced the government on extradition. Laureano Rentería, accused of bribing high officials for the leader Juan Carlos Ramírez Abadía, was found dead of cyanide poisoning in his cell on the day of his extradition in February 2007.
cite: Wikipedia, Norte del Valle Cartel (citing US DOJ indictment, 2004)

n: Cachiros video shows traffickers offering cash to Castro's brother-in-law
rank: Secretary of Congress; Libre party campaign
d: The Cachiros, a Honduran trafficking clan, negotiated with a senior figure in the ruling family's party. In video secretly recorded in 2013 and published by InSight Crime and Univision on 3 September 2024, Cachiros members including Devis Leonel Rivera Maradiaga offered Carlos Zelaya, brother-in-law of President Xiomara Castro, $650,000 for her 2013 campaign and discussed past bribes to former president Manuel Zelaya. Carlos Zelaya, then secretary of Congress, said he took no money and acted without Castro's knowledge. He and Defence Minister José Manuel Zelaya, Castro's nephew, resigned on 31 August 2024, days before the video appeared. Castro called the affair a coup plot.
cite: El Faro (4 Sep 2024); InSight Crime; AP via ABC News (Sept 2024)

n: Trafficker Alexander Ardón ran El Paraíso as mayor and funded the party
rank: Mayor of El Paraíso, Copán; National Party campaigns
d: A cocaine trafficker took over a Honduran border town by becoming its mayor and used the post to buy national protection. Alexander Ardón, a go-between for Colombian and Mexican traffickers, was mayor of El Paraíso, Copán, on the Guatemalan border, and was re-elected in 2009 with 94.7% of the vote; police said he posted cameras and armed guards at the town's entrances. US prosecutors said that from 2008 Tony Hernández offered protection in return for National Party campaign money, and that Ardón paid $1.5 million into Juan Orlando Hernández's 2013 campaign. Indicted in 2019, Ardón became the key US witness against both Hernández brothers.
cite: InSight Crime, 'How an ex-mayor could bring down Honduras' president' (Aug 2019); El Heraldo (Aug 2026)

n: Presidential candidate Mario Estrada sought Sinaloa Cartel campaign cash
rank: Presidential candidate (offered state posts and ports)
d: A Guatemalan presidential candidate tried to sell the state to the Sinaloa Cartel. Mario Estrada, who ran for president in 2018 and 2019 and at times polled in the top five, asked people he believed were cartel representatives for millions of dollars in drug money for his campaign. In return he promised, if elected, 'unfettered access' to Guatemala's airports and ports, high government posts for cartel members and a share of profits, and asked them to hire hitmen to kill rivals. The contacts were US informants. He pleaded guilty to cocaine importation conspiracy and on 11 February 2020 a New York court sentenced him to 15 years.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, press release (11 Feb 2020)

n: Texis Cartel: a mayor and a football boss accused, later acquitted
rank: Mayor of Metapán; legislators, police, judges
d: El Faro reported in 2011 that a trafficking network called the Texis Cartel, which moved drugs along El Salvador's northern border, was led by a sitting mayor and protected by officials. It named as founders José Adán Salazar ('Chepe Diablo'), president of the national football league, and Juan Umaña Samayoa, mayor of Metapán, and alleged support from other mayors, a legislator, and police, soldiers, judges and prosecutors paid to let shipments pass or drop charges. President Mauricio Funes ordered an investigation, and the US listed Salazar as a drug kingpin in 2014, then delisted him in 2017. In May 2021 a court acquitted all nine defendants of laundering $500 million.
cite: El Faro (2011); Wikipedia, Texis Cartel

n: Haiti's police chief Michel François indicted for cocaine bribes
d: US prosecutors charged that Colombian drug lords paid the head of Haiti's police under the military regime. Colonel Joseph-Michel François helped lead the 1991 coup against President Jean-Bertrand Aristide and then ran the police and secret police under General Raoul Cédras. In March 1997 the US indicted him for allegedly smuggling 33 tons of cocaine and heroin into the United States from his private airstrip in Haiti while taking bribes from Colombian traffickers. He denied the charges. Honduras, where he had fled, refused to extradite him in July 1997 for lack of evidence, and he died there in 2017.
cite: Wikipedia, Michel François (citing New York Times, 1997)

n: Royal Commission finds drug money ran through Pindling's cabinet
d: Colombian cocaine smugglers paid members of the Bahamian government to use the islands as a route to the US. Carlos Lehder, a Medellín Cartel co-founder, controlled Norman's Cay in the Exumas as a smuggling base. After an NBC report, 'The Bahamas: A Nation For Sale', a Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking and Government Corruption reported in 1984 wide corruption in the cabinet and police. It found that Prime Minister Lynden Pindling's spending from 1977 to 1984 was eight times his reported income and that he and his wife had received at least $57.3 million in cash. The commission did not find Pindling guilty, but five ministers resigned or were dismissed.
cite: Wikipedia, Lynden Pindling and Illegal drug trade in the Bahamas (citing New York Times; Royal Commission report 1984)

n: Minister Vere Bird Jr let Israeli guns pass Antigua to the Medellín Cartel
d: Agents of the Medellín Cartel used an Antiguan cabinet minister to obtain military weapons. Maurice Sarfati and the Israeli mercenary Yair Klein ordered Israeli arms in Antigua's name, with forged papers, as part of a plan to train and supply the forces of the cartel leader Gonzalo Rodríguez Gacha. An Israeli diplomatic note said the guns were shipped at the apparent instruction of minister Vere Bird Jr, son of the prime minister. After Colombia complained, an inquiry under Sir Louis Blom-Cooper, ordered in April 1990, reported that November and recommended Bird be barred from public office for life. He was removed from cabinet on 10 May 1990.
cite: Wikipedia, Vere Bird Jr. (citing Blom-Cooper inquiry report, 1990)

n: Cocaine Coup: trafficker Roberto Suárez financed Bolivia's 1980 junta
rank: Military junta; Minister of the Interior
d: Bolivia's leading cocaine trafficker helped pay for a military coup and then had his cousin in charge of the police. On 17 July 1980 General Luis García Meza seized power in what became known as the 'Cocaine Coup'. Roberto Suárez Gómez helped finance it, and many officers had ties to traffickers, with parts of the army acting as their protectors for bribes. Suárez's cousin, Colonel Luis Arce Gómez, became Minister of the Interior, giving Suárez political protection. US pressure isolated the regime, which fell in 1981. Arce Gómez was later jailed in the US for drug trafficking, and García Meza received a 30-year sentence for human rights crimes.
cite: Wikipedia, Luis García Meza; Wikipedia, Luis Arce Gómez; Wikipedia, Roberto Suárez Gómez

n: Bicho bosses' ledgers named 12 congressmen and 125 police in Rio
rank: Police, judges, congressmen and state officials
d: The bosses of the jogo do bicho, Rio de Janeiro's illegal numbers lottery, kept police and politicians on their side. Rio's attorney general Antônio Carlos Biscaia called the bosses' central commission 'a true Brazilian Mafia' that aimed to corrupt authorities and police, and in 1993 Judge Denise Frossard convicted the commission's members of criminal association. In March 1994 police raided Castor de Andrade's base in Bangu and seized 200 account books. The material implicated a former president, Rio's governor, the mayors of São Paulo and Rio, three judges, 12 congressmen, seven state legislators, 25 police commissioners and 100 police officers. Those named were not convicted.
cite: Wikipedia, Jogo do bicho (citing Folha de S.Paulo, Veja, New York Times 1994)

n: Federal raid finds bicho and slot-machine bosses paying judges and police
d: Brazil's federal police found that the bosses of Rio's illegal numbers game and slot-machine trade were paying people inside the justice system. On 12 April 2007 they arrested Antonio Petrus Kalil, Anísio Abraão David and Capitão Guimarães, then president of the league of Rio samba schools, with 24 others over illegal lotteries, bingo halls and slot machines. The raids allegedly uncovered payoffs to judges, police officers, prosecutors and lawyers, and about $6 million in cash was seized. The same families had been jailed in 1993 and freed on parole within three years.
cite: Wikipedia, Jogo do bicho (citing O Globo, Folha de S.Paulo, April 2007)

n: Rio state deputy TH Joias arrested as Comando Vermelho's man in assembly
rank: Rio de Janeiro State Legislative Assembly (Alerj)
d: Comando Vermelho (Red Command), Rio de Janeiro's oldest drug faction, is accused of having a representative in the state legislature. In 2025 police placed state deputy TH Joias in preventive detention for ties to the group, alleging he acted as its arm in the Legislative Assembly of Rio de Janeiro (Alerj). That September the MDB party's president said a state deputy allegedly involved with the faction would be expelled. A September 2025 report also cited investigations showing police officers escorting the faction's drug shipments. In October 2025 a police operation against the group in the Penha and Alemão favelas left more than 120 dead.
cite: Wikipedia, Comando Vermelho (citing G1, Folha de S.Paulo, 2025)

n: Caso Encuentro: Albanian mafia link reached Lasso's family circle
rank: State companies and President Lasso's campaign
d: Reporting in 2023 alleged that a drug-trafficking network linked to the Albanian mafia reached Ecuador's presidency through a businessman close to the president's family. The outlet La Posta published audio of Rubén Cherres, an associate of President Guillermo Lasso's brother-in-law Danilo Carrera, describing a scheme in state companies and saying he provided $1.5 million to Lasso's 2021 campaign; investigators later reported Cherres linked the Albanian mafia to Lasso's circle. A police inquiry into Cherres's drug ties had been dropped. Cherres was murdered on 31 March 2023. Facing impeachment, Lasso dissolved the National Assembly on 17 May 2023, forcing early elections.
cite: Wikipedia, Guillermo Lasso (citing La Posta, Primicias, El Universo 2023)

n: Los Choneros leader 'Fito' walks out of La Roca prison
d: Los Choneros, the gang that has held sway in Ecuador's prisons since 2011, ran its operations from inside them and is accused of buying the staff. Its leader José Adolfo Macías ('Fito'), serving 34 years, directed the gang by phone and internet from his cell. In January 2024 he vanished from La Roca prison in Guayaquil; guards were suspected of complicity, a perimeter fence had been cut days earlier, and a boat with guard uniforms and ammunition was found nearby. About 30 officials were arrested in a linked anti-corruption operation, and the government declared an 'internal armed conflict'. Fito was recaptured in June 2025 and agreed to extradition to the US.
cite: Wikipedia, Los Choneros (citing Primicias, Reuters, AP 2024–25)

n: US names three of Chávez's security chiefs as FARC drug helpers
rank: Military intelligence chief, DISIP intelligence director, former interior minister
d: The US Treasury said the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army that financed itself through cocaine, had senior Venezuelan security officials working for it. On 12 September 2008 it sanctioned Hugo Carvajal, head of military intelligence; Henry Rangel Silva, director of the DISIP intelligence service; and Ramón Rodríguez Chacín, a former Minister of the Interior. It accused Carvajal of protecting FARC drug loads from seizure, supplying weapons and giving it Venezuelan official documents. Rangel Silva later became defence minister and governor of Trujillo.
cite: US Treasury press release (12 Sep 2008), via Wikipedia, Hugo Carvajal

n: Corleonesi ally Vito Ciancimino ran Palermo's building permits
rank: Palermo public works assessor and mayor
d: Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia, had its own man in charge of Palermo's building permits. Vito Ciancimino, from Corleone and close to the Corleonesi bosses Bernardo Provenzano and Totò Riina, became the city's assessor for public works and building permits in 1959 and was mayor in 1970–71. The construction boom of those years, known as the 'Sack of Palermo', destroyed the city's green belt. After the informer Tommaso Buscetta testified, Ciancimino was arrested in 1984. In 1992 he was sentenced to 13 years for Mafia association and laundering, the first time an Italian politician was found guilty of working with the Mafia. In 2002 the city sought €150m in damages from him.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Vito Ciancimino' and 'Sack of Palermo' (citing Italian court records and press)

n: Mafia cousins Nino and Ignazio Salvo held Sicily's tax collection
d: Two members of Cosa Nostra, the cousins Nino and Ignazio Salvo, held the private concession to collect taxes for the region of Sicily. The concession, arranged through the Christian Democrat leader Salvo Lima, paid them 10% of what they collected, about three times the 3.3% national average. The informer Tommaso Buscetta revealed that both men belonged to the Mafia, and they were arrested on 12 November 1984. Nino died in 1986; Ignazio was convicted of Mafia association at the 1987 Maxi Trial and sentenced to seven years. Photographs from 1979 showed Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti with Nino Salvo, though Andreotti denied knowing the cousins. Ignazio was murdered by the Mafia in 1992.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ignazio and Nino Salvo' (citing police and Maxi Trial records)

n: Mafia votes put Antonio D'Alì in the Senate and Interior Ministry
d: Cosa Nostra helped elect a senator who then became a junior minister at Italy's Interior Ministry, the ministry that runs the police. Italy's highest court, the Court of Cassation, confirmed in December 2022 a six-year sentence for Antonio D'Alì, a Forza Italia senator for 24 years, for 'external complicity' in a mafia association (helping the Mafia without being a sworn member). The court found that in 2001 he made a pact under which the Mafia delivered votes for his re-election, which led to his appointment as interior under-secretary from 2001 to 2006. It also found he took part in a sham land sale arranged by the Trapani boss Matteo Messina Denaro. D'Alì surrendered at Opera prison.
cite: L'Indipendente, 15 Dec 2022; LiveSicilia (D'Alì surrenders at Opera prison)

n: Intelligence deputy Bruno Contrada convicted of aiding the Mafia
d: Former Mafia members said Cosa Nostra had a source high in Italy's civil intelligence service, SISDE. Bruno Contrada had headed Palermo's judicial police and later rose to deputy director of SISDE. He was arrested on 24 December 1992 after the informers Gaspare Mutolo and Giuseppe Marchese accused him of tipping off the Mafia about police operations and obstructing the capture of the boss Totò Riina. He was sentenced to ten years, a verdict upheld by the Court of Cassation in 2007. In 2015 the European Court of Human Rights ruled he had been convicted for conduct that was not clearly a crime at the time, and in 2017 Italy's top court annulled the conviction. He died in March 2026.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bruno Contrada'; ANSA, 14 Apr 2015 (ECtHR ruling)

n: Salvo Lima, Andreotti's man in Sicily, killed after Maxi Trial loss
d: Cosa Nostra treated Salvo Lima, Palermo's mayor in 1958–63 and 1965–68, later an MP, budget under-secretary and member of the European Parliament, as its link to national power. Lima was the Sicilian broker for Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti's faction of the Christian Democrats. A 1964 indictment described Palermo bosses seeking favours from him, and the Italian parliament's Antimafia Commission found in 1993 strong signs of his relations with Cosa Nostra. The informers Tommaso Buscetta and Gaspare Mutolo said Lima was expected to get the Maxi Trial convictions overturned. When the Supreme Court upheld them in January 1992, he was shot dead on 12 March 1992; Totò Riina and other bosses got life sentences for the killing.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Salvo Lima' (citing 1993 Antimafia Commission report and 2004 Cassation ruling on Andreotti)

n: Judge 'the sentence-slayer' Carnevale tried for helping the Mafia
rank: President, First Criminal Section, Court of Cassation
d: Prosecutors charged that Cosa Nostra had influence over the judge who heard Mafia appeals at Italy's highest court. Corrado Carnevale presided over the First Criminal Section of the Court of Cassation and overturned so many Mafia convictions that he was nicknamed 'l'ammazzasentenze', the sentence-slayer. Because of suspected collusion, he was kept off the final ruling in the Maxi Trial of hundreds of mafiosi in 1992 and another judge took his place. He was suspended in 1993 and in June 2001 sentenced to six years for 'external complicity' in a mafia association. The Court of Cassation acquitted him in October 2002, and he returned to work as a civil judge in 2007.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Corrado Carnevale'

n: Lombardy regional minister Zambetti bought 4,000 'Ndrangheta votes
d: The 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, sold a block of votes to a politician who then sat in the government of Lombardy, Italy's richest region. Prosecutors said Domenico Zambetti paid €200,000 to two 'Ndrangheta figures, Eugenio Costantino and Giuseppe D'Agostino, for about 4,000 preference votes in the 2010 regional election, which he won with 11,217 votes before becoming a regional assessore (minister). He was arrested in October 2012. In February 2017 a Milan court sentenced him to 13 years and six months for a 'political-mafia exchange', and the prosecutor said the deal had distorted the 2010 result. Costantino, described as a contact of the Di Grillo-Mancuso clan, received 16 and a half years.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 8 Feb 2017; LaPresse, 8 Feb 2017

n: 'Ndrangheta clans steered Reggio Calabria's public health authority
d: The 'Ndrangheta got inside the public body that runs hospitals for Reggio Calabria province. On 13 March 2019 Italy's cabinet dissolved the provincial health authority (ASP) for mafia infiltration and put it under commissioners, at the request of the prefect, the national government's local representative. In March 2021 Carabinieri arrested 14 people. Investigators said the Piromalli clan, with the Molè family, steered appointments of health directors, and firms linked to it monopolised supply of medical products to hospitals in Locri, Gioia Tauro, Polistena and Melito Porto Salvo through direct awards, with staff taking 2.5–5% commissions. Earlier reporting found convicted mafia employees still drawing pay and debts above €420m.
cite: ANSA, 13 Mar 2019; Domani, 23 Mar 2021; Il Fatto Quotidiano, 13 Mar 2019

n: Ostia's council dissolved for mafia infiltration; Fasciani clan convicted
d: Crime groups got inside the local government of Ostia, Rome's seaside district (Municipio X, a borough council of the city). On 27 August 2015 the national government dissolved the Ostia council for mafia infiltration, after its former chairman Andrea Tassone was arrested in June with 43 others in the 'Mafia Capitale' inquiry into a ring of gangsters, businessmen and politicians. In November 2019 Italy's Court of Cassation confirmed that the Fasciani family ran a mafia-type association in Ostia, with ten final convictions, including over 27 years for Carmine Fasciani. Rome's mayor called it the first clear recognition that a mafia existed in Rome. Police had seized €18.5m of assets, including beach businesses, in 2018.
cite: ANSA, 27 Aug 2015; Open, 29 Nov 2019

n: Sicily's President Raffaele Lombardo tried for Mafia ties, acquitted
rank: President of the Region of Sicily
d: Prosecutors charged that the elected head of Sicily's regional government had dealings with Cosa Nostra. Raffaele Lombardo became President of Sicily in April 2008 and resigned on 31 July 2012 while under investigation for external complicity with the Mafia and for handing out public money for political favours. On 19 February 2014 a court sentenced him to six years and eight months for mafia association. The case went through several appeals: he was acquitted at a second appeal trial in 2022, and in 2023 the Court of Cassation confirmed the acquittal. This was a separate case from that of his predecessor Salvatore Cuffaro, who was jailed for leaking investigation secrets.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Raffaele Lombardo'

n: Interior Minister Antonio Gava accused of trading favours for Camorra votes
d: Prosecutors in Naples accused a former Italian interior minister, the minister in charge of the police, of being tied to the Camorra, the Naples-area mafia. Antonio Gava, a Christian Democrat from Campania, was interior minister from April 1988 to October 1990. He was charged in 1993 with membership of a criminal organisation and arrested on 21 September 1994, accused of trading favours for votes gathered by the Camorra. He had also been involved in the 1981 release of the politician Ciro Cirillo, kidnapped by the Red Brigades, when politicians visited the jailed Camorra boss Raffaele Cutolo to ask him to negotiate. After 13 years of proceedings Gava was acquitted of all Camorra charges.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Antonio Gava'

n: Casalesi clan bribed Campania officials for 20 years to take toxic waste
d: The Casalesi clan of the Camorra paid local officials in Campania so that toxic waste could be dumped in their areas. The clan's waste broker Gaetano Vassallo admitted that for about 20 years he bribed local politicians and officials to accept the dumping. Industrial waste from northern Italy, including heavy metals, was mixed with household rubbish, buried or burned around Acerra, Nola and Marigliano, the area called the 'triangle of death'. From about 2005 the Camorra also bought land rented to the state waste contractor FIBE for storing waste bales. In June 2008 President Giorgio Napolitano said the Camorra had systematically moved toxic waste from northern industry into Campania.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Naples waste management crisis' (citing Vassallo testimony and D'Alisa et al.)

n: Montenegro's leader Djukanovic indicted in Italian cigarette-mafia case
d: Italian anti-mafia prosecutors in Bari charged that Montenegro's state, under its leader Milo Djukanovic, protected cigarette smugglers working with Italian crime groups. In October 2008 they indicted Djukanovic, then prime minister, with seven Serbian and Montenegrin and seven Italian suspects, over smuggling cigarettes from Montenegro to Puglia between 1994 and 2002 and helping talks between the Montenegrin mafia and a Puglia crime group over control of the trade. The EU estimated the smuggling cost it billions of euros in taxes. Prosecutor Giuseppe Scelsi said Djukanovic would not stand trial because of his immunity; a 2003 Italian ruling had already found he had head-of-state immunity. Djukanovic went on to lead Montenegro until 2023.
cite: OCCRP, Oct 2008 ('Djukanovic Indicted; Avoids Trial'); ICIJ/OCCRP 'The Montenegro Connection'

n: Businessman Marian Kočner's messages expose 13 Slovak judges
rank: Judges and the deputy justice minister
d: Marian Kočner, a Slovak businessman later charged with ordering the 2018 murder of the journalist Ján Kuciak, had judges and a deputy justice minister working for him, according to messages taken from his phone. On 11 March 2020 the National Criminal Agency detained 13 judges and a lawyer in 'Action Storm'. Those charged with corruption, interfering with court independence and abuse of power included former deputy justice minister Monika Jankovská and acting Supreme Court President Jarmila Urbancová. Former judges Vladimír Sklenka and Miriam Repáková confessed to cooperating with Kočner, and five accused were held in custody. The case led to a wider clean-up of Slovakia's courts.
cite: Slovak Spectator, 12 and 15 Mar 2020; RTVS, 16 Mar 2020

n: Oligarch Bödör's group allegedly ran Slovakia's police leadership
rank: Police President, NAKA and financial police chiefs
d: Slovak prosecutors charge that a businessman, Norbert Bödör, ran a criminal group whose members included the country's top police officers. In 'Očistec' (Purgatory), police detained eight former senior officials on 5 November 2020, including former Police President Tibor Gašpar, allegedly Bödör's right-hand man, and former heads of the National Criminal Agency (NAKA) and its financial and anti-corruption units. The group allegedly used police powers to blackmail businesspeople, obtain information on investigations and pass it to people close to the ruling Smer party. Two former officers confessed. The Special Prosecutor Dušan Kováčik was also charged with supporting the group. The trial continues.
cite: Slovak Spectator, Nov 2020; RTVS, 'Očistec trial' reports

n: Jovanjica: police and intelligence officers guarded a cannabis farm
rank: Serbian police and BIA intelligence officers
d: A Serbian businessman close to the ruling party is accused of running a cannabis farm with help from police officers and agents of the BIA, Serbia's security intelligence agency. Predrag Koluvija's company Jovanjica presented itself as an organic food producer; in November 2019 police raided it and found about 650 kg of dried marijuana and 65,000 stems. Koluvija had travelled in President Aleksandar Vučić's delegation to a 2019 Moscow business forum. Prosecutors charged him with leading a criminal group with police and intelligence officers among its members. He is on trial in two cases at Belgrade's Special Court for Organised Crime, and courts ordered many of his properties seized in 2023.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jovanjica case' (citing KRIK, BIRN, N1)

n: Marbella council dissolved after planning chief's bribery ring
who: Property developers via Juan Antonio Roca
d: A network built around Marbella's urban planning adviser, Juan Antonio Roca, took property developers' money in return for planning decisions from the city council. The council had been run since 1991 by Jesús Gil's GIL party; Gil himself was jailed in 2002 for diverting public funds. In March 2006 police arrested Roca, Mayor Marisol Yagüe, the deputy mayor and many councillors in 'Operación Malaya'. On 7 April 2006 Spain's government dissolved the council, the first time that power had been used against a council in Spanish democracy. In October 2013 a court convicted 53 people of bribery, fraud and laundering; Roca got 11 years and a fine of about US$300m.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Marbella City Council dissolution'; OCCRP, Oct 2013

n: Delyan Peevski made Bulgaria's security chief; US cites bribes
rank: Head of DANS state security agency
d: Delyan Peevski, a Bulgarian MP and media owner, was elected by parliament on 14 June 2013 to head DANS, the State Agency for National Security. Mass protests in Sofia followed, with crowds chanting 'Mafia', and he resigned the next day. By then his family's media group owned six of the 12 largest newspapers and controlled nearly 80% of print distribution. In June 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned him under the Global Magnitsky Act, which targets serious corruption. It said he had used influence peddling and bribes to protect himself from scrutiny and to control key institutions in Bulgaria. The UK later imposed its own anti-corruption sanctions.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Delyan Peevski' (citing US Treasury, June 2021)

n: Alleged 'Octopus' gang leader Aleksei Petrov advised Bulgaria's DANS
d: Bulgarian police said a man they accused of leading an extortion gang had been working inside the national security agency. Aleksei Petrov became an informant for DANS, the State Agency for National Security, in 2001 and an official adviser in 2008. On 10 February 2010 he was detained and accused of heading a criminal group called 'Octopus' engaged in racketeering and extortion. The charges were later narrowed to two cases from 1998 and 2000, the investigation was closed for lack of evidence in 2014, and he was acquitted in July 2021. He ran for president in 2011. Petrov was shot dead in Sofia on 16 August 2023.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Aleksei Petrov (businessman)'

n: Mkhedrioni militia of Jaba Ioseliani became Georgia's interior forces
d: An armed group accused of extortion and drug smuggling was given a place inside Georgia's state after it helped overthrow the government. Jaba Ioseliani founded the Mkhedrioni in 1989. It joined the 1991–92 coup against President Zviad Gamsakhurdia and was then given the role of interior forces and, later, semi-official status as the 'Georgian Rescue Corps'. Ioseliani sat in parliament with armed Mkhedrioni men as 'bodyguards'. Members ran roadblocks where drivers were 'fined', and were accused of extortion, robbery and drug smuggling. In 1995 Eduard Shevardnadze ordered the group disarmed; it was outlawed and Ioseliani was jailed until an amnesty in 2000.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mkhedrioni' (citing Jamestown Foundation and contemporary reports)

n: Tambov gang's Kumarin ran St Petersburg's city fuel company
d: The Tambov gang, a St Petersburg crime group, got control of the city's main fuel trader. The Petersburg Fuel Company (PTK) was formed in 1994 and administered by the city government; from 1998 to 1999 its deputy president was Vladimir Kumarin, named as the gang's leader. In 2001 Russia's interior minister Boris Gryzlov said the gang controlled up to 100 industrial enterprises, including PTK. The city legislature's speaker, Viktor Novosyolov, was alleged to be close to Kumarin before he was killed in a 1999 car bombing. Kumarin, jailed for racketeering in 1990–93, was sentenced in November 2009 to 14 years. A Spanish case against the gang's Spanish branch ended in acquittals in 2018.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Tambov Gang' (citing Vedomosti, 2009, and Gryzlov statement, 2001)

n: Crime groups controlled AvtoVAZ car sales through its managers
d: Criminal groups got control of sales at AvtoVAZ, maker of Lada cars and then Russia's largest carmaker, through close ties with part of its management. By 1995 car sales, distribution and spare parts were controlled by criminal organisations, which were also used to control workers and break strikes; some dealerships simply stole cars from the factory. Operation Cyclone, a 1997 investigation by Russia's Interior Ministry, found evidence that gangsters connected to AvtoVAZ had committed at least 65 murders of managers, dealers and rivals. By late 1996 the company was Russia's largest tax debtor, owing $2.4 billion, and workers went unpaid for months.
cite: Wikipedia, 'AvtoVAZ' (citing Interior Ministry Operation Cyclone, 1997)

n: US-sanctioned Gafur Rakhimov elected head of world amateur boxing
d: A man the US Treasury listed as a member of a transnational crime network became head of the International Boxing Association (AIBA), which then ran Olympic boxing. In February 2012 the Treasury sanctioned the Uzbek businessman Gafur Rakhimov among people it accused of belonging to the 'Brothers' Circle', a Eurasian criminal group. Rakhimov, who denies wrongdoing and has never been charged, was elected AIBA president in November 2018 despite criticism from the International Olympic Committee. In June 2019 the IOC suspended AIBA's recognition and ran boxing at the Tokyo Games itself. Rakhimov resigned on 15 July 2019. Boxing's Olympic place stayed in doubt for years afterwards.
cite: Wikipedia, 'International Boxing Association (amateur)' and 'Gafur Rakhimov' (citing US Treasury, Feb 2012; IOC, June 2019)

n: Mogilevich alleged to control Ukraine's gas middleman RosUkrEnergo
d: Ukrainian politicians and US diplomats suspected that the crime boss Semion Mogilevich, once on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list, controlled the company that supplied all of Ukraine's imported gas. RosUkrEnergo was half-owned by Russia's Gazprom and half by a group of Dmytro Firtash and Ivan Fursin; from 2006 to January 2009 it supplied all of Ukraine's gas imports from Russia and Central Asia and resold them to the state firm Naftogaz, earning over $785 million in profit in 2006. In November 2006 Yulia Tymoshenko said it was controlled by Mogilevich, and leaked US cables showed diplomats shared her suspicion. Mogilevich denies any link. A January 2009 deal cut RosUkrEnergo out.
cite: Wikipedia, 'RosUkrEnergo' and 'Semion Mogilevich' (citing leaked US diplomatic cables)

n: Hong Kong police officer Godber's flight exposed police graft syndicates
org_label: Illegal gambling, vice and drug operators
rank: Royal Hong Kong Police senior officers
d: In colonial Hong Kong, operators of illegal gambling, prostitution and drugs paid police, and stations were organised to profit from them. The system came to light in 1973 when Chief Superintendent Peter Godber, deputy commander for Kowloon, was found to hold about HK$4.3 million in overseas accounts and fled to London when asked to explain it. The public outcry led to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) being founded on 15 February 1974, reporting to the Governor rather than the police. Godber was extradited and jailed for four years in 1975. In 1978, 119 officers were made to leave the force and 24 were held on conspiracy charges.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Independent Commission Against Corruption (Hong Kong)' and 'Peter Godber'

n: Smuggler Lai Changxing bought Xiamen's officials and a police vice-minister
rank: Vice-minister of public security and Xiamen officials
d: A smuggling ring based in Xiamen corrupted hundreds of Chinese officials, up to a vice-minister of public security. Lai Changxing's Yuanhua Group was believed to have smuggled about US$10 billion of goods, including luxury cars and oil, into China, avoiding US$3.6 billion in taxes and fees. Officials were won over with bribes, banquets, jobs for relatives and blackmail; those named included Li Jizhou, deputy minister for public security. About 300 officials were put on trial and 14 people were executed in connection with the case. Lai fled to Canada in August 1999, was deported in July 2011 after a 12-year fight, and was sentenced to life in May 2012.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lai Changxing' (citing Xinhua and Canadian court records)

n: Saigon gang boss Nam Cam bought a police chief and a top prosecutor
rank: Police chief, deputy chief prosecutor, state radio head
d: Truong Van Cam, known as Năm Cam, ran Ho Chi Minh City's gambling dens, extortion and loan-sharking for about 15 years with officials on his side. At his 2003 trial, then Vietnam's largest, about 155 defendants included 13 senior police officers and two expelled members of the Communist Party's Central Committee. Phạm Sỹ Chiến, former deputy national chief prosecutor, and Trần Mai Hạnh, former head of state radio, were found guilty of taking bribes from Cam. Bùi Quốc Huy, city police chief in 1996–2001, was found guilty of negligence that enabled Cam's operations. Cam was executed in June 2004 for ordering a rival's killing in 2000.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Năm Cam' (citing 2003 trial reporting)

n: Inagawa-kai boss Ishii got billions in credit from Sagawa and brokers
rank: Sagawa Kyubin, Nomura and Nikko Securities
d: Susumu Ishii, head of the Inagawa-kai, one of Japan's largest yakuza groups, from 1985 to 1990, got large sums out of major Japanese companies. He received credit and loans totalling about $2.5 billion from the delivery firm Sagawa Kyubin, whose payments to politicians caused a corruption scandal from 1992 that helped bring down the ruling Liberal Democratic Party. Using $200 million in loans from Nomura and Nikko Securities, Japan's leading brokers, he bought 27 million shares in Tokyu Corporation and made a profit of almost $2 billion. When his links to the brokers became public, Nikko's president and Nomura's chairman and president resigned. Ishii died in 1991.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Susumu Ishii' and 'Sagawa Express' (citing The Independent, 1993; New York Times, 1994)

n: Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank lent ¥30bn to corporate racketeers
d: Sokaiya, corporate racketeers often tied to the yakuza who extort companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings, got money out of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, then one of Japan's largest banks. The bank's loans to sokaiya, granted during the late-1980s bubble, amounted to ¥30 billion. Tokyo prosecutors raided the bank in 1997, and its former president and chairman, Kuniji Miyazaki, hanged himself at home that year. In a separate case three top executives of Nomura Securities pleaded guilty to payments to a sokaiya who held enough Nomura shares to propose his own choice for the board. Japanese law bans benefits given for statements or votes at shareholder meetings.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank' and 'Sōkaiya'

n: Gang leader Lo Fu-chu co-chaired Taiwan's legislative judiciary committee
d: A self-described gang leader sat in Taiwan's parliament and helped run the committee that oversees the justice system. Lo Fu-chu called himself a leader of the Celestial Alliance, formed in the mid-1980s by mob bosses jailed together. He was an independent member of the Legislative Yuan from 1996 to 2002, leading an 11-member bloc. He joined its judicial committee in 1998 and became one of its three co-chairs in 2000, which drew wide protest; Justice Minister Liao Cheng-hao reportedly refused to attend while Lo sat on it. This was the period of 'black gold' politics, when a 1994–95 campaign led to 320 local councillors being prosecuted. Lo was convicted of stock manipulation in 2013.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lo Fu-chu' and 'Black gold (politics)'

n: Afghan counter-narcotics chief Daud accused of protecting smugglers
d: The official in charge of fighting Afghanistan's drug trade was accused of working for it. General Mohammad Daud Daud, a former commander under Ahmad Shah Massoud, became Afghanistan's Deputy Minister of Interior for Counter-narcotics and head of its Counter Narcotics Police. A 2009 Globe and Mail report and two books accused him of involvement in the narcotics trade and of using his post to give smugglers safe passage. His campaigns were also credited with cutting poppy cultivation in some provinces. He was never charged. Daud was killed in a bombing in Taloqan on 28 May 2011, claimed by the Taliban.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mohammad Daud Daud' (citing The Globe and Mail, 2009)

n: Heroin trade founder Ayub Afridi sat in Pakistan's National Assembly
d: A drug trafficker described as a primary founder of the Afghan heroin trade won a seat in Pakistan's parliament. Ayub Afridi smuggled gold and contraband, then moved weapons to the Afghan mujahideen and opium to laboratories in Pakistan's tribal areas. He won a National Assembly seat for Khyber Agency in 1990 as an independent and served until 1993. In December 1995 he was arrested in Pakistan over hashish shipped to Belgium, served about three and a half years in a US prison and paid a $50,000 fine, then was returned to Pakistan in 1999. A Pakistani court gave him seven years, but he was freed after a few weeks. He died in 2009.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ayub Afridi (drug lord)'

n: Brothels and casinos paid Queensland's police commissioner $700,000
who: Brothel, SP bookmaker and casino operators
d: Operators of brothels, illegal casinos and off-course 'SP' bookmakers paid Queensland's top police officer to protect them. The Fitzgerald Inquiry (1987–89) found long-term police and political corruption; detective Jack Herbert, the 'bagman' who collected bribes for Commissioner Terry Lewis from 1980, became its key witness. A jury found Lewis, commissioner from 1976 to 1987, had accepted bribes totalling $700,000 to protect these businesses and to block legal poker machines. He was sentenced to 14 years and stripped of his knighthood in 1993. Premier Joh Bjelke-Petersen resigned, ministers were jailed, and the inquiry led to the Criminal Justice Commission, a standing anti-corruption body.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Fitzgerald Inquiry' and 'Terry Lewis (police officer)' (citing Fitzgerald report, 1989)

n: Drug dealers paid Sydney's Kings Cross detectives, royal commission finds
rank: NSW Police Kings Cross detectives and Drug Squad
d: Drug traffickers in Sydney's Kings Cross paid regular cash to the detectives meant to police them. The Wood Royal Commission (1994–97) examined whether corruption in the New South Wales Police was 'systemic and entrenched'. Detective Trevor Haken, who collected payments from dealers including Bill Bayeh, agreed to work for the commission; recordings from his car contradicted detectives' sworn denials in 1995. The commission found hundreds of cases of bribery, drug dealing and evidence tampering in the Kings Cross detective division, and specialist units including the Drug Squad were implicated. Hundreds of officers were forced out, the police commissioner resigned, and its staff formed the Police Integrity Commission.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Wood Royal Commission' (citing the Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service final report, 1997)

n: NSW Premier Askin alleged to take weekly payoffs from Abe Saffron
org_label: Abe Saffron and Sydney crime syndicates
rank: Premier of New South Wales and police commissioner
d: Sydney's organised crime figures were alleged to have paid the premier of New South Wales and his police commissioner. After Sir Robert Askin, premier from 1965 to 1975, died in 1981, the National Times ran 'Askin: friend of organised crime', and David Hickie's book The Prince and the Premier alleged long-running payoffs, with Police Commissioner Norman Allan assisting. The Australian Taxation Office found that much of Askin's estate came from undisclosed income. In 2008 Alan Saffron, son of the crime boss Abe Saffron, wrote that his father paid Askin and Allan A$5,000 to $10,000 a week for years for illegal liquor, prostitution and gambling. None of this was tested in court.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Robert Askin' (citing National Times, 1981; Hickie; Alan Saffron, 2008)

n: Vohra report: crime syndicates ran a 'parallel government' in India
d: An official Indian report found crime syndicates had got inside politics and the civil service. After the March 1993 Bombay bombings, the government asked former Home Secretary N. N. Vohra to examine the links between criminals, politicians and officials, starting from intelligence on Dawood Ibrahim's gang. His October 1993 report said criminal networks were 'virtually running a parallel government', protected by politicians of all parties and by officials, with criminals elected to local bodies, state assemblies and Parliament. It said agencies kept such information to themselves and recommended a single point to collect it. Its annexes were never published; in 1997 the Supreme Court recommended a high-level committee to pursue prosecutions.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Vohra Report'

n: Customs and police bribed to land RDX for the 1993 Bombay bombings
rank: Customs and police officers, Raigad coast
d: Smugglers working for Dawood Ibrahim's crime syndicate, D-Company, paid customs and police officers to let about 3,000 kg of RDX explosive and weapons land at Shekhadi on the Raigad coast in February 1993. The explosives were used in the Bombay bombings of 12 March 1993. A special anti-terror (TADA) court convicted the officials in 2006–07: assistant customs commissioner R. K. Singh took over ₹780,000 and got nine years; customs superintendents and an inspector got seven to eight years; police sub-inspector Vijay Patil got life; and four constables got six years. Senior customs officer S. N. Thapa was also given life. Dawood Ibrahim and Tiger Memon have never been tried.
cite: Wikipedia, '1993 Bombay bombings' (citing TADA court verdicts, 2006–07)

n: Gangster Atiq Ahmed won five assembly terms and a Lok Sabha seat
d: A gang leader facing more than 160 criminal cases held elected office in Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, for most of 15 years. Atiq Ahmed of Prayagraj (Allahabad), known for extortion, kidnapping and murder, won the Allahabad West seat in the state assembly in 1989, 1991, 1993, 1996 and 2002, and was elected to the national parliament, the Lok Sabha, from Phulpur in 2004. He was convicted of kidnapping Umesh Pal, a witness in the 2005 murder of the legislator Raju Pal. On 15 April 2023, while in police custody in Prayagraj, he and his brother were shot dead on live television by men posing as journalists.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Atiq Ahmed'

n: Gangster Mohammad Shahabuddin held Siwan's Lok Sabha seat for 13 years
d: A gangster from Siwan in Bihar was elected to India's parliament four times. Mohammad Shahabuddin, a close aide of the Rashtriya Janata Dal leader Lalu Prasad Yadav, won the Ziradei seat in the Bihar assembly in 1990 and 1995 and represented Siwan in the Lok Sabha from 1996 to 2009. In 2005 it emerged he had declared 19 pending criminal cases when 34 were pending. He was sentenced to ten years for the 1996 attempted murder of Siwan's police superintendent, to life in 2007 for kidnapping a CPI-ML party worker, and to life in 2015 for a 2004 double murder. He died of COVID-19 in 2021.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mohammad Shahabuddin (Indian politician)'

n: Nepali minister Mirza Dilshad Beg tied to Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company
d: A member of Nepal's parliament who held ministerial posts was reported to work with Dawood Ibrahim's Indian crime syndicate, D-Company. Mirza Dilshad Beg, born in India, was elected from Kapilvastu in 1994, held posts in two governments and won two terms for the Rastriya Prajatantra Party. Reports linked him to D-Company and its lieutenant Chhota Shakeel, and to Pakistan's ISI intelligence agency, with activities including gun-running, drug trafficking, document forgery and sheltering fugitives. He was shot dead in Kathmandu on 29 June 1998; the rival gangster Chhota Rajan claimed the killing in an India Today interview, saying Beg was spreading terror in India for the ISI.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mirza Dilshad Beg' (citing India Today, 1998)

n: Ghanaian MP Eric Amoateng jailed in US for 136 lb heroin shipment
d: A sitting member of Ghana's parliament was part of a heroin smuggling operation into the United States. Eric Amoateng of the then-ruling New Patriotic Party took his seat for Nkoranza North in January 2005. On 12 November 2005 he was arrested in the US with an associate after seven boxes of pottery were found to contain 136 pounds of heroin, worth about US$6 million on the street. He pleaded guilty on 19 March 2007, resigned his seat, and on 12 December 2007 was sentenced to ten years in jail. The case was one of several in which West African drug networks were found to reach elected officials.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Eric Amoateng' (citing US court records and Ghanaian parliament)

n: Senator Buruji Kashamu sat in Nigeria's Senate while wanted by the US
d: A man the United States sought on drug charges became a senator and party chief in Nigeria. Buruji Kashamu was arrested in the UK in 1998 on drug-related charges; British authorities refused a US extradition request because a co-conspirator failed to identify him in a photo line-up. Back in Nigeria he became a People's Democratic Party leader in Ogun State and chaired its organising committee for the South West. He won the Ogun East Senate seat in 2015 with 99,540 votes and served until 2019. He was the PDP's candidate for Ogun governor in 2019. He died of COVID-19 in August 2020.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Buruji Kashamu'

n: Alleged crime leader Rysbek Akmatbayev elected to Kyrgyz parliament
d: A man described as a criminal leader won a seat in Kyrgyzstan's parliament and used it to challenge the government. Rysbek Akmatbayev had faced criminal charges, including murder, under President Askar Akayev. After Akayev's fall he was elected to parliament in April 2006 amid a power struggle in which several politicians, including his brother Tynychbek, were killed. He then led nationwide protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Felix Kulov. He was shot dead outside a mosque in Bishkek in May 2006, weeks after entering parliament.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Rysbek Akmatbayev'

n: Tajikistan's drug agency chief Mirzoyev jailed, drug ties alleged
rank: Head of the Drug Control Agency
d: The head of Tajikistan's Drug Control Agency, on the main route for Afghan heroin north, was charged with drug trafficking. General Ghaffor Mirzoyev had commanded the Presidential Guard from 1995 and later ran the drug agency. He was arrested in August 2004 with 15 supporters and charged with abuse of power, seizing state property and drug trafficking; about 3,000 weapons were found in Drug Control Agency stores. He was sentenced to life and stripped of his rank. Many said the arrests were political, while critics who accepted he was a corrupt official also said he had links to the narcotics trade.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ghaffor Mirzoyev'

n: Heroin baron Lo Hsing Han became the Myanmar junta's builder
who: Lo Hsing Han and Asia World
rank: Junta's ceasefire broker and state contractor
d: A heroin trafficker from Kokang became one of the Myanmar military government's main business partners. Lo Hsing Han was a leading 'China white' heroin dealer in the early 1970s. After 1989 the military intelligence chief Khin Nyunt used him to broker ceasefires with ethnic armies, and in return he received business openings and unofficial permission to run drugs; 17 new heroin refineries appeared within a year. His Asia World Company, founded in June 1992 and run by his son Steven Law, won contracts for roads, seaports and other infrastructure. In February 2008 the US sanctioned Lo, his son and companies they controlled as junta cronies. Lo died in 2013.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Lo Hsing Han' (citing The Irrawaddy and US Treasury, 2008)

n: Opium warlord Khun Sa traded his army for Yangon protection and business
d: Myanmar's military rulers made a secret deal with the region's best-known opium warlord, Khun Sa, who was under US indictment. By 1996 they agreed that if he surrendered his Mong Tai Army he would receive government protection and would not be extradited. He surrendered on 5 January 1996 and moved to Yangon with a large fortune. A US federal grand jury had indicted him on drug trafficking charges in January 1990 and the US had put a $2 million bounty on him. In Yangon he became a businessman with investments in Yangon, Mandalay and Taunggyi, a ruby mine and a Yangon–Mandalay highway, under military intelligence watch, until he died in 2007.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Khun Sa'

n: Fugitive Djoko Tjandra bribed police generals and a prosecutor
rank: Police generals and a state prosecutor
d: A fugitive tycoon paid Indonesian police generals and a prosecutor to help him escape a prison sentence. Djoko Tjandra fled in 2009, the day before the Supreme Court gave him two years over the Bank Bali scandal. In 2020, through the businessman Tommy Sumardi, he paid police Inspector General Napoleon Bonaparte and Brigadier General Prasetijo Utomo to remove his Interpol Red Notice and issue a travel letter that let him fly inside Indonesia. Prosecutor Pinangki Sirna Malasari took $500,000 for a plan to obtain a Supreme Court ruling clearing him. In 2021 Napoleon got 4.5 years, Prasetijo 3.5 years, Pinangki 10 years and Tjandra 4.5 years for bribery.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Djoko Tjandra' (citing Jakarta court verdicts, 2020–21)

n: Illegal jueteng gambling bosses paid President Estrada ₱5m a month
