d: Operators of jueteng, an illegal numbers game run across the Philippines, were accused of paying the country's president for protection. In October 2000 Luis 'Chavit' Singson, governor of Ilocos Sur, alleged that President Joseph Estrada received 5 million pesos a month in jueteng protection money and that Singson had given him 400 million pesos in gambling profits. On 13 November 2000, 115 members of the House signed an impeachment complaint. The Senate trial collapsed in January 2001, mass protests followed, the armed forces withdrew support and Gloria Macapagal Arroyo was sworn in on 20 January 2001. Estrada was later convicted of plunder in 2007 and pardoned weeks later.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Impeachment of Joseph Estrada' and 'Joseph Estrada'

n: Kuratong Baleleng-linked Parojinog family ran Ozamiz City Hall
rank: Mayor, vice-mayor and councillors of Ozamiz
d: A family linked by a senator to a crime syndicate held the main elected offices of Ozamiz, a city in Mindanao. Senator Panfilo Lacson said the father of Mayor Reynaldo Parojinog Sr. founded Kuratong Baleleng, a Mindanao organised-crime group. In August 2016 President Rodrigo Duterte named the mayor as involved in the drug trade, which he denied. On 30 July 2017 police raided the family's homes; 15 people died, including the mayor, his wife and a provincial board member. Vice-Mayor Nova Princess Parojinog-Echavez was arrested, and police said they found shabu (methamphetamine) and rifles. The family said police planted evidence, and the Commission on Human Rights investigated.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Reynaldo Parojinog' (citing Philippine press, 2017)

n: Zimbabwe's envoy Uebert Angel filmed offering gold-laundering route
d: An Al Jazeera investigation alleged that criminal money-launderers had Zimbabwe's own presidential envoy on their side. In March 2021 President Emmerson Mnangagwa appointed the preacher Uebert Angel as ambassador-at-large and presidential envoy to seek trade and investment. In 'Gold Mafia', broadcast in March 2023, undercover reporters posing as clients recorded Angel apparently offering to use his diplomatic status to bring illicit cash into Zimbabwe, swap it for mined gold and sell the gold abroad as clean money, saying 'gold we can do it right now'. Zimbabwe's Financial Intelligence Unit said in March 2023 that it found no evidence to support the claims.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Uebert Angel' (citing Al Jazeera Investigative Unit, March 2023)

n: Czech fugitive Krejčíř allegedly bought a judge and South African warders
d: Radovan Krejčíř, a Czech organised-crime figure, was accused of buying his way through two countries' justice systems. In 2005 he escaped during a police raid on his villa near Prague, an escape that led Czech Police President Jiří Kolář to resign. He moved to South Africa in 2007. The Czech Republic said South Africa refused his extradition because he had bribed the judge involved. Convicted in Johannesburg of attempted murder and kidnapping, he was sentenced to 35 years in February 2016. A September 2015 cell raid found weapons, and reports said R246 million was available for an escape plan that included R1.5 million paid to three prison warders.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Radovan Krejčíř'

n: Gang case Charl Kinnear was probing reached eight senior police officers
rank: SAPS senior officers and Crime Intelligence
d: Lieutenant Colonel Charl Kinnear, a Western Cape anti-gang detective, was investigating a gun racketeering case that tied the alleged crime boss Nafiz Modack to eight high-ranking officers of the South African Police Service. Kinnear was shot dead outside his Cape Town home on 18 September 2020. The man arrested had allegedly tracked his phone 2,116 times. Modack and two others were charged with the murder in 2021. The police oversight body IPID described a 'rogue unit' in Western Cape Crime Intelligence, and laid charges against National Police Commissioner Khehla Sitole for refusing to cooperate. Police guarding Kinnear's home had been withdrawn in December 2019 after an earlier grenade attempt.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Charl Kinnear' (citing IPID reports and South African press)

n: Triad boss 'Broken Tooth' Wan Kuok-koi chaired a Malaysian listed firm
d: Wan Kuok-koi, former leader of the Macau branch of the 14K triad (a Chinese crime society), got himself appointed chairman of a Malaysian listed company. Convicted in Macau in 1999 and released in 2012, Wan launched the World Hongmen History and Culture Association in Cambodia in 2018 with the Cambodian government's support, and in 2020 became chairman of Inix Technology Bhd. In December 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned him under the Global Magnitsky Act, along with his Dongmei Group and the Hongmen association, which it called a 14K front. Malaysian police later linked him to Nicky Liow, a businessman charged with money laundering. His Saixigang development on the Myanmar border became a base for scams.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Wan Kuok-koi' (citing US Treasury, Dec 2020)

n: Executed trafficker Freddy Budiman said he paid Indonesian drug agencies
rank: Police, BNN drug agency and customs
d: An Indonesian drug trafficker on death row claimed he had worked with the agencies meant to stop him. Freddy Budiman was sentenced to death in 2012 for importing 1.4 million ecstasy pills from China, and from prison he reportedly ran a dealer network and made his own drugs, while getting preferential treatment. In 2014 he told the human rights lawyer Haris Azhar that he had asked the police, the National Narcotics Agency (BNN) and the customs directorate to bring drugs into Indonesia for him. Azhar published the account shortly before Budiman was executed on Nusa Kambangan on 29 July 2016. The claims were not tested in court.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Freddy Budiman' (citing Haris Azhar/KontraS statement, July 2016)

n: Countrywide gave cut-price 'VIP' mortgages to US lawmakers and officials
rank: Senators, House members, Fannie Mae and agency staff
d: Countrywide Financial, then the largest US mortgage lender, gave hundreds of discounted 'VIP' home loans to members of Congress, their staff and other government employees, including staff of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the state-backed firms that bought its loans. A three-year investigation by the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, led by Darrell Issa, reported on 5 July 2012 that the programme was used to buy influence in Washington and to protect Countrywide's special arrangement with Fannie Mae, which gave it fee discounts. Recipients named included Senators Christopher Dodd and Kent Conrad and four House members. Countrywide's chief, Angelo Mozilo, called it another channel to compete for loans.
cite: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, 'How Countrywide used its VIP loan program to influence Washington policymakers' (5 July 2012); CNNMoney (5 July 2012)

n: Citigroup's lobbyists wrote most of a House bill on bank derivatives
d: Citigroup, one of the largest US banks, drafted much of a bill passed by the House Financial Services Committee in 2013 to weaken a rule it opposed. The 'push-out' rule in the Dodd-Frank Act, passed after the 2008 crash, required banks to move certain risky derivatives trades out of units backed by federal deposit insurance. On 23 May 2013 the New York Times reported that Citigroup's recommendations appeared in more than 70 lines of the committee's 85-line Swaps Regulatory Improvement Act (H.R. 992). The committee approved the bill 53 to 6. It would have let banks keep a wider range of derivatives in their insured arms.
cite: New York Times (23 May 2013), as reported by Mother Jones (24 May 2013); NPR, 'When lobbyists literally write the bill' (11 November 2013)

n: Goldman director chaired the New York Fed and bought Goldman shares
rank: Chairman, Federal Reserve Bank of New York
d: Stephen Friedman, a former Goldman Sachs chairman who still sat on its board, chaired the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the arm of the US central bank that supervises Wall Street, from January 2008. When Goldman became a bank holding company in September 2008 it came under the New York Fed's supervision, which made his board seat a breach of Fed policy. He was given a waiver that was not made public, and the Government Accountability Office later found he kept buying Goldman stock between November 2008 and January 2009 without the Fed's knowledge. Rolling Stone put the purchase at 52,000 shares. He resigned on 7 May 2009, saying the Fed did not need the distraction.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Stephen Friedman (economist)'; Sen. Bernie Sanders press release on GAO report GAO-12-18 (19 October 2011); UPI (8 May 2009)

n: JPMorgan's chief sat on the New York Fed board as it rescued his bank's deals
rank: Board of directors, Federal Reserve Bank of New York
d: Jamie Dimon, chief executive of JPMorgan Chase, sat on the board of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York while the Fed gave his bank emergency help during the 2008 crisis. Regional Fed banks are partly governed by directors drawn from the banks they oversee. A Government Accountability Office audit released on 19 October 2011 found at least 18 current and former Fed directors were tied to banks and firms that received emergency Fed loans. JPMorgan received $29 billion in financing to take over Bear Stearns in 2008, acted as a clearing bank for Fed lending programmes, and was given an 18-month exemption from risk-based capital rules. The audit called for tighter conflict-of-interest rules for Fed directors.
cite: US Government Accountability Office, GAO-12-18 (19 October 2011), summarised in Sen. Bernie Sanders press release; ABC News (October 2011)

n: J.P. Morgan's 'preferred list' sold cheap shares to Coolidge and a justice
d: J.P. Morgan & Co., then the most powerful US private bank, kept a 'preferred list' of influential friends who were offered newly issued shares at prices well below what the public paid. Senate hearings led by counsel Ferdinand Pecora in 1933 revealed that the list included former President Calvin Coolidge and Supreme Court Justice Owen Roberts. The hearings also showed J.P. Morgan himself had paid no income tax from 1930 to 1932. The practice was legal, but the revelations fed public pressure for the Glass-Steagall Act, which separated deposit banking from securities dealing, and the Securities Acts of 1933 and 1934.
cite: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Man Who Busted the Banksters'; Wikipedia, 'Ferdinand Pecora'; US Senate Banking Committee, Stock Exchange Practices hearings (1933)

n: Banker Andrew Mellon ran the US Treasury while keeping his company shares
d: Andrew Mellon, head of Pittsburgh's Mellon National Bank and Union Trust Company and a backer of Alcoa and Gulf Oil, served as US Treasury Secretary from March 1921 to February 1932 under three presidents. He pushed tax cuts on top incomes, and the Revenue Act of 1926 cut the top rate to 25 percent. On 6 January 1932 Congressman Wright Patman began impeachment proceedings, charging that Mellon broke federal conflict-of-interest laws by keeping non-banking shares while in office. Before the case went further, President Hoover moved Mellon to the post of ambassador to the United Kingdom.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Andrew Mellon'; Bloomberg Opinion, Justin Fox (27 January 2017); Federal Reserve History, 'Andrew W. Mellon'

n: Payday-lender donor Mulvaney ran the US consumer finance watchdog
rank: Acting Director, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
d: Mick Mulvaney, who received nearly $63,000 from payday lenders for his congressional campaigns, was named acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the US agency that polices lenders, in November 2017. At the bureau he froze new investigations, slowed existing ones and scaled back enforcement against payday, car-loan and other lenders. In April 2018 he told about 1,300 bankers at an American Bankers Association conference that as a congressman he had met lobbyists who gave him money and mostly not those who did not. Senator Elizabeth Warren asked for an ethics inquiry into whether donations shaped CFPB decisions.
cite: CNBC (24 April 2018); Office of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, letter to Mulvaney (27 April 2018)

n: Japan's banks paid Finance Ministry inspectors for advance tip-offs
org_label: Sanwa Bank, Asahi Bank affiliate and other banks
d: Japanese banks entertained and paid Ministry of Finance bank inspectors in return for advance notice of inspections. On 26 January 1998 Tokyo prosecutors arrested Koichi Miyagawa, chief of the ministry's finance inspection office, and his colleague Toshimi Taniuchi. Miyagawa allegedly took ¥1,804,838 in bribes from an Asahi Bank affiliate plus a ¥4.4 million discount on a flat; Taniuchi allegedly took ¥1.61 million in meals and golf from Sanwa Bank. In return they told banks the dates of inspections and which branches would be checked. Prosecutors raided the ministry and several banks, and Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka resigned two days later.
cite: Japan Times (26, 27 and 28 January 1998); Spokesman-Review (28 January 1998)

n: Latvian bank's owners bribed central bank chief and ECB member
rank: Governor, Bank of Latvia; ECB Governing Council
d: Shareholders of Trasta Komercbanka, a Riga bank, paid Ilmārs Rimšēvičs, governor of the Bank of Latvia and a member of the European Central Bank's Governing Council, for help with Latvia's financial regulator. In 2010 a shareholder offered him a paid fishing trip to Kamchatka; in 2012 two shareholders approached him again and he asked for €500,000, of which €250,000 was paid. Bank representatives later went to Latvia's anti-corruption bureau, which detained Rimšēvičs in February 2018. On 20 December 2023 the Riga District Court sentenced him to six years in prison and confiscated property; businessman Māris Martinsons, the go-between, got five years.
cite: LSM, 'Former Latvian central bank governor Rimšēvičs sentenced to 6 years in prison' (20 December 2023); Baltic Times (December 2023)

n: Banker Ilan Shor paid Moldova's ex-PM Filat to let him take a state bank
rank: Former Prime Minister; government decision on Banca de Economii
d: Ilan Shor, a businessman named by investigators as the main figure in Moldova's $1 billion bank fraud, testified that he paid former prime minister Vlad Filat $250 million. About $190 million was for the government not to use its pre-emptive rights in Banca de Economii, the state-controlled savings bank, which let Shor's investors take control of it. The $1 billion vanished from Banca de Economii, Unibank and Banca Socială in 2014, a loss equal to about 12 percent of Moldova's GDP. On 27 June 2016 a Chișinău court sentenced Filat to nine years for corruption and abuse of office. The central bank governor resigned in 2015 saying politicians had interfered in the inquiry.
cite: bne IntelliNews, 'Moldovan ex-premier Filat jailed for 9 years in $1bn bank fraud case' (June 2016); Wikipedia, '2014 Moldovan bank fraud scandal'

n: Tycoon Truong My Lan paid Vietnam's bank inspection chief $5.2m
rank: Head of inspection and supervision, State Bank of Vietnam
d: Truong My Lan, chair of the property group Van Thinh Phat, paid the head of the State Bank of Vietnam's inspection and supervision department to protect Saigon Commercial Bank (SCB), which Lan secretly controlled. The State Bank is Vietnam's central bank and banking supervisor. Do Thi Nhan received $5.2 million through an intermediary after meeting Lan, then told her inspection team to adjust data and keep SCB off the list of banks under special monitoring, though she knew its condition. On 11 April 2024 a court sentenced Nhan to life in prison and Lan to death, alongside about 85 other defendants.
cite: The Investor (Vietnam), 'Former State Bank of Vietnam inspection chief receives life sentence in Van Thinh Phat scandal' (11 April 2024); RFA (11 April 2024)

n: Financier Xiao Jianhua paid Chinese officials to evade financial supervision
d: Xiao Jianhua, a Chinese-Canadian billionaire, and his conglomerate Tomorrow Holdings, which owned banks, insurers and brokerages, gave Chinese officials shares, property, cash and other assets worth more than 680 million yuan (about $100 million) between 2001 and 2021. A Shanghai court said on 19 August 2022 that the payments were meant to 'evade financial supervision and seek illegitimate interests'. Xiao was convicted of bribery, illegally taking public deposits and misusing entrusted funds, and sentenced to 13 years; Tomorrow Holdings was fined a record 55.03 billion yuan ($8.1 billion). Xiao had not been seen in public since 2017, and in July 2020 regulators seized nine of the group's financial institutions.
cite: Al Jazeera / Reuters (19 August 2022); NBC News (19 August 2022)

n: Goldman bankers bribed Malaysian and Abu Dhabi officials for 1MDB bonds
rank: Officials of Malaysia's 1MDB fund and Abu Dhabi state funds
d: Goldman Sachs bankers paid bribes to officials in Malaysia and Abu Dhabi to win the bond business of 1MDB, a Malaysian state investment fund. Between 2011 and 2013 Goldman sold about $6.5 billion of 1MDB bonds and earned about $600 million in fees, around ten times the normal rate; billions were then stolen from the fund. Tim Leissner, Goldman's Southeast Asia chairman, pleaded guilty in 2018 to paying the bribes and was sentenced to two years in May 2025. His deputy Roger Ng was convicted in 2022. In October 2020 Goldman agreed to pay $2.9 billion to authorities in the US, Malaysia, Singapore and the UK, and its Malaysian arm pleaded guilty.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Goldman Sachs' and 'Tim Leissner'; US Department of Justice (October 2020); Wikipedia, '1MDB scandal'

n: National City Bank took Haiti's gold, central bank and finances for decades
who: National City Bank of New York
rank: Haiti's national bank and public finances
d: National City Bank of New York, forerunner of Citigroup, took control of Haiti's national bank and, with US troops, of its public finances. It bought into the bank from 1910 and owned all its shares by 1920. Its lobbyist Roger Farnham pressed Washington to intervene, and in December 1914 eight US Marines removed $500,000 in gold from the bank to a Wall Street vault. US forces occupied Haiti from 1915 for 19 years. A 1922 New York loan, approved by a president the US installed, came with US management of Haiti's finances until repaid; over a decade about a quarter of revenue went on debts held by National City and an affiliate. US financial control lasted until 1947.
cite: New York Times, 'Invade Haiti, Wall Street urged. The U.S. obliged.' ('The Ransom' series, 2022), republished by bdnews24

n: European bondholders took over Ottoman tax collection
d: European holders of Ottoman government bonds, chiefly British and French, got their own body placed inside the Ottoman state to collect its revenue. The Ottoman Empire had stopped paying its foreign debt, and the Decree of Muharrem of 15 October 1881 created the Ottoman Public Debt Administration. Bondholders from Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Austria and the Netherlands, along with Ottoman bondholders, were represented on it, and it was given special rights to collect various taxes and customs duties inside the empire to pay creditors. It turned part of the empire's tax system into an agency run for foreign lenders.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ottoman public debt'; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Decree of Muharrem'

n: Creditor powers placed commissioners over Egypt's debt payments
d: Egypt's European creditors placed their own commissioners over its finances through the Caisse de la Dette Publique (Public Debt Fund), set up by a decree of Khedive Isma'il on 2 May 1876 after Egypt fell behind on its loans. The commissioners represented Austria-Hungary, France and Italy, joined by Britain in 1877 and Russia and Germany in 1885. Its work covered collecting debt payments, how taxes were raised and what Egypt could afford to pay. Alongside it France and Britain ran 'dual control' of Egypt's finances until Britain occupied the country alone in 1882. The Caisse lasted about 64 years, until an Anglo-Egyptian agreement abolished it on 17 July 1940.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Caisse de la Dette Publique'

n: Six creditor powers' commission ran Greek tax revenue for 38 years
d: Greece's creditor states placed a six-member International Financial Commission inside the Greek state to take its revenues and repay loans. Greece had declared bankruptcy in 1893 and then lost the 1897 war with the Ottoman Empire, which required reparations and a new loan of 151.3 million francs. Law 2519 of 23 February 1898 gave the commission, representing Britain, France, Austria-Hungary, Germany, Russia and Italy, control of the salt, oil, match, playing-card, cigarette-paper and Naxos emery monopolies, the tobacco tax, stamp duties and Piraeus port duties. It also assessed state agencies' tax collection. It stayed in Athens until 1936 and in the 1920s handled League of Nations lending.
cite: Wikipedia, 'International Financial Commission'

n: Peru's bondholders took its railways and guano under the Grace Contract
d: Holders of Peru's defaulted government bonds, organised in the London-based Peruvian Corporation, took control of Peru's main state assets. Under the Grace Contract, drafted in 1886 and ratified in 1890, the corporation took over the bonds in exchange for its own shares and received the use of Peru's state railways, mainly the Southern and Central Railways, for 66 years, plus up to 2 million tons of guano from certain islands. Peru also agreed to pay it 33 annual payments of $400,000. A 1907 change extended the railway leases to run until 1973 and cut the payments to 30.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Peruvian Corporation'

n: Dawes Plan put creditor nominees on half the Reichsbank's board
org_label: Allied creditor states and Wall Street lenders (Dawes Plan)
d: Under the Dawes Plan, Germany's First World War creditors placed their own representatives inside its central bank and railway to secure reparation payments. Germany had been declared in default in January 1923. The Reichstag passed the plan on 29 August 1924 and it took effect on 1 September. The Reichsbank was reorganised under creditor supervision and made independent of the German government, with a board of seven creditor-state representatives and seven Germans, and the national railway became a corporation under creditor supervision. Germany received an 800 million Reichsmark loan as the central bank's capital, about half raised through Wall Street bond issues. The Young Plan replaced it in 1929.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Dawes Plan'

n: New York bankers took Nicaragua's national bank, railway and customs
rank: National Bank, National Railway and customs of Nicaragua
d: New York bankers, backed by the US government, took control of Nicaragua's main financial institutions in exchange for loans. Around the 1911 Knox-Castillo proposal they lent $15 million and later advanced another $1.5 million, took Nicaragua's National Bank as collateral and gained a 51 percent stake in the National Railway, while President Taft appointed the collector of Nicaragua's customs. When President Adolfo Díaz faced a revolt in July 1912 and asked for help, US Marines landed in August 1912; they stayed until 1925, returned in 1926 and remained until 1935. US diplomatic records describe the loan contracts with American bankers.
cite: Historical Text Archive, 'Nicaragua and U.S. intervention'; US Office of the Historian, Foreign Relations of the United States 1913, 'Financial affairs: conclusion of a loan contract with American bankers'

n: League of Nations loan put Austria's economy under foreign supervision
d: In October 1922 Austria accepted a League of Nations loan of 650 million gold Kronen, guaranteed by Britain, France, Italy and Czechoslovakia, on condition that the League oversee its economy. Chancellor Ignaz Seipel also promised that Austria would not seek union with Germany for 20 years. The League's supervision of Austrian finances lasted until March 1926, and in the two years after the loan the state budget was brought into balance.
cite: Wikipedia, 'First Austrian Republic'

n: IMF and World Bank placed foreign co-signers inside Liberia's state firms
d: Under the Governance and Economic Management Assistance Program (GEMAP), launched in September 2005, foreign financial controllers were placed inside Liberia's main state enterprises with power to co-sign their major transactions. The programme was designed and funded by the IMF, the World Bank, the US Treasury and USAID, and agreed between Liberia's government and an international contact group, after a 2005 European Commission audit of the central bank and five state firms. Non-Liberian controllers sat in the National Port Authority, the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company, Roberts International Airport and the Forestry Development Authority. Signing authority returned to the Liberian government in October 2009.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Governance and Economic Management Assistance Program'

n: Jakob Fugger's money bought Charles V's election as emperor
rank: Prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire
d: Jakob Fugger, an Augsburg banker, financed the payments that made Charles of Habsburg Holy Roman Emperor. More than 850,000 guilders went to the prince-electors, the seven rulers who chose the emperor; Fugger supplied about 550,000, the Welser house about 150,000 and Italian bankers the rest. The rival, Francis I of France, had offered 300,000. Charles was elected unanimously on 28 July 1519. By 1521 he owed Fugger more than 600,000 guilders and repaid part by giving his firm the silver and copper mines of Tyrol, and in 1523 a quicksilver concession at Almadén. At the 1523 Imperial Diet Fugger reminded Charles that he could not have won the crown without Fugger's help.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jakob Fugger'

n: Banca Romana's secret loans to Italian politicians toppled Giolitti
d: Banca Romana, one of Italy's note-issuing banks, lent money, often interest-free, to politicians for their election campaigns and to newspapers, in return for favours. Under its governor Bernardo Tanlongo it had 135 million lire in notes in circulation against a legal limit of 75 million, and had printed another 40 million in duplicate-numbered notes. The bank failed in January 1893. Documents implicated Prime Minister Giovanni Giolitti, who had tried to make Tanlongo a senator, which would have given him immunity, and former premier Francesco Crispi. Giolitti resigned on 24 November 1893. Tanlongo was acquitted in 1894, but the scandal led to the founding of the Bank of Italy.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Banca Romana scandal'

n: Second Bank of the United States paid and lent to members of Congress
who: Second Bank of the United States
d: The Second Bank of the United States, a privately run national bank headed by Nicholas Biddle, used loans and retainer fees to win support in Congress for renewing its charter. Senator Daniel Webster reportedly received an annual fee for defending the bank. Senator George Poindexter of Mississippi received a $10,000 loan after backing renewal, and another $8,000 while the first was unpaid, in breach of the bank's charter. The bank also gave money to Henry Clay and to pro-bank newspaper editors before the 1832 election. Congress passed the renewal, but President Andrew Jackson vetoed it on 10 July 1832 and in 1833 removed federal deposits from the bank.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bank War'

n: Panama Canal financiers paid off French deputies and a minister
d: The French Panama Canal Company, through the financiers Jacques de Reinach and Cornelius Herz, paid bribes to members of parliament and a minister to get approval to raise money from the public. Ferdinand de Lesseps was accused of paying bribes in 1888 to permit a stock issue; Reinach handled right-wing deputies and Herz the radicals. When the company collapsed, about 800,000 French investors lost around 1.8 billion gold francs. Before his death in 1892 Reinach gave a list of bribed deputies to the newspaper La Libre Parole, and inquiries found 104 legislators involved. Former minister Charles Baïhaut was sentenced to five years; most others were acquitted.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Panama scandals'

n: Financier Stavisky's protection reached France's prime minister
d: Alexandre Stavisky, a financier who sold worthless bonds tied to the municipal pawnshop of Bayonne, had protection from people in the French state. His fraud trial, opened in 1927, was postponed again and again, and he was granted bail 19 times. He fled in December 1933 and was found dead in Chamonix on 8 January 1934. His dealings with many officials then came to light, and Prime Minister Camille Chautemps resigned after it emerged that he had shielded Stavisky. Right-wing protests followed; on 6 February 1934 police fired on a crowd in Paris and killed 17 people, and Chautemps's successor Édouard Daladier was also forced out.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Stavisky Affair'

n: Bank of Crete owner Koskotas paid Greek ministers; two convicted
d: George Koskotas, owner of the Bank of Crete, said he paid Greek ministers and Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou in return for state money. He claimed PASOK government figures ordered state companies to deposit about $35 million in his bank, which went on bribes and media purchases, and that over $200 million missing from the bank was taken with ministers' help. On 28 September 1989 parliament indicted Papandreou and four ministers, the first indictment of a Greek prime minister. In 1992 a special court acquitted Papandreou by seven votes to six, but sentenced former finance minister Dimitris Tsovolas to two and a half years and George Petsos to ten months. Koskotas got 25 years.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Koskotas scandal'

n: Bank of Italy governor Fazio rigged a takeover for banker Fiorani
d: Antonio Fazio, governor of the Bank of Italy, Italy's central bank and bank supervisor, used his office to favour Gianpiero Fiorani's Banca Popolare Italiana in the 2005 contest to take over Banca Antonveneta, against a bid from the Dutch bank ABN AMRO. Published wiretaps of calls showed his support for the Italian bid. Fiorani was arrested on 14 December 2005; Fazio was put under investigation for insider trading two days later and resigned on 19 December, and Mario Draghi replaced him. In May 2011 an Italian court sentenced Fazio to four years in prison for market rigging in the Antonveneta takeover, and a Milan court fined him €1.5 million.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Antonio Fazio'

n: Pakistan's spy agency paid politicians through Mehran Bank in 1990
d: Pakistan's military intelligence agency, the ISI, used Mehran Bank and its owner Yunus Habib to pass money to politicians in the 1990 election to stop Benazir Bhutto winning. Payments of up to 140 million rupees were reportedly made through Habib, authorised by ISI chief Lieutenant-General Asad Durrani, in a scheme started by army chief General Mirza Aslam Beg. The officers formed the Islami Jamhoori Ittehad alliance with Nawaz Sharif as leader. Mehran Bank later collapsed and Habib was jailed for fraud in 1995. On 19 October 2012 Pakistan's Supreme Court, ruling on a petition by Air Marshal Asghar Khan, found Beg and Durrani had violated the constitution.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Asghar Khan case'

n: Golkar treasurer's firm drew $80m from Indonesia's bank rescue agency
d: Era Giat Prima, a debt-collecting firm owned by tycoon Djoko Tjandra and run by Setya Novanto, deputy treasurer of the ruling Golkar party and part of President B.J. Habibie's re-election team, used officials of the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA) to extract a fee from Bank Bali. IBRA held Bank Bali's Rp904.6 billion claim on two failed banks; its deputies approved payment on 1 June 1999 while its chairman was abroad, and the firm took Rp546 billion (about $80 million). Part went to Habibie's campaign. After the scandal broke the fee was returned, parliament rejected Habibie's accountability speech, and an IBRA deputy, Pande Lubis, was later jailed for four years.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bank Bali scandal'

n: Goldman partner Gensler steered the US law that freed derivatives
rank: Under Secretary of the Treasury for Domestic Finance
d: Gary Gensler, who spent 18 years at Goldman Sachs and became a partner there, moved into the US Treasury as Under Secretary for Domestic Finance from April 1999 to January 2001. In that post, under Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers, he campaigned for the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000, which exempted over-the-counter derivatives, privately traded financial contracts such as credit default swaps, from regulation. Such contracts were central to the 2008 crisis. Gensler later chaired the Commodity Futures Trading Commission from 2009 to 2014 and the Securities and Exchange Commission from 2021 to 2025.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Gary Gensler'

n: Goldman banker Kashkari ran the $700bn TARP bank bailout
rank: Assistant Secretary of the Treasury for Financial Stability (TARP)
d: Neel Kashkari, an investment banker at Goldman Sachs from 2002 to 2006, was named by Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson, Goldman's former chief executive, to run the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), the US government's 2008 fund for rescuing banks. As interim Assistant Secretary of the Treasury for Financial Stability from 6 October 2008 to 1 May 2009, he oversaw the programme that put public money into Wall Street banks. He was replaced by Herbert Allison in May 2009.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Neel Kashkari'

n: Goldman lobbyist Mark Patterson became the Treasury's chief of staff
rank: Chief of staff to the Treasury Secretary
d: Mark Patterson, a lobbyist for Goldman Sachs from 2004 until April 2008, became chief of staff to Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner in February 2009, weeks after Barack Obama took office. Patterson had worked on Obama's campaign and transition team, coordinating Senate confirmations. He stayed in the post until Jack Lew replaced him after Geithner's departure in 2013, then joined the law firm Perkins Coie.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Mark A. Patterson'

n: Goldman vice chairman Zoellick picked as World Bank president
d: Robert Zoellick moved from Goldman Sachs, where he was vice chairman, international, from June 2006, to the presidency of the World Bank, the international lender that funds development projects and attaches policy conditions to its loans. President George W. Bush nominated him on 30 May 2007 to replace Paul Wolfowitz, under the custom that the United States picks the bank's president. He led the World Bank from 1 July 2007 to 30 June 2012. He had earlier been a Goldman adviser from 1999 to 2001, and returned as chairman of its international advisers from 2013 to 2016.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Robert Zoellick'

n: Mnuchin's OneWest Bank chief Otting became the top US bank regulator
d: Joseph Otting, chief executive of OneWest Bank from 2010 to 2015, where he worked with its founder Steven Mnuchin, became Comptroller of the Currency, the regulator of US national banks, on 27 November 2017, while Mnuchin was Treasury Secretary. On 20 May 2020 his office finalised a rewrite of rules under the 1977 Community Reinvestment Act, which requires banks to lend in poorer neighbourhoods, broadening what counts as such lending. Community groups said it would cut lending in low-income areas. Congresswoman Maxine Waters suggested the rewrite was shaped by the reinvestment complaints OneWest faced in its merger with CIT. Otting left in May 2020.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Joseph Otting'

n: Carlyle dealmaker Quarles eased Fed oversight of mid-sized banks like SVB
rank: Vice Chair for Supervision, Federal Reserve
d: Randal Quarles, a managing director of the private equity firm Carlyle Group focused on financial-services deals, and founder of the investment firm Cynosure Group, became the Federal Reserve's first Vice Chair for Supervision, the official in charge of bank oversight, from 13 October 2017 to 13 October 2021. Under him, banks moved into the stricter large-bank oversight group only once their assets consistently averaged more than $100 billion, instead of $50 billion. The New York Times reported this delayed Silicon Valley Bank's move into tighter supervision. Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in March 2023.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Randal Quarles' (citing the New York Times)

n: Hedge fund manager Bessent at the US Treasury halted the CFPB
org_label: Soros Fund Management and Key Square Group
rank: Secretary of the Treasury; acting CFPB director
d: Scott Bessent, chief investment officer of Soros Fund Management from 2011 to 2015 and founder of the hedge fund Key Square Group in 2015 with $2 billion from George Soros, was confirmed as US Treasury Secretary on 27 January 2025. As acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in February 2025 he ordered the agency to halt all work. He backs easing the supplementary leverage ratio, a capital rule for large banks, and in August 2026 the Treasury repealed its implementation of the Corporate Transparency Act, which had required companies to disclose their real owners. He said he would cut ties with Key Square.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Scott Bessent'

n: Citigroup executive Jack Lew became US Treasury Secretary
d: Jack Lew, chief operating officer of Citigroup's Alternative Investments unit, a proprietary trading group, from June 2006, later became US Treasury Secretary, serving from 28 February 2013 to 20 January 2017. Citigroup had been rescued with $45 billion from the TARP bailout after losing $27.7 billion. At his Senate confirmation hearing Lew was questioned about more than $900,000 in bonuses he received at Citigroup. As Treasury Secretary he chaired the Financial Stability Oversight Council, which oversees risks from the largest banks.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jack Lew'; NPR (13 February 2013)

n: Goldman's António Borges led IMF Europe, then Portugal's privatisations
rank: IMF European Department director; Portugal's privatisation overseer
d: António Borges, vice chairman of Goldman Sachs International from 2000 to 2008 and afterwards a Goldman managing director and adviser, became director of the IMF's European Department in November 2010, as the IMF lent to Greece, Ireland and Portugal. A year later, in November 2011, Prime Minister Pedro Passos Coelho appointed him to oversee Portugal's privatisations, the renegotiation of public-private partnerships and the restructuring of state firms and banks. These measures were conditions of the bailout from the troika, the European Commission, European Central Bank and IMF. He moved from Goldman to the lender and then to the borrowing government carrying out its terms.
cite: Wikipedia, 'António Borges'

n: Ex-Goldman and JPMorgan trader ran Greece's debt agency in the crisis
rank: General Manager, Public Debt Management Agency
d: Petros Christodoulou, a former trader at Goldman Sachs (1987–88) and J.P. Morgan (1989–98) and treasurer of the National Bank of Greece, became head of Greece's Public Debt Management Agency, which issues and manages the state's borrowing, on 25 February 2010, as the Greek debt crisis began. He led negotiations on the 2012 restructuring of Greek government debt, which cut it by about €106.5 billion. In June 2012 he returned to the National Bank of Greece, one of the banks holding Greek bonds, as deputy chief executive.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Petros Christodoulou'

n: Lehman's Spain chief de Guindos ran Spain's bank bailout, then the ECB
rank: Minister of Economy; ECB vice president
d: Luis de Guindos, an adviser to Lehman Brothers in Europe from 2006 and director of its Spanish and Portuguese bank until its collapse in 2008, became Spain's Minister of Economy on 21 December 2011. In that post he negotiated the European Union's €100 billion rescue of Spain's failing savings banks. He left the ministry on 7 March 2018 and became Vice-President of the European Central Bank on 1 June 2018, a post he held until 31 May 2026, where he worked on banking stability across the euro area.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Luis de Guindos'

n: Citibank veteran Shaukat Aziz ran Pakistan's finances and privatised its banks
d: Shaukat Aziz, who worked for Citibank for about 30 years and rose to executive vice-president, was asked by military ruler Pervez Musharraf to run Pakistan's economy and became finance minister on 6 November 1999. He held the post until 2007 and was also prime minister from 28 August 2004 to 15 November 2007. He carried out the privatisation programme from 2001 and is credited with putting about 80 percent of the banking sector into private hands. An attempt to sell Pakistan Steel Mills was blocked by the Supreme Court in 2006.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Shaukat Aziz'

n: BankBoston's Meirelles ran Brazil's central bank, then joined JBS's owners
d: Henrique Meirelles spent 28 years at BankBoston, heading its Brazilian business and then serving as president of BankBoston worldwide from 1996 to 1999 and of FleetBoston's global banking. He became president of the Central Bank of Brazil in 2003 and stayed until 2010. In 2012 he joined the board of J&F, the Batista family's holding company that controls the meatpacker JBS and Banco Original, later chairing it. On 12 May 2016 he became President Michel Temer's finance minister, serving until April 2018.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Henrique Meirelles'

n: Hariri's Merrill Lynch banker Salameh ran Lebanon's central bank for 30 years
d: Riad Salameh, who worked at Merrill Lynch from 1973 to 1993 and managed the personal portfolio of Rafic Hariri, was appointed governor of Lebanon's central bank, Banque du Liban, by Hariri as prime minister in August 1993. He held the post for 30 years. From 2016 he ran 'financial engineering' swaps with commercial banks to draw in dollars and hold the currency peg; the peg broke down in 2019. France and Switzerland opened money-laundering inquiries in 2021, and in August 2023 the US, UK and Canada sanctioned him. He was arrested on 3 September 2024, charged with embezzling $42 million of public funds, and released on bail of over $14 million in 2025.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Riad Salameh'

n: IMF official Ouattara was pressed on Côte d'Ivoire as its economic chief
d: Alassane Ouattara, director of the IMF's African Department from 1984 to 1988 and then governor of the regional central bank BCEAO, was placed at the head of Côte d'Ivoire's economic policy under IMF pressure. In April 1990 the IMF pressed President Félix Houphouët-Boigny to accept him as chair of a committee on economic stabilisation, and on 7 November 1990 he became prime minister, still under the IMF's programme. He later returned to the IMF as Deputy Managing Director from 1994 to 1999, and has been president of Côte d'Ivoire since April 2011.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Alassane Ouattara'

n: World Bank finance chief Moeen Qureshi made Pakistan's caretaker PM
d: Moeenuddin Ahmad Qureshi, who had worked for the IMF, served as executive vice-president of the International Finance Corporation and was the World Bank's senior vice-president for finance from 1981 to 1987, was appointed Pakistan's caretaker prime minister after a military-brokered deal forced out both the prime minister and the president. Living in the United States, he was in Singapore when President Ghulam Ishaq Khan asked him to form a technocratic government. Serving from 18 July to 19 October 1993, he devalued the rupee, raised food prices, made the State Bank of Pakistan autonomous and published a list of taxpayers before handing over after elections.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Moeenuddin Ahmad Qureshi'

n: World Bank vice-president installed as Panama's president by a rigged vote
d: Nicolás Ardito Barletta, the World Bank's vice-president for Latin America and the Caribbean from 1978 to 1984, became president of Panama in October 1984 as the candidate of the military-backed government coalition. His 1,713-vote win was widely seen as the product of manipulated results; independent estimates suggested his opponent Arnulfo Arias would have won a fair count. In office he announced austerity measures to meet IMF loan conditions, including a 7 percent tax on services, and reversed some after strikes. He resigned on 27 September 1985 after the murder of government critic Hugo Spadafora and disputes with military commanders.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Nicolás Ardito Barletta Vallarino'

n: World Bank's Sri Mulyani went straight back to Indonesia's treasury
d: Sri Mulyani Indrawati moved repeatedly between the international lenders and Indonesia's finance ministry. She was an IMF executive director from 2002 to 2004, then finance minister from 2005 to 2010, when she left to become one of the World Bank's three managing directors, responsible for work in 74 countries. She left the World Bank on 27 July 2016 and the same day President Joko Widodo reappointed her finance minister. She served under Widodo and then President Prabowo Subianto until he dismissed her on 8 September 2025.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Sri Mulyani Indrawati'

n: World Bank vice-president Derviş took over Turkey's economy in the 2001 crash
rank: Minister of State for Economic Affairs
d: Kemal Derviş, who spent about 22 years at the World Bank and rose to vice-president, was brought in as Turkey's Minister of State for Economic Affairs in March 2001, during a severe financial crisis, under Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit. He designed a three-year recovery programme, strengthened the central bank and secured about $20 billion in loans from the IMF and World Bank. Inflation fell from near 70 percent in the 1990s to 12 percent by 2003. He resigned in August 2002 and entered parliament for the Republican People's Party; in 2005 he became head of the UN Development Programme.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kemal Derviş'

n: US-funded fund head Jaresko made Ukraine's finance minister same day
org_label: Western NIS Enterprise Fund / Horizon Capital
d: Natalie Jaresko, an American former US State Department official who had served at the US embassy in Kyiv, ran the Western NIS Enterprise Fund, which invested USAID money in Ukrainian and Moldovan businesses, from 2001, and in 2006 co-founded Horizon Capital, which took over managing it. On 2 December 2014 she was given Ukrainian citizenship on the same day she was appointed Ukraine's Minister of Finance. She served until April 2016 and oversaw a debt restructuring that included a 20 percent cut on privately held government bonds. In 2017 she became executive director of Puerto Rico's federal financial oversight board.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Natalie Jaresko'

n: Banker Jacques Necker, a lender to the crown, took over France's treasury
d: Jacques Necker, a Geneva-born banker and partner in the Thellusson bank in Paris, lent money to the French government through annuities and lotteries from 1768 to 1776, then took charge of its finances. In October 1776 he was named director of the royal treasury and on 29 June 1777 its director-general; as a Protestant he could not hold the title of Controller-General. He refused a salary and financed the state mainly through loans at high interest rather than higher taxes. In 1781 he published the Compte rendu au roi, the first public summary of royal income and spending, and was dismissed on 19 May 1781.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jacques Necker'

n: ICICI veteran Buch chaired India's market regulator amid conflict claims
rank: Chairperson, Securities and Exchange Board of India
d: Madhabi Puri Buch, who worked at ICICI Bank from 1989 and was chief executive of ICICI Securities from 2009 to 2011, became the first private-sector head of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the stock-market regulator, on 1 March 2022, after five years as a board member. In August 2024 Hindenburg Research alleged that she and her husband had held stakes in offshore funds that it said Vinod Adani used in Adani Group shares, which SEBI was investigating. The Congress party alleged she kept receiving ICICI benefits while at SEBI. She and ICICI denied the claims. Her term ended in February 2025, and in May 2025 the Lokpal ombudsman dismissed complaints for lack of evidence.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Madhabi Puri Buch'

n: Ombudsman: ECB chief's seat in bankers' Group of Thirty risked undue influence
d: The Group of Thirty, a private club whose 30 members include heads of large private banks alongside central bank governors from about 19 countries, had the President of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, as a member. The ECB is the central bank and main bank supervisor of the euro area. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman, Emily O'Reilly, asked Draghi to leave the group, saying his membership could be seen as giving its banking members undue influence. The group's members have also included two presidents of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Group of Thirty'

n: Croatia's Sanader accused of Hypo bank commission; later acquitted
d: Ivo Sanader, later Croatia's prime minister, was charged with taking a commission of nearly $695,000 from Austria's Hypo Alpe-Adria-Bank for arranging a loan from it in 1995, when he was deputy foreign minister. Croatia's anti-corruption office USKOK investigated payments from Hypo in the 1990s. In November 2012 he was sentenced to ten years in a combined verdict covering the Hypo case and a separate MOL case; the Supreme Court cut the term in 2014, and the Constitutional Court quashed the verdict in 2015 over procedural errors. On retrial he was acquitted in the Hypo case, and in 2025 the High Criminal Court upheld the acquittal.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ivo Sanader'

n: Chinese energy firm's NGO paid ex-UN Assembly president Kutesa $500,000
rank: President of the UN General Assembly (just ended term)
d: Patrick Ho, head of a Hong Kong charity funded by the Shanghai oil conglomerate CEFC China Energy, used the charity's standing at the United Nations to reach Sam Kutesa, Uganda's foreign minister, who had just finished a term as President of the UN General Assembly. Ho had $500,000 wired through New York to an account Kutesa named, dressed up as a gift to a charitable foundation, and Kutesa later steered a Ugandan bank acquisition towards CEFC. Ho also offered Chad's president $2 million in cash hidden in gift boxes for oil rights, which was refused. The charity held special consultative status with the UN Economic and Social Council. A New York jury convicted Ho of bribery and money laundering on 5 December 2018.
cite: US Department of Justice, SDNY press release, 5 Dec 2018; OCCRP, Dec 2018

n: Saddam's Iraq gave the UN Oil-for-Food chief oil allocations, inquiry found
d: Saddam Hussein's government is accused of buying the head of the United Nations programme meant to control its oil sales. The Oil-for-Food Programme, launched in December 1996, let sanctioned Iraq sell oil to buy food and medicine under UN supervision. Its director, Benon Sevan, solicited oil allocations from Iraq between 1998 and 2001 for a small trading company, African Middle East Petroleum, according to the inquiry led by former US Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker. Kofi Annan suspended Sevan in February 2005 and he resigned. In January 2007 US prosecutors indicted him for bribery and wire-fraud conspiracy, alleging about $160,000 in kickbacks. Sevan denied wrongdoing and stayed in Cyprus, out of reach of extradition.
cite: JURIST, Jan 2007; Fox News/AP, 5 Aug 2005 (Volcker interim findings)

n: Contractors paid UN procurement officer Yakovlev nearly $1m for contracts
rank: UN procurement officer; chair of UN budget oversight committee
d: Companies seeking United Nations supply contracts paid a UN purchasing officer, the Russian Alexander Yakovlev, to help them win. The UN's inquiry into the Oil-for-Food Programme found $950,000 in illegal payments from winners of UN contracts worth $79 million, paid into an offshore account he controlled in Antigua. The UN lifted his diplomatic immunity and he pleaded guilty to conspiracy, wire fraud and money laundering in August 2005. A second Russian diplomat, Vladimir Kuznetsov, who had chaired the UN's budget oversight committee, was convicted in March 2007 of laundering Yakovlev's bribes through an offshore company he set up in 2000. The case led the UN to order a review of its procurement office.
cite: Al Jazeera, 9 Aug 2005; Fox News/AP, 7 Mar 2007; Probe International, Aug 2005

n: Iraq paid Tongsun Park to lobby the UN Secretary-General on Oil-for-Food
d: Saddam Hussein's government paid the South Korean businessman Tongsun Park, already known from the 1970s 'Koreagate' bribery of US congressmen, to use his access to the United Nations leadership. In 1992 Samir Vincent, an Iraqi-born American working unofficially for Baghdad, recruited Park to help set up a programme easing sanctions on Iraq. Park acted as a go-between with Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, a friend, and the Oil-for-Food Programme began in late 1996, partly after his lobbying. He received about $2 million. In July 2006 a US federal jury convicted him of conspiracy, the first conviction from the Oil-for-Food investigation, and in February 2007 he was sentenced to five years in prison.
cite: Wikipedia 'Tongsun Park', citing US court records 2006–07; NPR, Jan 2007

n: CIA's agent Arkady Shevchenko served as UN Under-Secretary-General
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency had a source in the second rank of the United Nations Secretariat. Arkady Shevchenko, a Soviet diplomat, was the UN's Under-Secretary-General for Political Affairs from July 1973 to June 1978, a post the Soviet Union filled by custom. From about 1975 he passed Soviet secrets to the CIA while working in the UN's top political office and formally representing Moscow's interests there. When Moscow recalled him on 31 March 1978 he defected to the United States on 10 April 1978. He described the arrangement in his 1985 book 'Breaking With Moscow'. The case showed how national intelligence services used UN posts.
cite: Wikipedia 'Arkady Shevchenko'; Shevchenko, Breaking With Moscow (Knopf, 1985)

n: East German spy 'Topaz' took NATO's war plans from inside its headquarters
d: East Germany's foreign intelligence service, the HVA, placed a spy inside NATO's headquarters in Brussels. Rainer Rupp, a West German hired by NATO in 1977, rose quickly through its staff and, under the code names Mosel and later Topaz, passed material to East Berlin until 1989. He photographed about 10,000 pages, including deployment plans for cruise and Pershing II missiles, and handed over MC 161, the document summarising NATO strategy and its assessment of the Warsaw Pact. He was arrested in 1993 while on holiday in Germany, and sentenced to 12 years in prison in 1994.
cite: Wikipedia 'Rainer Rupp'; Reuters archive, 1994

n: Soviet spy Georges Pâques became deputy head of NATO's press service
d: Georges Pâques, a French official who had spied for the Soviet Union since 1944, joined NATO in October 1962 as deputy head of its press service. He was arrested on 10 August 1963 in the wake of the 'Martel affair', a Soviet defector's disclosures to the West. At his 1964 trial in Paris he admitted espionage and was sentenced to life imprisonment. He served seven years before being pardoned by his old friend Georges Pompidou, by then President of France. The case was one of several in the 1960s that showed Soviet services placing long-term agents in Western governments who could then be posted into NATO itself.
cite: Wikipedia 'Georges Pâques', citing French trial reporting 1964

n: GRU officer posing as a Brazilian tried to start a job at the ICC
d: Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, tried to place an officer inside the International Criminal Court in The Hague, the court that tries war crimes. Sergey Cherkasov had built a false Brazilian identity, Victor Muller Ferreira, using a forged birth certificate, and in April 2022 he flew to the Netherlands to take up a post at the court. The Dutch security service AIVD judged him a serious threat; he was refused entry at Schiphol and sent back to Brazil, where he was convicted of using forged documents. The AIVD published his real identity, an unusual step meant to warn other institutions.
cite: Wikipedia 'Sergey Cherkasov', citing AIVD statement June 2022 and Brazilian court rulings

n: CIA used UN weapons inspectors in Iraq to spy on Saddam, reports said
d: United States intelligence is reported to have used UNSCOM, the United Nations commission that inspected Iraq's weapons after the 1991 Gulf War, as cover to spy on Iraq's leadership. In January 1999 the Washington Post reported that CIA engineers posing as UN technicians had installed eavesdropping equipment at Iraqi sites without the knowledge of UNSCOM's chairman, Richard Butler, and that the system helped track Saddam Hussein's movements. Former inspector Scott Ritter made similar accusations. Butler denied that foreign agencies 'piggybacked' on the commission. Iraq had long said UNSCOM was a cover for espionage. Inspectors had withdrawn in 1998 and UNSCOM was disbanded in 1999 and replaced by a new body, UNMOVIC.
cite: Wikipedia 'UNSCOM', citing Washington Post, Jan 1999

n: UN inquiry: nine UNRWA staff in Gaza may have joined the 7 October attack
d: Members of armed Palestinian groups were found among the staff of UNRWA, the UN agency that runs schools and aid for Palestinian refugees and is headquartered in Amman and Gaza. In January 2024 Israel alleged that 12 UNRWA employees took part in the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023; UNRWA fired them and major donors suspended funding. The UN's internal investigators, OIOS, concluded in 2024 that nine staff may have been involved, and they were dismissed; evidence was insufficient for nine others. A separate review led by Catherine Colonna found Israel had not shown evidence for its wider claim that many staff belonged to armed groups. In October 2024 Israel's parliament banned UNRWA from operating in Israel.
cite: Wikipedia 'UNRWA and Israel', citing UN OIOS findings Aug 2024 and Colonna review 22 Apr 2024

n: Nazi SS chiefs took over Interpol and ran it from Berlin
rank: Presidency and headquarters of the ICPC (Interpol)
d: Nazi Germany took control of the International Criminal Police Commission, the body that became Interpol, which shares police information between countries. After Germany annexed Austria in 1938 the Vienna-based commission came under German control and most member states stopped supporting it. From 1938 to 1945 its presidents were all SS generals: Otto Steinhäusl, Reinhard Heydrich, Arthur Nebe and Ernst Kaltenbrunner, the last executed after the Nuremberg trials. By November 1941 it had offices at Am Kleinen Wannsee 16 in Berlin, and its headquarters moved to Berlin in 1942. The organisation was re-founded after the war, and Interpol's own history acknowledges the period.
cite: Wikipedia 'Interpol', citing Interpol history and academic sources

n: Microsoft partners joined national committees to vote its format into ISO
rank: National committees voting in the ISO standards process
d: When Microsoft sought approval of its Office Open XML document format as an international standard at ISO, the Geneva-based body that sets world standards, national committees that cast each country's vote saw sudden new members. In Sweden, Microsoft admitted an employee had asked two partner companies to join the Swedish Standards Institute committee and vote yes in return for 'marketing contributions'; the institute annulled Sweden's vote in 2007. In Norway the committee grew from about seven members to 30, and 13 of 23 members resigned in October 2008 after the vote was changed to approval. Similar complaints of 'committee stuffing' came from Switzerland, Poland and Portugal. The format was approved in April 2008 and published in November 2008.
cite: Wikipedia 'Standardization of Office Open XML', citing Computer Sweden, SIS statement 2007 and national press

n: NSA steered a weakened encryption standard through NIST and ISO
rank: Editor of national and international encryption standards
d: The US National Security Agency used its place in standards-setting bodies to have a random-number generator it could likely predict, Dual_EC_DRBG, adopted as an encryption standard by the US standards agency NIST in 2006, and by ANSI and ISO. Encryption depends on unpredictable random numbers. Leaked NSA documents reported by the New York Times in September 2013 showed the agency had become the sole editor of the standard. In December 2013 Reuters reported that the NSA paid RSA Security $10 million to make the generator the default in widely used software; RSA denied knowingly colluding. NIST told users to stop using it, removed it in April 2014 and formally withdrew it in June 2015.
cite: Wikipedia 'Dual_EC_DRBG', citing New York Times Sept 2013, Reuters Dec 2013, NIST 2014–15

n: AIIB spokesman quits saying Communist Party members dominate the bank
rank: Management of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank
d: The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, a Beijing-based development bank with over 100 member countries, was accused by its own spokesman of being run from inside by the Chinese Communist Party. In June 2023 Bob Pickard, a Canadian who was the bank's communications director, resigned, left China and said party members dominated the bank, acted as an 'in-house secret police' and filtered what reached its president, Jin Liqun. Canada froze its ties with the bank the same day and opened a review, widened in December 2023 to cover governance and safeguards. The bank called the claim 'baseless' and launched an internal investigation. The case is listed as contested: the allegation is from a named insider and has not been tested.
cite: Wikipedia 'Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank', citing Reuters and Government of Canada statements, June and Dec 2023

n: Industry-tied experts on EU food-safety agency panels, auditors found
who: Food and chemical industry, incl. ILSI
rank: Expert panels and board of the European Food Safety Authority
d: Experts tied to the food and chemical industries sat on the panels of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), the EU agency in Parma that gives the scientific advice on which EU food, pesticide and additive rules are based. In 2012 the European Court of Auditors criticised EFSA for 'frequent conflicts of interests', some undeclared, and several of them involved the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI), a research group founded and funded by food companies including Coca-Cola. The campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory counted 58% of EFSA experts with conflicts of interest in 2013 and 46% in 2017. EFSA tightened its independence rules after the findings.
cite: Wikipedia 'European Food Safety Authority', citing European Court of Auditors special report 2012 and Corporate Europe Observatory 2013, 2017

n: Hezbollah seized west Beirut and won a cabinet veto in 2008
d: Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Shia party and armed group, won a veto inside Lebanon's government by force in 2008. In early May 2008 the cabinet declared Hezbollah's private fibre-optic telephone network illegal and removed the security chief of Beirut airport, Brigadier General Wafic Shkeir, seen as close to Hezbollah. Its leader Hassan Nasrallah called this a 'declaration of war'; from 8 May its fighters and allies took over much of west Beirut, and about 70 to 110 people were killed. The government withdrew both decisions on 10 May. The Doha Agreement of 21 May gave Hezbollah and its allies a 'blocking third' of cabinet seats, enough to veto decisions, which shaped Lebanese governments for years after.
cite: Wikipedia '2008 Lebanon conflict' and 'Hezbollah', citing UN, Human Rights Watch and Doha Agreement text

n: Houthi movement took over Yemen's state and runs it through its own council
rank: Head of state functions (Supreme Political Council) and cabinet
d: The Houthi movement, a Zaydi Shia armed group from northern Yemen, took control of Yemen's capital and its state institutions. Its fighters captured Sanaa's government buildings on 21 September 2014; in December they evicted oil company officials, blocked the port director in Hodeidah and fired four provincial governors. After President Hadi resigned on 22 January 2015, the Houthis declared parliament dissolved and on 6 February 2015 issued a 'constitutional declaration' putting their Revolutionary Committee in charge. On 28 July 2016 they and allies set up the Supreme Political Council, which performs head-of-state functions and appoints the cabinet in Sanaa. The UN called it a clear violation of Yemen's constitution. It still governs most of Yemen's population.
cite: Wikipedia 'Houthi takeover in Yemen' and 'Supreme Political Council', citing UN statements and Reuters

n: Iran-founded Badr militia's commander Bayan Jabr ran Iraq's Interior Ministry
d: The Badr Organization, a Shia militia formed in Iran in 1982 under Iranian officers to fight Saddam Hussein, moved its people into Iraq's police after 2003. Most of its fighters reportedly joined the new army and police, and its parent party, SCIRI, took the Interior Ministry, which runs the police. Interior Minister Bayan Jabr was a former Badr commander. In 2006 the UN's human rights chief said hundreds of people had been tortured or executed under the ministry; Badr was accused of running a secret prison and sectarian killings, and many police commandos were suspected of being former Badr members. A German government-funded institute, SWP, has called Badr Iran's most important instrument in Iraqi politics.
cite: Wikipedia 'Badr Organization' and 'Bayan Jabr', citing UN human rights office 2006, Knight Ridder Mar 2006, SWP

n: Badr's Qasim al-Araji became Iraq's interior minister and security adviser
rank: Minister of Interior; National Security Adviser
d: A senior member of the Badr Organization, the Iraqi militia created with Iran's Revolutionary Guards, held the top posts over Iraq's police and security policy. Qasim al-Araji, who trained in Revolutionary Guards camps and fought on Iran's side in the Iran–Iraq war, had been detained twice by US forces, in 2003 and 2007, on suspicion of commanding militia forces and released for lack of evidence. Parliament approved him as Interior Minister on 30 January 2017, replacing another Badr member, Mohammed al-Ghabban. He served until October 2018 and in July 2020 became National Security Adviser, holding that post until June 2026. Badr thus kept the Interior Ministry across successive governments.
cite: Wikipedia 'Qasim al-Araji', citing Iraqi parliament records and leaked US cables

n: Quds Force adviser al-Muhandis sat in Iraq's parliament and ran the PMF
rank: MP; deputy chairman, Popular Mobilization Commission
d: Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, a military adviser to Iran's Quds Force (the foreign arm of the Revolutionary Guards), held posts inside the Iraqi state. A Kuwaiti court sentenced him to death in absentia in 2007 for the 1983 Kuwait bombings. He was elected to Iraq's parliament in 2005 for the Dawa Party, and in 2014 became deputy chairman of the Popular Mobilization Commission, the state body that pays and commands the Popular Mobilization Forces, a militia umbrella formally part of Iraq's armed forces. He also led Kata'ib Hezbollah, which the US designated a terrorist group in 2009, and was designated himself. He was killed with Quds Force head Qasem Soleimani in a US strike near Baghdad airport on 3 January 2020.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis' and 'Popular Mobilization Forces', citing US Treasury 2009 and Kuwaiti court 2007

n: Quds Force-backed Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq holds Iraqi state brigades and seats
rank: PMF brigades 41–43 of Iraq's armed forces; parliament
d: Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, an Iraqi Shia militia funded, trained and guided by Iran's Quds Force and Hezbollah, has its fighters inside Iraq's state forces. Its units serve as the 41st, 42nd and 43rd Brigades of the Popular Mobilization Forces, which Iraqi law makes part of the armed forces and pays from the state budget. Founded in 2006 by Qais al-Khazali after splitting from Muqtada al-Sadr's Mahdi Army, it also sits in parliament, running in 2018 inside the Fatah Alliance. By March 2007 Iran was reportedly supplying $750,000 to $3 million a month. On 3 January 2020 the US designated it a Foreign Terrorist Organization and sanctioned Qais and Laith al-Khazali, citing the violent suppression of protests.
cite: Wikipedia 'Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq', citing US State Department designation, Jan 2020

n: Sadrist deputy health minister accused of using hospitals for death squads
d: The Sadrist movement of the cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose militia was the Mahdi Army, placed its member Hakim al-Zamili as Iraq's Deputy Health Minister from May 2006 to April 2007. During the sectarian war he was accused of running death squads that used ambulances and hospitals to kidnap and murder Sunni Arabs, and of kidnapping a fellow deputy minister, Ammar al-Saffar, in November 2006. US troops arrested him in February 2007, accusing him of channelling money to militias. He was cleared after key witnesses failed to appear, which was linked to alleged intimidation. He returned to parliament in 2010 and became First Deputy Speaker in January 2022.
cite: Wikipedia 'Hakim al-Zamili', citing Washington Post, Mar 2008

n: Janjaweed-born RSF made a state force; its chief Hemedti reached the top
rank: Deputy head of Sudan's Sovereignty Council; state paramilitary
d: The Rapid Support Forces, built in August 2013 from the Janjaweed militias that Sudan's government had used in Darfur, were placed inside the state under the intelligence service and army, and their leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, rose to the top of government. In 2017 he used the RSF to take Darfur gold mines, and his firm al-Junaid became Sudan's biggest gold trader. After the 2019 coup against Omar al-Bashir he became deputy head of the ruling council and joined the Sovereignty Council on 21 August 2019. RSF forces killed about 100 protesters in Khartoum on 3 June 2019. In April 2023 the RSF went to war with the army. On 7 January 2025 the US found it had committed genocide.
cite: Wikipedia 'Rapid Support Forces' and 'Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo', citing US State Department, Jan 2025

n: Rebel CNDP folded into Congo's army; ICC suspect Ntaganda made a general
d: The CNDP, a Tutsi rebel group in eastern Congo's North Kivu, was absorbed into the Congolese army, and its chief of staff, Bosco Ntaganda, served as a general despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant. A UN expert group reported in 2011 that he profited from several mines, including through a 'parallel' mine police at Rubaya. In April 2012 he and about 300 loyal troops left the army, the start of the M23 rebellion. He surrendered at the US embassy in Kigali in March 2013. The ICC convicted him of 18 counts, including murder, rape and child recruitment, and in November 2019 sentenced him to 30 years, its longest sentence at that time.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bosco Ntaganda', citing UN Group of Experts 2011 and ICC judgment 2019

n: Kahanist Ben-Gvir, convicted of backing a terror group, became police minister
d: A leader of the Kahanist movement, which follows the banned anti-Arab Kach party, was given ministerial control of Israel's police. Itamar Ben-Gvir was Kach's youth coordinator and was convicted in 2007 of incitement to racism and of supporting a terrorist organisation, Kach. His party Otzma Yehudit is seen as Kach's ideological successor. Under the coalition deal of late 2022 he became head of a new National Security Ministry over the police, including the Border Police in the West Bank. The cabinet reappointed him in March 2025 over the Attorney General's objections. On 10 June 2025 the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Norway froze his assets and banned travel, accusing him of inciting settler violence.
cite: Wikipedia 'Itamar Ben-Gvir', citing Times of Israel and UK government statement, 10 Jun 2025

n: Settler leader Smotrich given control of West Bank civil administration
rank: Minister in the Defence Ministry over West Bank civil affairs
d: The settler movement, which builds Israeli communities in the occupied West Bank, gained control of the government office that governs land and building there. Bezalel Smotrich grew up in the Beit El settlement, lives in Kedumim and co-founded Regavim, a group that pursues legal action against Palestinian building. Under the November 2022 coalition deal he received a Defence Ministry post with authority over civil affairs in the West Bank, and in February 2023 was entrusted with much of its administration; his stated aim is to expand settlements and merge their administration with Israel's. He announced the 3,400-home E1 plan in August 2025. Several states, including the UK on 10 June 2025, sanctioned him for inciting settler violence.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bezalel Smotrich', citing Times of Israel, Reuters and UK government, 2022–2025

n: Azov commander Vadym Troyan became Kyiv police chief, then deputy minister
rank: Kyiv region police chief; acting head of National Police; deputy interior minister
d: Members of the Azov movement, a nationalist militia founded in 2014 by Andriy Biletsky, who had led the far-right Patriot of Ukraine and Social-National Assembly, moved into top police posts. Azov was first a volunteer unit funded through the Interior Ministry and on 11 November 2014 was made part of the National Guard. On 31 October 2014 its deputy commander Vadym Troyan was appointed police chief of Kyiv region. He went on to be first deputy and acting head of the National Police and, from February 2017 to September 2019, a deputy minister of internal affairs. Biletsky himself was elected to parliament in 2014. The appointments drew criticism because of the movement's far-right origins.
cite: Wikipedia 'Azov Brigade' and 'Vadym Troyan', citing Ukrainian government decrees and press

n: Svoboda, heir to a Social-National party, held deputy PM and two ministries
rank: Deputy Prime Minister; agriculture and environment ministers; three governors
d: Svoboda, an ultranationalist party descended from the Social-National Party of Ukraine, which in the 1990s was accused of neo-Nazism for recruiting skinheads and using neo-Nazi symbols, placed its members in Ukraine's government after the 2014 revolution. In the Yatsenyuk government formed on 27 February 2014, Oleksandr Sych became Deputy Prime Minister, Ihor Shvaika Minister of Agrarian Policy and Andriy Mokhnyk Minister of Environment. In early March party members were made governors of the Poltava, Ternopil and Rivne regions. Svoboda left the coalition on 24 July 2014, its ministers resigned on 12 November 2014, and President Poroshenko dismissed the three governors on 18 November.
cite: Wikipedia 'Svoboda (political party)', citing Ukrainian government records 2014

n: Militant tendency, a Trotskyist group inside Labour, ran Liverpool council
rank: Liverpool City Council leadership; three MPs
d: Militant, a Trotskyist group organised around its newspaper, worked secretly inside the Labour Party, a method called entryism, to take over its branches and seats. A Labour inquiry found in June 1982 that it breached party rules, and five of its editorial board were expelled in February 1983. In May 1983 Militant-backed councillors took Liverpool City Council, with Derek Hatton as deputy leader. The council set an illegal deficit budget in June 1985 and in September issued redundancy notices to about 30,000 workers. Forty-seven councillors were surcharged; their appeal failed in 1987. Militant supporters won seats as Labour MPs: Terry Fields and Dave Nellist in 1983 and Pat Wall in 1987.
cite: Wikipedia 'Militant tendency', citing Labour NEC Hayward-Hughes report 1982 and House of Lords 1987

n: Up to 15% of UDR soldiers in loyalist groups, army intelligence estimated
d: Loyalist paramilitary groups, the UVF and UDA, had members inside the Ulster Defence Regiment, a British Army regiment recruited in Northern Ireland. A 1973 report, 'Subversion in the UDR', believed to be from British military intelligence, estimated that 5–15% of UDR soldiers were or had been members of 'Protestant extremist groups' and called the regiment their 'best single source of weapons'. About 315 UDR weapons had gone missing by 1976. Dual membership was banned in November 1972 and 171 UDA-linked soldiers were discharged by 1975. Two serving UDR soldiers took part in the 1975 Miami Showband killings. In 1989 the Stevens inquiry into collusion arrested 28 UDR soldiers. The regiment was merged into the Royal Irish Regiment in 1992.
cite: Wikipedia 'Ulster Defence Regiment', citing 'Subversion in the UDR' (1973) and Stevens Inquiry (1989)

n: Glenanne gang: UVF killers included serving UDR soldiers and RUC police
rank: RUC police officers and UDR soldiers
d: The Glenanne gang was a loyalist group that drew on the UVF's Mid-Ulster Brigade together with serving soldiers of the Ulster Defence Regiment and officers of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Northern Ireland's police; 25 soldiers and officers were named as members. Active from 1972 to 1980, it is estimated to have killed about 120 people, almost all Catholic civilians. A 2006 international panel led by Professor Douglas Cassel examined 76 killings and found evidence of police or soldier involvement in 74, and that some senior officers knew and did not act. Irish judge Henry Barron concluded that UDR and RUC members took part in or knew of preparations for the 1974 Dublin and Monaghan bombings. Families won a court ruling in 2019 for an independent inquiry.
cite: Wikipedia 'Glenanne gang', citing Cassel report 2006, Barron reports 2003, NI Court of Appeal 2019

n: Irish ministers Haughey and Blaney sacked over alleged arms plan for IRA
rank: Minister for Finance; Minister for Agriculture; army intelligence officer
d: The Arms Crisis of 1970 was an alleged plan by two serving Irish cabinet ministers and an army intelligence officer to bring in weapons for republicans in Northern Ireland, linked to the IRA and the Northern Citizen Defence Committees. Taoiseach Jack Lynch dismissed Finance Minister Charles Haughey and Agriculture Minister Neil Blaney on 6 May 1970 after they refused to resign; Kevin Boland resigned in protest, saying Lynch and Defence Minister Jim Gibbons had known. Captain James Kelly of army intelligence was involved. Charges against Blaney were dropped, and in October 1970 Haughey, Kelly and two others were found not guilty of conspiracy. Haughey later became Taoiseach. The case is listed as contested because the trial ended in acquittal.
cite: Wikipedia 'Arms Crisis', citing Irish trial record 1970

n: Spain's Supreme Court found party Batasuna was part of ETA and banned it
rank: Seats in the Basque and municipal assemblies
d: ETA, the Basque armed separatist group, used the party Batasuna to hold elected seats and public money, Spanish courts found. Judge Baltasar Garzón suspended the party in August 2002 to investigate its links with ETA. In 2003 Spain's Supreme Court declared Batasuna illegal, a ruling confirmed by the Constitutional Court; a court found it had financed ETA with public funds, and the EU lists it as part of ETA. Batasuna lost its elected representatives, and in 2009 neither it nor parties seen as its proxies could stand in the Basque election. In July 2009 the European Court of Human Rights upheld the ban, saying its ties to ETA could be seen 'objectively as a threat to democracy'.
cite: Wikipedia 'Batasuna', citing Spanish Supreme Court 2003 and ECtHR Herri Batasuna and Batasuna v. Spain, 30 Jun 2009

n: Alleged IRA spy ring at Stormont; accused Sinn Féin official was MI5's agent
rank: Sinn Féin office at the Northern Ireland Assembly
