d: On 4 October 2002 police raided Sinn Féin's offices at Stormont, seat of the Northern Ireland Assembly, and arrested its head of administration Denis Donaldson and two others, alleging an IRA intelligence ring there. The power-sharing government collapsed ten days later and Northern Ireland returned to direct rule from London. Prosecutors dropped the charges on 8 December 2005 as no longer in the public interest. That month Donaldson confirmed he had been a British MI5 informer for over twenty years and called the spy ring a fiction. He was shot dead in County Donegal on 4 April 2006; the Real IRA later claimed responsibility. Devolution returned in 2007.
cite: Wikipedia 'Stormontgate', citing PSNI, Public Prosecution Service 2005 and Donaldson's statement

n: Oath Keepers list held 370 serving police and 100 military members
rank: Police and military personnel; elected officials
d: The Oath Keepers, an anti-government militia that recruits from police and the military, had members working in law enforcement and the armed forces. In September 2021 hackers took its membership files and Distributed Denial of Secrets released data on about 38,000 apparent members, including applications from serving police officers, some filed after the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol. In September 2022 the Anti-Defamation League found that over 370 names appeared to be current law enforcement employees and over 100 current military personnel, and dozens of elected officials were also linked. Founder Stewart Rhodes was convicted of seditious conspiracy on 29 November 2022 and sentenced to 18 years; his sentence was commuted in January 2025.
cite: Wikipedia 'Oath Keepers', citing ADL report Sept 2022 and US DOJ

n: Germany dissolved a special forces company over far-right extremists in it
rank: Kommando Spezialkräfte (KSK), Germany's army special forces
d: Far-right extremists built up inside the KSK, the German army's elite special forces unit based in Calw. Federal police reportedly uncovered in 2018 a plot involving KSK soldiers to kill prominent politicians and attack immigrants on a 'Day X', and prosecutors investigated neo-Nazi gestures at a KSK farewell party. In June 2020 Defence Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer announced that the 2nd Commando Company would be dissolved and not replaced, after what the ministry described as a notable build-up of right-wing extremists in the unit, and she spoke of a 'toxic leadership culture'.
cite: Wikipedia 'Kommando Spezialkräfte', citing German Defence Ministry, June 2020

n: Islamic Jihad cell inside Egypt's army assassinated President Sadat
rank: Army officers at the presidential parade
d: Egyptian Islamic Jihad, an armed Islamist group, had a cell inside Egypt's army led by Lieutenant Khalid al-Islambuli, which used its place in a military parade to kill President Anwar Sadat. A September 1981 round-up of more than 1,500 people had missed the cell. On 6 October 1981, at the Cairo parade marking the 1973 crossing of the Suez Canal, the squad rode in an army truck towing artillery, stopped it in front of the reviewing stand and attacked with grenades and gunfire. Nineteen people were tried; on 15 April 1982 five were executed, including al-Islambuli, an army sergeant, and the plot's leader Muhammad Abd al-Salam Faraj. Hosni Mubarak became president.
cite: Wikipedia 'Assassination of Anwar Sadat', citing Egyptian trial records 1982

n: Bomber inside Iran's PM office killed the president and prime minister
rank: Secretary of the PM's office and of the Supreme National Security Council
d: On 30 August 1981 a bomb in the office of Iran's prime minister killed President Mohammad-Ali Rajai, Prime Minister Mohammad-Javad Bahonar, the police chief and five others. The bomb was attributed to Masoud Keshmiri, who held the post of secretary of Bahonar's office and of the Supreme National Security Council, and who left Iran on a false passport. Iran said he was an agent of the People's Mojahedin (MEK), an armed opposition movement; no group claimed the attack. Two months earlier, on 28 June 1981, a bomb at the ruling Islamic Republican Party's headquarters, planted by a man who got a job there as a sound engineer, had killed about 70 officials including the Chief Justice.
cite: Wikipedia '1981 Iranian Prime Minister's office bombing' and 'Hafte Tir bombing'

n: Breakaway Tiger commander Karuna made Sri Lanka's integration minister
d: The leader of an armed group that fought alongside Sri Lanka's forces was brought into parliament and the cabinet. Vinayagamoorthy Muralitharan, known as Karuna Amman, had been the Tamil Tigers' top commander in the east before breaking away in July 2004 and forming the TMVP, which fought the Tigers with the Sri Lankan army. UNICEF and Human Rights Watch accused the group of recruiting child soldiers, and rights groups linked it to disappearances; he denied this. He became an MP in October 2008, Minister of National Integration in March 2009 and a vice-president of the ruling SLFP in April 2009. In March 2025 the UK sanctioned him over alleged wartime abuses.
cite: Wikipedia 'Karuna Amman', citing UNICEF, Human Rights Watch and UK FCDO, Mar 2025

n: Fascist Iron Guard given Romania's interior ministry and every county prefecture
rank: Deputy Prime Minister; Interior and three other ministries; all 50 prefects
d: The Iron Guard, Romania's fascist Legionary Movement, was placed inside the state when General Ion Antonescu formed the 'National Legionary State' on 14 September 1940. Its leader Horia Sima became Deputy Prime Minister; the Guard took the Interior, Education, Foreign Affairs and Religious Affairs ministries, most senior ministry posts, the Bucharest police command and the prefect's office in all fifty counties. On 27 November 1940 Guardists killed 64 former officials held at Jilava prison. On 20 January 1941 it attempted a coup together with a pogrom in Bucharest, murdering about 200 Jews at the city slaughterhouse. Antonescu put down the revolt, expelled the Guard from government and more than 9,000 people were arrested.
cite: Wikipedia 'National Legionary State', citing Romanian and Holocaust historians

n: German-backed coup put the Arrow Cross movement in charge of Hungary
d: The Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist movement, was installed in power by Nazi Germany. When Regent Miklós Horthy moved to leave the war, Germany launched Operation Panzerfaust in October 1944, detained him and forced his abdication; Arrow Cross leader Ferenc Szálasi became 'Leader of the Nation' and prime minister the same day, heading a government dominated by his party until March 1945. Arrow Cross death squads killed up to 38,000 Hungarian Jews in under three months, many shot on the bank of the Danube, and its officers helped Adolf Eichmann restart deportations from Budapest. After the war Hungarian courts convicted its leaders; Szálasi and three associates were hanged in March 1946.
cite: Wikipedia 'Arrow Cross Party', citing Hungarian People's Tribunal records and Holocaust histories

n: French generals led a putsch in Algeria; army officers then ran the OAS
rank: Generals and colonels of the French army
d: Supporters of keeping Algeria French had their people at the top of the French army and used them against the government. On 21–26 April 1961 four generals, Maurice Challe, Edmond Jouhaud, André Zeller and Raoul Salan, seized Algiers with units including the Foreign Legion's 1st Parachute Regiment, to stop President de Gaulle ending the Algerian War. The putsch failed; Challe and Zeller got 15 years, and Salan and Jouhaud were sentenced to death in absentia. Salan and colonels such as Yves Godard and Antoine Argoud then led the OAS, a clandestine armed group that killed Algiers police chief Roger Gavoury in May 1961 and tried to kill de Gaulle at Petit-Clamart in August 1962.
cite: Wikipedia 'Algiers putsch of 1961' and 'Organisation armée secrète', citing French military tribunal records

n: Nigeria's president said Boko Haram had members in his government and army
rank: Army, police and branches of government
d: Boko Haram, the jihadist group fighting in north-east Nigeria, had sympathisers inside the Nigerian state, according to the country's own president. On 8 January 2012 President Goodluck Jonathan said publicly that the group had infiltrated the army and the police as well as the executive and legislative branches of government. He named no individuals. Coming from the head of state, it amounted to an admission that the security forces themselves had been penetrated. It is listed as possible because the claim came from the head of state but no specific infiltrators were publicly identified at the time.
cite: Wikipedia 'Boko Haram', citing BBC News and Reuters, 8 Jan 2012

n: Russia's bribes bought the head of world biathlon, inquiry found
rank: President and Secretary General, International Biathlon Union
d: Russian officials bought the leadership of the International Biathlon Union (IBU), the Salzburg-based body that runs the Olympic sport of skiing and shooting, an independent inquiry found. Anders Besseberg of Norway had been IBU president for 25 years when he and his deputy, Secretary General Nicole Resch, were accused in 2018 of taking Russian bribes; both left that year. The External Review Commission, set up by the IBU's new leaders, reported in January 2021 that Besseberg received at least $200,000 in cash, hunting trips and other favours, and in return defended Russian athletes, attacked Russia's critics and blocked efforts to root out Russian doping. Austrian and Norwegian prosecutors opened criminal investigations.
cite: Wikipedia 'International Biathlon Union', citing IBU External Review Commission report, Jan 2021

n: Serving army officer Purohit co-founded Hindu nationalist Abhinav Bharat
rank: Lieutenant Colonel, Indian Army military intelligence
d: Abhinav Bharat, a Hindu nationalist group, counted a serving Indian Army intelligence officer, Lieutenant Colonel Prasad Shrikant Purohit, among its founders, and Maharashtra's anti-terrorism squad said serving and retired army officers had taken the group over. The squad linked Purohit and Sadhvi Pragya Singh Thakur to the bombings of 29 September 2008 in Malegaon and Modasa, which killed six people. Purohit said he had joined the group to gather intelligence as part of his job, and an army court of inquiry heard 59 witnesses say so. Thakur was later elected a BJP MP. In 2025 a special court of the National Investigation Agency acquitted all seven accused, finding conspiracy not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abhinav Bharat', '2008 Malegaon blasts' and 'Prasad Shrikant Purohit', citing Maharashtra ATS and NIA court

n: Committee of Union and Progress seized the Ottoman government in 1913
rank: Grand Vizier and War, Interior and Navy ministries
d: The Committee of Union and Progress, an oath-bound secret society that began among military medical students in Constantinople in 1889, took over the Ottoman government by force. Members were organised in cells, swore absolute obedience to a Central Committee, and placed officers in the army and party-chosen 'responsible secretaries' over provincial officials. On 23 January 1913, in the Raid on the Sublime Porte, CUP men forced Grand Vizier Kâmil Pasha to resign at gunpoint, and the War Minister was killed. Three members, Talât (Interior), Enver (War) and Cemal (Navy), then ran the empire as a one-party regime. The society's Special Organisation, answering to the Central Committee, was used in the policies that led to the genocide of Armenians, Pontic Greeks and Assyrians. Many members were court-martialled after 1918.
cite: Committee of Union and Progress (Wikipedia, citing Zürcher, Hanioğlu and others)

n: Secret officers' club Hanahoe took South Korea's army and presidency
rank: President; army command; Defence Security Command
d: Hanahoe was a secret club of South Korean army officers, formed by graduates of the 11th Korea Military Academy class and topped up with three or four hand-picked members from each later class. Its members, led by Chun Doo-hwan and Roh Tae-woo, formed the core of the group that seized control of the army on 12 December 1979 and the government in May 1980; Chun became president from 1980 to 1988, and Roh succeeded him. On 8 March 1993, new President Kim Young-sam abruptly dismissed the army chief of staff and the Defence Security Command chief and broke up the club. In 1996 Chun was sentenced to death, later commuted to life, and Roh to 17 years; both were pardoned in December 1997.
cite: Hanahoe and Chun Doo-hwan (Wikipedia, citing Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Hankyoreh, Korea Times); Asia Economy, 30 Nov 2023

n: Secret Ba'ath Military Committee seized Syria; member Assad later ruled
rank: Head of state; defence ministry; army
d: The Military Committee was a secret body of Syrian army officers, formed in 1958 by Captain Abd al-Karim al-Jundi, Lieutenant-Colonel Muhammad Umran, Major Salah Jadid and Captain Hafez al-Assad. Members swore not to disclose its existence even to other officers, and kept it hidden from their own Ba'ath Party leaders. The committee carried out the coup of 8 March 1963 that brought the Ba'ath Party to power, and then held the real power inside the ruling Revolutionary Command council, as a 'junta within a junta'. Jadid ousted the party's civilian leaders in February 1966, with Assad becoming defence minister. Assad seized power in November 1970 and was president from 1971 until his death in 2000; his son Bashar ruled until December 2024.
cite: Military Committee of the Ba'ath Party; Hafez al-Assad (Wikipedia, citing Seale 1990, Rabinovich 1972)

n: Free Officers' secret army cells overthrew Egypt's king and ruled
d: The Free Officers were a clandestine network of junior Egyptian army officers, begun as a small cell by veterans of the 1948–49 Palestine war and led from 1950 by Gamal Abdel Nasser. They recruited inside the army and enlisted a respected general, Mohamed Naguib, as their public face. On 23 July 1952 they seized power and forced King Farouk to abdicate, ending British control. Their Revolutionary Command Council ran the state; the monarchy was abolished on 18 June 1953, Nasser became prime minister in February 1954 and president soon after, ruling until his death in 1970. The council's successor, the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, still sits at the top of Egypt's state, and the model was copied by officers' groups in Iraq and Libya.
cite: Free Officers movement (Egypt); Gamal Abdel Nasser (Wikipedia); Al-Ahram Online

n: Iraq's secret Free Officers ended the monarchy; Qasim became premier
rank: Prime Minister; defence and interior ministries
d: The Iraqi Free Officers were a secret underground group of army officers, modelled on Egypt's Free Officers and led by Brigadier Abdul-Karim Qasim. Qasim and Colonel Abdul Salam Arif planned and timed a revolt using army units under their command. On 14 July 1958 their forces took Baghdad; Arif announced the revolution on the radio, and King Faisal II and Crown Prince Abd al-Ilah were killed at the palace, ending Iraq's Hashemite monarchy. Qasim made himself Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, and Arif became Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior. The coup began a long period in which officers' factions decided who governed Iraq.
cite: 14 July Revolution (Wikipedia)

n: Gaddafi's Free Unionist Officers took Libya in a 1969 army coup
rank: Revolutionary Command Council; head of state
d: The Free Unionist Officers were a group of about 70 young Libyan army officers, organised by Muammar Gaddafi inside the army and supported by enlisted men, mostly from the Signal Corps. On 1 September 1969, while King Idris was in Turkey, they launched a bloodless coup from Benghazi, abolished the monarchy and declared a republic. A twelve-member Revolutionary Command Council of the plotters formed the government, with Gaddafi as its chairman and de facto head of state. He ruled Libya for 42 years, until his death in 2011.
cite: 1969 Libyan revolution (Wikipedia)

n: Khana Ratsadon, formed by students in Paris, ended Siam's absolute monarchy
d: Khana Ratsadon, the People's Party, was founded in Paris in February 1927 by seven Siamese students, including Pridi Banomyong and Plaek Khittasangkha (later Phibunsongkhram). It grew to about 102 military officers and civilians in four branches. On 24 June 1932 its members, using army units, staged a bloodless revolution against King Prajadhipok and replaced absolute monarchy with a constitutional one. Members then held Thailand's prime ministership for about two decades, among them Phahon Phonphayuhasena (1933–1938) and Phibunsongkhram (1938–1944). The party split into civilian and military wings and dissolved in 1947, but the army's habit of taking power by coup dates from this event.
cite: Khana Ratsadon (Wikipedia)

n: Sakurakai: secret society in Japan's General Staff plotted two coups
d: The Sakurakai, or Cherry Blossom Society, was a secret society of Imperial Japanese Army officers founded in September 1930 by Lieutenant Colonel Kingoro Hashimoto, chief of the Russian section of the Army General Staff, with Captain Isamu Chō; Kuniaki Koiso, later prime minister, was a leading figure. It began with about ten General Staff officers and grew to more than 50 by February 1931 and possibly several hundred by October 1931. Its aim was to overthrow party government and install military rule. With civilian ultranationalists it tried to do so twice in 1931, in the March Incident and the Imperial Colours Incident. Its leaders were arrested and the society was dissolved, but such plots helped push Japan towards military-dominated government.
cite: Sakurakai (Wikipedia)

n: Blue Shirts: Chiang's secret officers' society inside the Kuomintang
rank: Army, ruling party and intelligence bureau
d: The Blue Shirts Society was a secret ultranationalist faction set up in 1932 by Chiang Kai-shek inside his Nationalist party, the Kuomintang, mainly from young army officers who had trained at the Whampoa Military Academy. Membership was strictly secret and Chiang never publicly acknowledged it. Its members spread through the military and the party, competing with a civilian faction, the CC Clique, and some joined the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, the regime's espionage and assassination service. Membership peaked at about 10,000 in 1935. In 1938 the new Three Principles of the People Youth Corps was placed largely under Blue Shirt influence.
cite: Blue Shirts Society (Wikipedia, citing Jeffrey Crean)

n: RAM officers' movement inside Philippine army toppled Marcos, then hit Aquino
d: The Reform the Armed Forces Movement (RAM) was founded on 23 July 1982 by junior Philippine officers from the Military Academy class of 1971, led by Gregorio Honasan, who was also chief security officer to Defence Minister Juan Ponce Enrile; Enrile reportedly approved its formation. About 300 officers, mostly from the 1971–1984 classes, revealed themselves in 1985. In February 1986 RAM, backed by Enrile, planned to oust Ferdinand Marcos; when the plot was discovered, Enrile and Fidel Ramos took refuge in the military camps, and the crowds that gathered became the People Power Revolution. RAM then attempted six coups against Corazon Aquino's government. Members received an amnesty in 1996; in 2021 three former members were convicted of murdering labour leader Rolando Olalia.
cite: Reform the Armed Forces Movement (Wikipedia)

n: San Martín's secret lodge made and unmade Argentina's early governments
d: José de San Martín, Carlos María de Alvear and José Matías Zapiola, officers back from Spain, set up a secret lodge in Buenos Aires in 1812, later called the Lautaro Lodge. Its secrecy means historians are unsure whether it was truly Masonic or a political group. The lodge organised the Revolution of 8 October 1812, in which San Martín's and Alvear's troops backed the removal of the First Triumvirate and its replacement by a Second Triumvirate. Lodge co-founder Alvear later became Supreme Director, the head of government, and San Martín backed fellow lodge member Juan Martín de Pueyrredón for the same post. San Martín set up a branch in Chile under the Lautaro name after his army crossed the Andes.
cite: José de San Martín; Lautaro Lodge (Wikipedia)

n: Secret officers' lodge GOU behind Argentina's 1943 coup and Perón's rise
rank: Presidency; war ministry; labour secretariat; police
d: The United Officers' Group (GOU) was a secret nationalist association of Argentine army officers, mostly colonels and lieutenant colonels, formed in March 1943; members swore an oath of loyalty. Most historians credit it with a crucial role in the coup of 4 June 1943, though some, such as Robert Potash, play this down. Members then took key posts: Juan Perón became head of the Labour Department, Minister of War and, in July 1944, Vice President; Emilio Ramírez became Buenos Aires police chief; Luis Perlinger became interior minister. In February 1944 the GOU dissolved itself to free members from their oath to President Ramírez, who was then forced out. Perón used the labour post to build union support and won the presidency in 1946.
cite: Revolution of 1943; Juan Perón (Wikipedia, citing Potash and Félix Luna)

n: Chávez's secret army cell MBR-200 recruited 2,367 troops, then took power
rank: Army battalions; later presidency and intelligence service
d: Hugo Chávez founded a secret movement inside Venezuela's army on 17 December 1982 with fellow officers Felipe Acosta Carlez and Jesús Urdaneta, swearing an oath under the Samán de Güere tree. Starting as a study circle, it recruited officers and planned a coup; by 4 February 1992, when it tried to seize power, about 2,367 military personnel from 10 army battalions were involved. The coup failed, but the movement became Chávez's Fifth Republic Movement, and he was elected president in 1998, taking office in February 1999 and ruling until his death in 2013. Co-founder Urdaneta was put in charge of the national intelligence service, and fellow 1992 plotters Francisco Arias Cárdenas and Hernán Grüber Odremán became governors of Zulia and Caracas.
cite: Revolutionary Bolivarian Movement-200; Hugo Chávez (Wikipedia)

n: RADEPA officers' lodge put its member Villarroel in Bolivia's presidency
d: Razón de Patria (RADEPA) was a faction of young Bolivian army officers founded in 1934 by Bolivian prisoners of war held in Paraguay during the Chaco War. It backed military involvement in politics and wanted to limit foreign control of Bolivia's natural resources. From September to December 1943 it coordinated in secret with the Revolutionary Nationalist Movement (MNR), and on 20 December 1943 the two overthrew President Enrique Peñaranda. RADEPA member Gualberto Villarroel became head of state, later proclaimed constitutional president in 1944, and MNR figures such as Víctor Paz Estenssoro took cabinet posts. On 21 July 1946 crowds stormed the presidential palace and killed Villarroel.
cite: Gualberto Villarroel (Wikipedia)

n: Clandestine UME society enrolled nearly half Spain's officers before 1936
rank: Officer corps of the Republican army
d: The Unión Militar Española (UME) was a clandestine, pro-fascist society of officers inside the armed forces of the Spanish Republic, formed in late 1933 by Colonel Emilio Rodríguez Tarduchy and soon led by Captain Bartolomé Barba Hernández. It first drew younger, junior officers, but by early 1936 it was estimated to include almost half of all serving officers, many also in the Falange. UME member Valentín Galarza opened contact with General Franco in 1935. In early 1936 the UME placed itself at the disposal of General Mola's conspiracy and joined the plans for the July 1936 coup, which began the Civil War; most members joined the Nationalist forces. It is also linked to killings that helped trigger the war.
cite: Unión Militar Española (Wikipedia)

n: Golden Square colonels steered Iraq's cabinets, then seized power in 1941
d: The Golden Square was a cabal of four pro-Axis Iraqi officers, Salah al-Din al-Sabbagh, Kamil Shabib, Fahmi Said and air force chief Mahmud Salman, part of a wider 'Circle of Seven' and encouraged by German and Italian envoys including Fritz Grobba. Because Iraqi governments of the 1930s needed army backing to survive, these officers held real power over who governed. On 1 April 1941 they and Rashid Ali al-Gaylani overthrew the regent's government and set up a 'National Defence Government'. Britain invaded in the Anglo-Iraqi War that followed; the plotters fled, and all four were later returned to Iraq and executed.
cite: Golden Square (Iraq) (Wikipedia)

n: Can Lao: Nhu's secret party placed cells across South Vietnam's state
rank: Army, police, civil service and assembly
d: The Cần Lao Party was set up on 2 September 1954 by Ngô Đình Nhu and his brother Ngô Đình Diệm, who became South Vietnam's president; Nhu was its general secretary. It worked covertly through cells whose members often knew only a few others. Members were placed in the army, civil service, police, national assembly, schools and media, and membership grew from about 10,000 in 1955 to 1,386,757 active members in 1962. Historian Bernard Fall called it 'a state within a state'. After the November 1963 coup in which Diệm and Nhu were killed, the party was banned and dissolved.
cite: Cần Lao (Wikipedia, citing Bernard Fall)

n: Orange Order members held every Northern Ireland premiership, 1921–69
rank: Prime Minister and cabinet of Northern Ireland
d: The Orange Order, a Protestant fraternal society, held a formal place inside Northern Ireland's ruling Ulster Unionist Party: when the Ulster Unionist Council was formed in 1905 the Order had 50 of its 200 seats, a link it kept until 2005. From 1921 to 1969 every Prime Minister of Northern Ireland was an Orangeman, all but three cabinet ministers were, and 87 of the 95 MPs who never reached cabinet were members. Prime Minister James Craig said in 1934 that he was 'an Orangeman first and a politician and a member of this parliament afterwards' and spoke of 'a Protestant Parliament and a Protestant State'. The Unionist party, led by Orangemen, governed without interruption until direct rule from London in 1972.
cite: Orange Order (Wikipedia, citing Ulster Unionist Council history and Craig's 1932–34 speeches)

n: Secret IRB recruited Irish Volunteer leaders and launched the 1916 Rising
d: The Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB), a secret oath-bound society founded in 1858 to win an independent Irish republic, backed the founding of the Irish Volunteers militia in November 1913 and then recruited the Volunteers' senior members into the IRB, so that a body with no stated republican aim could be used for one. A secret IRB Military Committee of Tom Clarke, Seán Mac Diarmada, Joseph Plunkett, Thomas MacDonagh and Patrick Pearse planned a rising, and in January 1916 the IRB Supreme Council fixed Easter Sunday as its date. The Easter Rising followed. Michael Collins later served as president of the IRB Supreme Council from 1920 to 1922, and its council voted 11–4 to accept the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty.
cite: Irish Republican Brotherhood (Wikipedia)

n: IRB faction inside Ireland's National Army purged after 1924 mutiny
d: After the Irish Civil War, the Irish Republican Brotherhood, a secret oath-bound society, re-formed in 1923 as a faction inside the Free State's National Army, backing Minister for Defence Richard Mulcahy against a rival group of officers, the 'Old IRA'. The rivalry over the IRB's hold on army posts led to the Army Mutiny of 1924. In its aftermath Mulcahy resigned and Kevin O'Higgins, acting head of government, dismissed other IRB members from the army. The IRB then dissolved itself, and the episode helped establish civilian control over the Irish army.
cite: Irish Republican Brotherhood (Wikipedia)

n: Black Dragon Society counted ministers and generals; army used its network
rank: Cabinet ministers; senior army officers; intelligence
d: The Black Dragon Society (Kokuryūkai) was an ultranationalist society founded in 1901 by Uchida Ryōhei as the successor to Tōyama Mitsuru's Gen'yōsha, with the stated aim of keeping Russia north of the Amur River. Its members included Japanese cabinet ministers, senior army officers and intelligence operatives. The Imperial Japanese Army used the society's network for espionage, sabotage and assassination during the Russo-Japanese War, the annexation of Korea and the Siberian Intervention, and it organised Manchurian guerrillas against Russian forces. The American occupation authorities ordered it disbanded in 1946.
cite: Black Dragon Society (Wikipedia)

n: Bavarian Illuminati placed members in state bodies until banned in 1785
rank: Civic and state governing bodies; court officials
d: The Illuminati were a secret society founded on 1 May 1776 by Adam Weishaupt, a professor at the University of Ingolstadt in Bavaria, and four students. It recruited heavily among lawyers, academics, churchmen and officials, and its members came to hold seats in many civic and state governing bodies, where some court officials reportedly favoured fellow members. About 650 members can be verified at the end of 1784, and the true total was perhaps about 1,300. Elector Charles Theodore banned it and other secret societies by edicts from 1784; the edict of 2 March 1785 effectively ended it. The government seized its papers in 1786–87 and published them in 1787.
cite: Illuminati (Wikipedia)

n: Rosicrucian Wöllner made Prussia's minister of justice and religion
rank: Minister of Justice; head of the Office for Worship
d: Johann Christoph von Wöllner was a supreme director of circles of the Order of the Golden and Rosy Cross, a secret Rosicrucian society, and a friend of fellow member Johann Rudolph von Bischoffswerder; King Frederick William II of Prussia was himself a member under the order name Ormesus. In 1788 the king made Wöllner Minister of Justice and head of the Office for Worship. Under the decree of 9 July 1788 he helped set up a commission to oversee religious activity across Prussia, with powers to confiscate money and property. Frederick the Great had earlier called him 'a treacherous and intriguing priest'.
cite: Johann Christoph von Wöllner (Wikipedia)

n: Carbonari officers forced a constitution on the King of Naples
d: The Carbonari were a secret revolutionary society whose members in the Kingdom of Naples included nobles, priests, landlords, government officials and army officers. On 1 July 1820 two officers, Michele Morelli and Joseph Silvati, led cavalry regiments towards Nola, and General Guglielmo Pepe and many other officers and officials joined. King Ferdinand I agreed to grant a constitution and a parliament. The Holy Alliance sent an Austrian army in February 1821 that defeated the movement; Morelli and Silvati were sentenced to death and Pepe went into exile.
cite: Carbonari (Wikipedia, citing Villari 1911)

n: Carbonária's 40,000 members drove Portugal's 1910 republican revolution
d: The Portuguese Carbonária was a secret, anti-clerical revolutionary society, refounded in 1896 by Artur Augusto Duarte da Luz de Almeida and organised in a hierarchy of cells with military training. It took part in plots against the monarchy; King Carlos I and his heir Luís Filipe were assassinated on 1 February 1908 in a conspiracy involving the Carbonária. By 1910 the society had about 40,000 members, and it played a key role in the revolution of 5 October 1910 that ended the monarchy and created the Portuguese Republic.
cite: Carbonária (Wikipedia)

n: Sun Yat-sen's secret Tongmenghui became the core of China's ruling party
d: The Tongmenghui was a secret society and underground resistance movement founded in Tokyo on 20 August 1905 by Sun Yat-sen, Song Jiaoren and others, by merging Sun's Xingzhonghui, the Guangfuhui and other revolutionary groups. Its members organised against the Qing dynasty, and after the 1911 Xinhai Revolution Sun became Provisional President of the new Republic of China in January 1912. In August 1912 the Tongmenghui formed the nucleus of the Kuomintang, the Nationalist party that later ruled China and then Taiwan.
cite: Tongmenghui (Wikipedia)

n: La Cagoule: secret society funded by industrialists infiltrated French army
d: La Cagoule was a secret far-right society founded in 1936 by Eugène Deloncle, organised in military-style cells whose members swore an oath on pain of death. It was funded by industrialists including L'Oréal founder Eugène Schueller and Louis Renault. Through Georges Loustaunau-Lacau's Corvignolles network it infiltrated parts of the French army to obtain weapons, and it carried out assassinations and the bombing of two employers' buildings on 11 September 1937 to blame communists. It planned to overthrow the Popular Front government in November 1937; police had infiltrated it, and about 70 men were arrested. Member Joseph Darnand later led the Vichy regime's Milice.
cite: La Cagoule (Wikipedia)

n: US envoy Poinsett used York Rite lodges to reshape Mexico's cabinet
d: Joel Roberts Poinsett, the first United States minister to Mexico, promoted the York Rite branch of Freemasonry there, which was tied to US political interests and became one of three competing Masonic strands in Mexican politics. He used his connection with the York Rite lodges to pressure President Guadalupe Victoria into removing allies such as Lucas Alamán from his cabinet. Some historians call this the first US 'soft' coup in Latin America, saying it installed a compliant government that dropped plans for a naval expedition against Spanish-held Cuba and Puerto Rico. Poinsett became caught up in Mexico's political turmoil and was recalled in 1829–30.
cite: Joel Roberts Poinsett (Wikipedia)

n: Irish bishops' secret objections killed a health scheme; minister resigned
d: Ireland's Catholic bishops, led by Archbishop John Charles McQuaid of Dublin, steered the cabinet of Taoiseach John A. Costello to drop the Mother and Child Scheme, Health Minister Noël Browne's 1950 plan for free health care for mothers and children up to 16. On 5 April 1951 McQuaid told Costello the scheme was 'opposed to Catholic social teaching', and Costello told McQuaid he would accept the Church's view even if it brought down the government. Browne was left alone in cabinet and resigned on 11 April 1951. The next day The Irish Times published the private correspondence between the bishops and ministers, revealing how far the hierarchy had decided government policy.
cite: Mother and Child Scheme (Wikipedia)

n: Santamaria's Catholic 'Movement' took hold of Labor unions; party split
rank: Australian Labor Party and trade unions
d: The Catholic Social Studies Movement, founded in Victoria in 1941 by B. A. Santamaria with the backing of Archbishop Daniel Mannix, gained a large influence over the 'Industrial Groups', anti-communist factions organised by Catholic members inside the Australian Labor Party and its trade unions from the late 1940s. After the 1954 federal election Labor leader H. V. Evatt turned on the 'Groupers', saying they held disproportionate influence in the party. This led to the 1955 Labor split: many Groupers resigned or were expelled, several unions left, and they formed what became the Democratic Labor Party. The split and the DLP's preferences to the Liberals are described as a major reason Labor stayed out of federal power for almost 30 years.
cite: Industrial Groups (Wikipedia)

n: Jamaat-e-Islami activists given judicial jobs under Zia, Pakistan
d: Jamaat-e-Islami, Pakistan's main Islamist movement, became seen as the ideological and political arm of General Zia-ul-Haq's military government after 1977, with members at times holding cabinet posts including information and broadcasting. Journalist Owen Bennett-Jones writes that 'tens of thousands of Jamaat activists and sympathisers were given jobs in the judiciary', and that these appointments kept Zia's Islamisation agenda alive after his death in 1988. Jamaat also backed Zia's support for the war against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan. Zia later distanced himself from the party over elections.
cite: Jamaat-e-Islami Pakistan (Wikipedia, citing Owen Bennett-Jones, Pakistan: Eye of the Storm)

n: Haqqania seminary graduates fill the Taliban government's ministries
rank: Interior, foreign, higher education and other ministries
d: Darul Uloom Haqqania, a Deobandi seminary at Akora Khattak in Pakistan nicknamed the 'University of Jihad', has supplied much of the leadership of Afghanistan's Taliban. After the Taliban took power in August 2021 its graduates held senior posts including acting Interior Minister Sirajuddin Haqqani, acting Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi, Higher Education Minister Abdul Baqi Haqqani and Hajj Minister Noor Mohammad Saqib; the school said the justice and water ministers and various governors, commanders and judges were also alumni. Its chancellor Samiul Haq, called the 'Father of the Taliban', wrote in 2015 that about 90 percent of the religiously educated people in the Taliban government were graduates or sons of graduates. The seminary reserves 400 places for Afghan students.
cite: Darul Uloom Haqqania (Wikipedia, citing Rassler and Brown; Samiul Haq 2015)

n: Brotherhood leader Turabi made Sudan's attorney general; Islamists placed
d: Hassan al-Turabi, who had taken control of Sudan's Muslim Brotherhood and led its political arm, the Islamic Charter Front, was brought back by President Gaafar Nimeiry under a 1977 'National Reconciliation' and made Justice Minister and Attorney General in 1979. His movement took a 'top down' approach, placing party members in high posts in government and the security services. Turabi became Nimeiry's foreign-affairs adviser in 1983 and was instrumental in institutionalising sharia law in northern Sudan; Nimeiry's September 1983 laws imposed it on the whole country and set off renewed civil war in the south. This groundwork preceded the 1989 coup that Turabi is alleged to have designed.
cite: Hassan al-Turabi; Gaafar Nimeiry (Wikipedia)

n: Sudan's Free Officers took power in 1969; Nimeiry led their council
rank: Revolutionary Command Council; head of state
d: Sudan's Free Officers were a clandestine group of army officers on the Egyptian model. On 25 May 1969 Colonel Gaafar Nimeiry, commanding the Khartoum garrison, joined other Free Officers in overthrowing the civilian government of Ismail al-Azhari, in what they called the 'May Revolution'. Nimeiry made himself chairman of their Revolutionary Command Council and ruled Sudan until 1985, later bringing Islamists into government and imposing sharia law across the country in September 1983.
cite: Gaafar Nimeiry (Wikipedia)

n: RSS-founded think tank VIF supplied Modi's security adviser and PMO chiefs
rank: National Security Adviser; Prime Minister's Office
d: The Vivekananda International Foundation (VIF), a Delhi think tank set up in December 2009 by Vivekananda Kendra, an organisation of the RSS-led Hindu nationalist family (Sangh Parivar), supplied several of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's top officials in 2014. Its founding director, former Intelligence Bureau chief Ajit Doval, became National Security Adviser; Nripendra Misra became Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, and P. K. Mishra Additional Principal Secretary. Other VIF figures went to the NITI Aayog planning body, the Lieutenant Governor's post in Delhi, the state broadcaster Prasar Bharati and the national journalism institute. The VIF says it has no formal links to the RSS or BJP. Doval remains National Security Adviser.
cite: Vivekananda International Foundation (Wikipedia, citing Tehelka Aug 2014, The Caravan Nov 2017, Business Standard Jun 2014)

n: RSS 'dual membership' of ministers Vajpayee and Advani broke India's government
d: After the Janata Party won India's 1977 election, former leaders of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, the RSS's political wing, took major posts: Atal Bihari Vajpayee became External Affairs Minister and L. K. Advani Information and Broadcasting Minister. Other Janata leaders pressed them to give up their membership of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, while in government. Vajpayee, Advani and other former Jana Sangh members chose to stay in the RSS. The dispute fed the collapse of Prime Minister Morarji Desai's government, which resigned on 19 July 1979, and the RSS-linked members then founded the Bharatiya Janata Party in 1980.
cite: Janata Party (Wikipedia)

n: RSS full-timer of 17 years Khattar made Haryana's chief minister
rank: Chief Minister of Haryana; Union Minister
d: Manohar Lal Khattar joined the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation that trains and supplies cadres for the BJP, in 1977 and became a full-time organiser (pracharak) about three years later, working in that role for 17 years before the RSS moved him to the BJP in 1994. Elected to the Haryana assembly for the first time in 2014, he was sworn in as the state's Chief Minister on 26 October 2014, the BJP's first in Haryana, and held the post until 2024. On 10 June 2024 he became Union Minister of Power and of Housing and Urban Affairs in Modi's government.
cite: Manohar Lal Khattar (Wikipedia)

n: Heritage's 1981 Mandate for Leadership: 60% of 2,000 proposals acted on
rank: Reagan cabinet; Interior Secretary; NEH chair
d: The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank in Washington, wrote a 20-volume, roughly 3,000-page programme for Ronald Reagan's incoming administration, Mandate for Leadership, with more than 2,000 recommendations for moving the federal government in a conservative direction. Reagan handed out copies at his first cabinet meeting, and the administration hired contributors including James G. Watt, who became Secretary of the Interior, and William Bennett, who became chair of the National Endowment for the Humanities and later Education Secretary. According to its authors, about 60 percent of the proposals had been implemented or begun by the end of Reagan's first year. Heritage has produced a Mandate for each new conservative administration since, most recently Project 2025.
cite: Mandate for Leadership (Wikipedia, citing Washington Post 16 Nov 1980 and New York Times 2002)

n: PNAC think tank's signatories took 10 posts in Bush's Iraq-war government
who: Project for the New American Century
rank: Vice President; Defence Secretary; Deputy Defence Secretary
d: The Project for the New American Century (PNAC), a Washington think tank founded in 1997 by William Kristol and Robert Kagan, called in an open letter to President Clinton in January 1998 for the removal of Saddam Hussein; signatories included Donald Rumsfeld, Paul Wolfowitz, Elliott Abrams and John Bolton. Ten of the 25 people who signed its 1997 statement of principles then served in George W. Bush's administration, among them Vice President Dick Cheney, Defence Secretary Rumsfeld and Deputy Defence Secretary Wolfowitz; Scooter Libby became Cheney's chief of staff and Bolton UN ambassador. Shortly after 11 September 2001 PNAC urged Bush to remove Saddam, and its members supported the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Some scholars argue its influence on the decision has been exaggerated.
cite: Project for the New American Century (Wikipedia, citing Abelson and Parmar)

n: ADF lawyers wrote Mississippi's abortion law that ended Roe v. Wade
rank: State legislation; Mississippi Attorney General's legal team
d: Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF), a Christian conservative legal organisation, wrote the model for Mississippi's 15-week abortion ban, a law designed to provoke a legal challenge to Roe v. Wade. When it was challenged, ADF lawyers joined the Mississippi Attorney General's legal team to defend it, and in Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) the Supreme Court overturned Roe and Casey and returned abortion law to the states. ADF says it authored at least 130 bills in 34 states in 2022, of which more than 30 became law, and its members wrote model 'bathroom bills'. Former ADF attorney Mike Johnson became Speaker of the House of Representatives on 25 October 2023.
cite: Alliance Defending Freedom (Wikipedia, citing ADF 'Who We Are', The Nation, NBC News 2021, CBS News 2023)

n: Pentagon watchdog: six senior officers endorsed Christian Embassy in uniform
rank: Generals and colonels at the Pentagon
d: Christian Embassy, an evangelical group affiliated with Campus Crusade for Christ (now Cru) and founded in 1975 to minister to members of Congress, officials and diplomats, filmed a promotional video in 2004 in which seven military officers, in uniform at the Pentagon, endorsed it. After the video went online in November 2006 the Military Religious Freedom Foundation asked the Defence Department's Inspector General to investigate. The Inspector General's July 2007 report found that six senior officers, four generals and two colonels, had improperly endorsed and taken part in a non-federal group while in uniform, some implying they spoke for senior military leaders; a chaplain was found to have given the group a 'selective benefit', and one general had called it a 'quasi-federal entity'.
cite: Christian Embassy (Wikipedia, citing DoD Inspector General report, July 2007)

n: Scientology's secret Project Normandy aimed to take control of Clearwater
rank: Clearwater city government and local media
d: The Church of Scientology ran a secret operation, Project Normandy, to take control of Clearwater, Florida, by infiltrating city offices and local media. A front group, the 'United Churches of Florida', bought the Fort Harrison Hotel for $3 million, which became the church's headquarters. A 'Top Secret' internal document of 5 December 1975 set the aim of working out whom to penetrate and 'handle' to establish 'area control'. The plan was found in a 1977 FBI raid on Scientology offices and reported by the Clearwater Sun in November 1979. The church had also tried to entrap Mayor Gabriel Cazares in a sex scandal and staged a fake hit-and-run; he sued, and the church settled in 1986. Clearwater remains its main base.
cite: Project Normandy (Wikipedia, citing Clearwater Sun 3 Nov 1979)

n: Claremont's John Eastman wrote Trump's plan to block the 2020 count
rank: President's legal strategy; Vice President's certification role
d: John Eastman, founder and director of the Claremont Institute's Center for Constitutional Jurisprudence and a former chair of a Federalist Society practice group, wrote memos at the request of someone in the Trump administration arguing that Vice President Mike Pence could hold up certification of the 2020 election, calling the vice president 'the ultimate arbiter'. Pence rejected the argument when they met on 5 January 2021. In March 2022 federal judge David O. Carter found it 'more likely than not' that Eastman and Trump plotted to obstruct the certification. Eastman was indicted in Georgia in August 2023, but those charges were dropped in November 2025, when Trump also pardoned him. The California Supreme Court ordered him disbarred on 15 April 2026.
cite: John C. Eastman (Wikipedia, citing Eastman v. Thompson ruling March 2022 and California State Bar Court)

n: Adam Smith Institute papers became the poll tax and rail privatisation
d: The Adam Smith Institute, a London free-market think tank founded in 1977 by Madsen Pirie and Eamonn Butler, wrote policy that British governments turned into law. It published Douglas Mason's proposal to replace local rates with a flat per-head charge, and its papers of 1981–1985 set out the basis of the poll tax, introduced as the Community Charge in Scotland in 1989 and in England and Wales in 1990, then abolished after protests. Its 1987 paper The Right Lines proposed competing private train franchises on a separately owned network, which John Major's government enacted. Its 1981–83 Omega Project produced 19 papers, one per government department. The Thatcher government relied on it, the Centre for Policy Studies and the IEA for policy.
cite: Adam Smith Institute (Wikipedia)

n: Fabian Society got 229 members into Parliament in 1945 and shaped policy
d: The Fabian Society, a socialist society founded in London in 1884 to move Britain gradually towards socialism by working through institutions, had 229 of its members elected to the House of Commons at the 1945 general election, which brought Clement Attlee's Labour government to power; Attlee and Hugh Dalton were among Fabians in Labour's leadership. Sidney Webb, a leading Fabian, had earlier written the constitution of the Labour Representation Committee, which borrowed heavily from the society's founding documents. Its Fabian Colonial Bureau, set up in October 1940 with Rita Hinden as secretary, strongly influenced the colonial policy of the Attlee government from 1945 to 1951.
cite: Fabian Society (Wikipedia)

n: Fundación Mediterránea economists took over Argentina's economy ministry
d: Domingo Cavallo used the Fundación Mediterránea, a business-funded think tank in Córdoba, to prepare a team of economists to take over Argentina's economy, and backed Carlos Menem's 1989 presidential bid. Cavallo, who had briefly led the central bank in 1982, became Economy Minister in February 1991 and brought that team into the ministry. On 1 April 1991 he signed the Convertibility law that fixed the peso at one US dollar, and he served until 1996. Recalled as minister in March 2001, he froze bank deposits in late November 2001, measures known as the 'corralito', shortly before Argentina's economic collapse and record debt default.
cite: Domingo Cavallo (Wikipedia)

n: Gremialista leader Guzmán drafted Pinochet's 1980 constitution
rank: Constitutional commission; adviser to the junta
d: Jaime Guzmán founded the Movimiento Gremial, a Catholic conservative student movement, at the Catholic University of Chile's law school in March 1967. After the 1973 coup he became a trusted adviser to General Augusto Pinochet without holding an official post, and was legal adviser to the Ortúzar Commission, formed on 26 September 1973 to draft a new constitution. He is called the principal architect of the 1980 Constitution, approved in a plebiscite under the dictatorship, which governed Chile for four decades. He founded the Independent Democratic Union (UDI) party in 1983 and was assassinated in 1991. Chileans voted to replace the constitution in 2020 but rejected two drafts.
cite: Jaime Guzmán (Wikipedia)

n: IPES think-tank chief Golbery founded Brazil's SNI spy service after 1964
who: IPES / Golbery do Couto e Silva
rank: Head of the National Information Service; presidential chief of staff
d: The Institute for Research and Social Studies (IPES) was a conservative think tank founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1962 by business leaders Augusto Trajano de Azevedo Antunes and Antônio Gallotti. It ran anti-government propaganda and worked to co-opt organisations opposing President João Goulart, and a 1963 parliamentary inquiry investigated it. General Golbery do Couto e Silva headed the institute. After the military coup of 31 March 1964 Golbery became the first head of the new National Information Service (SNI), the regime's intelligence agency, from June 1964 to 1967, and later chief of staff of the presidency from 1974 to 1981. In 1966 the regime declared IPES an 'entity of public utility'.
cite: Instituto de Pesquisas e Estudos Sociais; Golbery do Couto e Silva (Wikipedia)

n: Harvard advisers steered Russia's privatisation; Harvard paid $26.5m
d: The Harvard Institute for International Development (HIID) received $40.4 million from USAID, without normal competitive bidding, for a 1992–1997 project led by economist Andrei Shleifer and lawyer Jonathan Hay to help rebuild Russia's economy, including advising on the privatisation of state industry. Oversight was later described as lax. In 1997 USAID ended a $14 million grant after Shleifer was accused of helping his wife's investments in Russia while advising its government. The US government sued, and in 2005 Harvard agreed to a $26.5 million settlement. The Russia scandal was one reason a Harvard task force recommended closing HIID in 2000.
cite: Harvard Institute for International Development (Wikipedia)

n: Matsushita Institute trained 66 politicians, including two prime ministers
who: Matsushita Institute of Government and Management
d: The Matsushita Institute of Government and Management was founded on 21 June 1979 by Kōnosuke Matsushita, the founder of Panasonic, with his own money, to 'cultivate young leaders to guide Japan into the twenty-first century'. It is known for training young people to win elections. By 2006, 66 of its 213 graduates had won elected office, including 28 members of the House of Representatives. Its graduates include Democratic Party Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda, Liberal Democratic Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and Seiji Maehara and Itsunori Onodera.
cite: Matsushita Institute of Government and Management (Wikipedia)

n: 'Kaduna Mafia' network said to fill Nigeria's top military-era posts
rank: Central bank governor; defence and finance ministries; chief of staff
d: The 'Kaduna Mafia' is a name, popularised by journalist Mvendaga Jibo, for a loose network of northern Nigerian civil servants, businessmen, intellectuals and officers based in Kaduna that took shape after 1966. People named as members held top posts: Shehu Musa Yar'Adua as Chief of Staff, Supreme Headquarters (1976–1979), Adamu Ciroma as Central Bank Governor (1975–1979) and later Finance Minister, Iya Abubakar as Defence Minister, and Mamman Daura as editor of the New Nigerian. The network is said to have had its greatest success under Obasanjo's military regime and to have returned under the Yar'Adua and Buhari governments. Most claims of its control are hedged, and its membership is unknown.
cite: Kaduna Mafia (Wikipedia, citing Fagbola 1987, William Graf 1988, Daily Trust 2016)

n: Ex-NU chairman Wahid elected president by NU-dominated party, Indonesia
d: Abdurrahman Wahid led Nahdlatul Ulama (NU), Indonesia's largest Muslim organisation with tens of millions of followers, as chairman from 1984 to 1999. In 1998 he approved the creation of the National Awakening Party (PKB), which was dominated by NU members and made him head of its advisory council. The PKB named him its presidential candidate in February 1999, and on 20 October 1999 the People's Consultative Assembly elected him Indonesia's fourth president by 373 votes to 313 over Megawati Sukarnoputri. He was impeached and removed on 23 July 2001.
cite: Abdurrahman Wahid (Wikipedia)

n: ICMI under minister Habibie moved Muslim intellectuals into Suharto's state
rank: Civil service and central ministries; vice-presidency
d: The Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals (ICMI) was formed in 1990 under B. J. Habibie, then Minister of Research and Technology, with President Suharto's permission as he courted Islamic support. In return for backing the regime, ICMI gained influence over policy and administration: its members moved into the civil service and central ministries, and it helped set up religious courts, Bank Muamalat and the newspaper Republika. By 1994 it had about 80,000 members. Critics, including groups in Nahdlatul Ulama, called it a lobby for Suharto's regime and a vehicle for Habibie, who became vice-president in 1998 and then president when Suharto resigned.
cite: Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals (Wikipedia)

n: ABIM Islamic youth founder Anwar entered cabinet and Islamised schooling
rank: Education and finance ministries; Deputy Prime Minister
d: Anwar Ibrahim co-founded the Malaysian Islamic Youth Movement (ABIM) in 1971 and was its second president. In 1982 he joined Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's party UMNO, on advice that Mahathir was committed to Islamisation, and entered government. He became Minister of Culture, Youth and Sports in 1983, Agriculture in 1984, Education in 1986, Finance in 1991 and Deputy Prime Minister in 1993. As Education Minister he made many curriculum changes, and analysts link the rise of social conservatism and Islamism among Malays to the Islamisation of schooling under him. He became Prime Minister in 2022.
cite: Anwar Ibrahim (Wikipedia)

n: Sasson report: state ministries built illegal settler outposts
rank: Housing, defence, education and energy ministries; WZO settlement division
d: An official report commissioned by Prime Minister Ariel Sharon and written by former senior prosecutor Talia Sasson, published on 8 March 2005, found that Israeli state bodies had spent millions of shekels supporting unauthorised West Bank settlement outposts, against the government's own rules. The Defence Ministry approved trailers to start outposts; the Housing Ministry supplied 400 mobile homes, some placed on private Palestinian land; the World Zionist Organization's settlement division, the Education Ministry and the Energy Ministry also helped. The settler movement Gush Emunim, founded in 1974, and its building arm Amana drove the outposts, and Amana received about 100 million shekels in state money in 2013–2015. In 2017 Gush Emunim co-founder Pinchas Wallerstein was appointed to head a committee on legalising outposts.
cite: Sasson Report; Gush Emunim (Wikipedia)

n: CIA directed Iran's 1953 coup, including bribes to members of parliament
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), with British help, bribed members of Iran's parliament and organised the security forces to remove Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh in August 1953, after he nationalised Iran's oil. A CIA internal history released by the National Security Archive in August 2013 says the coup 'was carried out under CIA direction as an act of US foreign policy'. The plan, codenamed TPAJAX, also included propaganda against Mossadegh, persuading the Shah to cooperate and stirring up demonstrations. General Fazlollah Zahedi replaced Mossadegh, and the CIA arranged to pay his new government $5 million within days. The Shah ruled as a close US ally until the 1979 revolution.
cite: Foreign Policy, 19 Aug 2013; Al Jazeera, 20 Aug 2013 (CIA history released by the National Security Archive)

n: CIA secretly funded Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party
d: The CIA secretly gave money to Japan's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), which has governed Japan for most years since 1955, and to its members during the 1950s and 1960s. Former intelligence officers described the payments to The New York Times in 1994: the aim was to make Japan a bulwark against communism and undermine the Japanese left, and the CIA also recruited informers inside the party. In July 2006 the State Department's official history series, Foreign Relations of the United States, formally acknowledged the covert funding for the first time, saying it was meant to keep an LDP-led government in power. Some money also went to moderate Socialists. The LDP denies receiving it.
cite: New York Times News Service via Deseret News, 9 Oct 1994; Japan Times, 20 Jul 2006 (FRUS vol. XXIX part 2)

n: CIA paid over half of Frei's campaign costs in Chile's 1964 election
d: The CIA paid slightly more than half the cost of Eduardo Frei's Christian Democratic campaign in Chile's 1964 presidential election, without Frei being told. The US Senate's Church Committee, which investigated US intelligence abuses, set this out in its 1975 report 'Covert Action in Chile 1963–1973'. It counted about $13.4 million spent in that decade, $8 million of it on elections and party support, including money for chosen congressional candidates in 1965 and 1968–69 and about $4 million for opposition parties in 1971–73. The CIA also funded the newspaper El Mercurio. On 15 September 1970 President Nixon ordered the CIA to help organise a military coup against the elected president, Salvador Allende.
cite: US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence Activities (Church Committee), 'Covert Action in Chile 1963–1973', 1975

n: CIA handed 'bags of money' to Italian politicians before the 1948 vote
d: The CIA delivered cash to chosen Italian politicians — Christian Democrats, Republicans and other pro-American parties — to pay campaign costs such as posters and pamphlets before Italy's April 1948 general election. F. Mark Wyatt, a CIA officer involved, described the 'bags of money' in a later interview and said guidance on whom to back came partly from Christian Democrat leader Alcide De Gasperi. The Christian Democrats won about 48% of the vote and the Communist-led Popular Democratic Front 31%. A US Defense Department draft history says the CIA then gave an average of $5 million a year in covert aid in Italy from the late 1940s to the early 1960s.
cite: F. Mark Wyatt interview, CNN Cold War series (National Security Archive); US DoD draft history cited in 'CIA activities in Italy'

n: CIA-funded Gehlen Organization became West Germany's spy service, the BND
d: The Gehlen Organization, a spy network built after 1945 by Reinhard Gehlen, the Wehrmacht's former intelligence chief on the Eastern Front, worked with the newly created CIA from 1947, and the CIA supplied its money, cars and aircraft. On 1 April 1956 the organisation was turned into West Germany's official foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), with Gehlen as its first president until 1968. It employed hundreds of former Nazi Party members, and Gehlen told a Bundestag committee in 1953 that about 40 of its staff came from the SS and SD, the Nazi party's armed and security branches. The CIA's own declassified history describes the relationship.
cite: CIA history 'CIA and the Origins of the BND, 1945–49' (declassified); Wikipedia, 'Gehlen Organization'

n: CIA paid King Hussein of Jordan millions a year for 20 years
d: The CIA made secret yearly payments of millions of dollars to King Hussein of Jordan for about 20 years, The Washington Post reported in February 1977. Hussein had been king since 1952, so the payments covered most of his reign up to then. President Jimmy Carter halted them a few days before the story ran. The report gave no exact figure. It appeared while Washington was still dealing with the Senate Church Committee's 1975–76 inquiry into the CIA, and US officials began assessing what the disclosure would mean for relations with Jordan, a close US ally in the Middle East.
cite: Washington Post, Feb 1977, as reported by Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 22 Feb 1977

n: CIA delivered bags of cash to Afghan President Karzai's office
d: The CIA delivered cash in bags to the office of Afghanistan's President Hamid Karzai for more than a decade from the start of the 2001 war, The New York Times reported in April 2013, citing sources who put the total at tens of millions of dollars. The sources said much of it went on to Karzai's relatives, associates, politicians and warlords. Karzai confirmed receiving what he called 'small amounts' and said he was grateful; his palace said the money was used for charitable purposes. Some Afghan senators called the payments a breach of national sovereignty. Karzai had earlier admitted taking similar cash from Iran.
cite: New York Times, 28 Apr 2013; NPR, 1 May 2013

n: Iran paid cash to Afghan President Karzai's chief of staff
d: Iran's government gave bags of cash to Umar Daudzai, chief of staff to Afghanistan's President Hamid Karzai, The New York Times reported in October 2010, describing a steady stream of money meant to buy his loyalty and promote Iran's interests inside the presidential palace. Karzai confirmed the payments two days later. He said Iran handed over €500,000 to €700,000 at a time, once or twice a year, and that the money was transparent and paid for the costs of running the president's office. The payments reportedly stopped after Karzai signed a strategic partnership agreement with the United States.
cite: New York Times, 23 Oct 2010; Foreign Policy, 25 Oct 2010; NPR, 1 May 2013

n: CIA paid Peru's spy chief Vladimiro Montesinos at least $10 million
rank: De facto head of National Intelligence Service (SIN)
d: The CIA gave Vladimiro Montesinos, unofficial head of Peru's National Intelligence Service (SIN) under President Alberto Fujimori, at least $10 million in cash from 1990 to September 2000, plus surveillance equipment, the Center for Public Integrity reported in 2001. The money went to a narcotics intelligence unit that Montesinos founded and personally controlled. When the CIA reported his alleged corruption, other US agencies told it to keep working with him. Military intelligence sources said CIA-supplied equipment was used to tap opposition figures, journalists and officers. Montesinos fled after a September 2000 video showed him paying a $15,000 bribe, and Fujimori resigned on 20 November 2000.
cite: Center for Public Integrity, 28 Jul 2001

n: Panama's military ruler Manuel Noriega was on the CIA payroll
d: Manuel Noriega, commander of Panama's armed forces and the country's de facto ruler in the 1980s, was paid at least $300,162 by the CIA for passing it secrets and carrying out other US intelligence operations, according to court documents disclosed in May 1991 ahead of his drug-trafficking trial in Miami. US forces had invaded Panama in December 1989 and taken him to the United States. The disclosure showed that the man in charge of Panama's military and intelligence apparatus had been a paid US source while he also took money from drug traffickers. He was convicted in April 1992.
cite: Tampa Bay Times, 31 May 1991; The Nation, 'April 9, 1992: Manuel Noriega Is Convicted'

n: CIA funded Burnham's party to unseat Cheddi Jagan in British Guiana
d: The CIA secretly funded Forbes Burnham's and Peter D'Aguiar's parties to remove the elected leftist premier Cheddi Jagan in British Guiana, the British colony that became Guyana. The State Department's official history records about $2.08 million approved for covert action there from 1962 to 1968: money and campaign expertise before the December 1964 election, funds linked to the 1964 general strike and help registering opposition voters, while Washington urged Britain to adopt proportional representation and delay independence. The anti-Jagan coalition won in 1964 and the CIA kept funding Burnham as premier. He became the first prime minister of independent Guyana in May 1966.
cite: US State Department, Foreign Relations of the United States 1964–68, vol. XXXII, editorial note 370

n: CIA's LITEMPO network counted two future presidents of Mexico
d: Winston Scott, CIA station chief in Mexico City from 1956, recruited 12 agents inside the Mexican government between 1956 and 1969 under a programme called LITEMPO, an unofficial channel for sensitive political information. Documents published by the National Security Archive in October 2006 identify Gustavo Díaz Ordaz, president from 1964 to 1970 and a personal friend of Scott, as LITEMPO-2, and Luis Echeverría, then a deputy minister at the interior ministry (Gobernación) and president from 1970 to 1976, as LITEMPO-8. Fernando Gutiérrez Barrios of the DFS, Mexico's political police, was LITEMPO-4. The network was active during the 1968 Tlatelolco massacre of students, on which Scott's reporting proved inaccurate.
cite: National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 204, 18 Oct 2006

n: Guatemalan colonel linked to two killings was a paid CIA source
d: Lieutenant Colonel Julio Roberto Alpirez of Guatemala's army was a paid CIA source at the time of two killings he was linked to: that of US citizen Michael DeVine near his ranch in June 1990, and the disappearance and apparent murder in 1992 of guerrilla Efraín Bámaca Velásquez, husband of American lawyer Jennifer Harbury. In April 1995 the acting CIA director, William Studeman, admitted the agency had failed to tell Congress what it knew. Reports said the CIA paid Alpirez up to $44,000 after learning of his alleged role in the DeVine case. The President's Intelligence Oversight Board reviewed the CIA's Guatemalan relationships in a report of 28 June 1996.
cite: Los Angeles Times via Spokesman-Review, 6 Apr 1995; Intelligence Oversight Board, Report on the Guatemala Review, 28 Jun 1996

n: CIA funded Mobutu and Congo's governments after moving against Lumumba
rank: Head of government and army chief
d: From August 1960 the CIA ran a covert political programme in the Congo, first to keep Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba out of power and then to keep chosen pro-Western leaders in office. The State Department's official history records covert funds to Joseph Mobutu's College of Commissioners from late 1960 and payments to Mobutu himself until September 1966. The CIA also paid for the 1961 parliamentary session that approved Cyrille Adoula's government, then funded that government through two parliamentary crises. About $11.7 million was approved for covert action in the Congo from 1960 to 1968, $5.8 million of it for political action. Mobutu ruled the country from 1965 to 1997.
cite: US State Department, Foreign Relations of the United States 1964–68, vol. XXIII, editorial note 1

n: Sarkozy convicted of conspiring to seek Gaddafi's money for 2007 campaign
d: Aides to Nicolas Sarkozy, then France's interior minister, met Libya's intelligence chief Abdullah al-Senussi, brother-in-law of the ruler Muammar Gaddafi, in secret in 2005 to seek money for Sarkozy's 2007 presidential campaign, a Paris court found. On 25 September 2025 it convicted Sarkozy of criminal conspiracy covering 2005–2007 and sentenced him to five years in prison, the first such sentence for a former French president. Claude Guéant received six years and Brice Hortefeux two. The court acquitted Sarkozy of corruption and illegal campaign financing, saying there was no proof Libyan money reached the campaign. The case began with a 2012 Mediapart report. Sarkozy denies wrongdoing and is appealing.
cite: Al Jazeera, 25 Sep 2025; PBS NewsHour, 25 Sep 2025

n: Saddam's Iraq allegedly paid the head of the UN Oil-for-Food programme
d: Benon Sevan, the UN official who ran the Oil-for-Food programme, allegedly took about $160,000 in bribes from Saddam Hussein's government. The programme let sanctioned Iraq sell limited amounts of oil to buy food and humanitarian goods; Iraq abused it by selling oil on the black market and bribing officials. An independent inquiry led by former US Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker made the allegations public in August 2005. In January 2007 US prosecutors in New York indicted Sevan for bribery and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, saying the money came through the brother of former UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali. Kofi Annan had suspended Sevan in 2005. He denies the charges and lives in Cyprus.
cite: Jurist, Jan 2007; Independent Inquiry Committee (Volcker), interim report, Aug 2005

n: East German spy Günter Guillaume was Chancellor Brandt's personal aide
d: Günter Guillaume, an agent of East Germany's foreign intelligence service, the HVA (part of the Stasi, the East German Ministry of State Security), became a personal assistant to West German Chancellor Willy Brandt, giving East Berlin a source inside the head of government's office. He was supervised by the HVA's chief, Markus Wolf. West German authorities arrested Guillaume on 24 April 1974, and Brandt, whose policy of opening relations with East Germany had defined his government, resigned as chancellor on 6 May 1974, less than two weeks later.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Guillaume affair'; Deutschlandmuseum, 'A spy at the heart of the West German government', 24 Apr 1974

n: Stasi agent rose to deputy head of the BND's Soviet section
d: Gabriele Gast, on the books of East Germany's foreign intelligence service, the HVA, since 1968, joined West Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), on 1 November 1973. She worked in the section analysing the Soviet Union and by 1986 was its deputy head; her reports went to the Chancellor's office and the foreign and defence ministries. She passed the HVA copies of 49 detailed Western intelligence reports, including analysis of the Reagan–Gorbachev summit. Exposed after East Germany's collapse, she was arrested in September 1990 and sentenced in 1991 to six years and nine months in prison. She was released on probation in 1994.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Gabriele Gast' (Bavarian High Court sentence, 1991)

n: SPD chief whip Karl Wienand convicted of spying for East Germany
d: Karl Wienand, chief whip of the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in West Germany's parliament, the Bundestag, from 1967 to 1974, was convicted in 1996 by the Düsseldorf regional court of spying for East Germany's Ministry of State Security (the Stasi). He was sentenced to two and a half years and fined the 1 million Deutschmarks he had received. In 1973 Wienand had admitted paying Christian Democrat MP Julius Steiner 50,000 marks to abstain in the 1972 no-confidence vote against Chancellor Willy Brandt. The Federal Court of Justice rejected his appeal in 1997, and President Roman Herzog commuted the prison term to probation on health grounds. Wienand denied spying until his death in 2011.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Karl Wienand' (Düsseldorf regional court, 1996)

n: Former Israeli energy minister Gonen Segev spied for Iran
rank: Former energy minister and Knesset member
d: Gonen Segev, Israel's minister of energy and infrastructure in 1995–96 and a former member of the Knesset, Israel's parliament, was recruited by Iranian embassy officials in Nigeria in 2012. He met Iranian intelligence handlers, travelled to Iran twice, received encrypted communications equipment and passed them information. Israel's Shin Bet security service and police announced his arrest in June 2018, after he was refused entry to Equatorial Guinea and sent to Israel. On 9 January 2019 he pleaded guilty to espionage under a deal that dropped the more serious charge of aiding an enemy in wartime, and in February 2019 he was sentenced to 11 years in prison.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Gonen Segev' (Shin Bet statement, Jun 2018; Jerusalem District Court plea, Jan 2019)

n: Israel ran US Navy intelligence analyst Jonathan Pollard as a spy
d: Jonathan Pollard, a US Navy intelligence analyst hired in 1979, passed classified material to Israel from June 1984 until the FBI arrested him on 21 November 1985, just after he left Israel's embassy in Washington. His handler was Rafi Eitan, head of Lekem, an Israeli scientific-intelligence bureau. Israel paid him $10,000 in cash at the start and then a salary that reached $2,500 a month. He was sentenced to life in prison on 4 March 1987. Israel apologised in 1987, gave him citizenship in 1995 and admitted in 1998 that he had been its agent. He was paroled on 20 November 2015.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jonathan Pollard' (US District Court sentence, 1987)

n: Nasser's son-in-law and Sadat's aide Ashraf Marwan was a Mossad source
rank: Presidential aide, Secretary for Foreign Relations
d: Ashraf Marwan, son-in-law of Egypt's President Gamal Abdel Nasser and later part of President Anwar Sadat's inner circle, offered his services at Israel's embassy in London in 1969 and was taken on as a source by Mossad, Israel's foreign intelligence service, in 1970. He passed Egyptian war plans and minutes of high-command meetings and warned of the coming 1973 war. In February 1974 Sadat made him Secretary to the President for Foreign Relations. His role was revealed in 2002; some argued he was a double agent, but historian Uri Bar-Joseph's work established him as a genuine Mossad spy. He died after falling from his London balcony on 27 June 2007.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ashraf Marwan' (Uri Bar-Joseph, The Angel; inquest, 2010)

n: Mossad agent Eli Cohen entered Syria's ruling circle under a false name
d: Mossad trained Eli Cohen, an Egyptian-born Israeli, and gave him the identity of a Syrian businessman, Kamel Amin Thabet. He lived in Buenos Aires from 1961, presenting himself as a source of money for Syria's Ba'ath Party, and moved to Damascus in February 1962. There he hosted ministers, businessmen and officers, lent money to officials and heard them discuss army plans, and he reported Syrian positions on the Golan Heights and a plan to divert the Jordan River's headwaters. He was reportedly on a short list for deputy defence minister. Syrian security caught him on 24 January 1965; a military court sentenced him to death and he was hanged in Damascus on 18 May 1965.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Eli Cohen'

n: Labour minister John Stonehouse was a Czechoslovak agent, MI5 history says
d: John Stonehouse, a Labour MP who served in Harold Wilson's governments as Minister of Technology, Postmaster General and Minister of Posts and Telecommunications between 1967 and 1970, allegedly began spying for Czechoslovakia in 1962. In 1969 Wilson told him of a defector's claim that he was a Czechoslovak agent, which Stonehouse denied. The official history of MI5, Britain's security service, published in 2009, supported the allegation, and in December 2010 it emerged that Margaret Thatcher had agreed in 1980 to keep the matter quiet because there was not enough evidence for a trial. In March 1968 Stonehouse had negotiated a technology cooperation agreement with Czechoslovakia.
cite: Christopher Andrew, The Defence of the Realm (MI5 authorised history), 2009; Wikipedia, 'John Stonehouse'

n: Conservative MP Ray Mawby sold Commons information to Czechoslovak spies
d: Ray Mawby, Conservative MP for Totnes from 1955 to 1983 and assistant Postmaster General in 1963–64, was paid by Czechoslovakia's military intelligence service under the code name 'Laval'. He received £100 for each piece of information and signed a receipt for one payment. He handed over hand-drawn floor plans of the Prime Minister's office in the House of Commons and details of who guarded it, lists of parliamentary committees and information on fellow politicians, and promised to ask questions in the Commons for his handlers. The meetings ran for about a decade and ended in November 1971. The BBC revealed the case on 28 June 2012 from Czech security files.
cite: BBC, 28 Jun 2012 (Czech security service files); Wikipedia, 'Ray Mawby'

n: State Department analyst Kendall Myers spied for Cuba for decades
rank: Analyst, Bureau of Intelligence and Research
d: Walter Kendall Myers worked as a Europe analyst in the US State Department's own intelligence unit, the Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR), which prepares analysis for the Secretary of State, from 2000 until he retired in 2007. US authorities charged that he and his wife had spied for Cuba for nearly three decades. They were arrested in June 2009 after an FBI undercover operation, and in July 2010 he was sentenced to life in prison without parole. Cuba's intelligence service thereby had a source inside the department that sets US policy towards Cuba.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Walter Kendall Myers' (US District Court, Jul 2010)

n: Rwandan officer James Kabarebe commanded Congo's army in 1997–98
d: James Kabarebe, a Rwandan army officer, was chief military strategist of the rebellion that brought Laurent-Désiré Kabila to power in Kinshasa on 17 May 1997, and Kabila then made him chief of staff of the Congolese army. While he held the post, units in eastern Congo recruited more Banyamulenge, Banyarwanda and former Rwandan army troops. Fearing a coup, Kabila dismissed him around 27 July 1998.
