On 4 August 1998 Kabarebe led an airborne assault on Kitona air base with about 3,000 Rwandan and Ugandan soldiers, starting the Second Congo War's push on the capital; Zimbabwean, Namibian and Angolan forces stopped them from taking Kinshasa.
cite: Wikipedia, 'James Kabarebe'

n: Apartheid police spy became deputy director of a Geneva aid fund
rank: Deputy director, International University Exchange Fund
d: Craig Williamson, an officer of apartheid South Africa's Security Branch police, persuaded the director of the International University Exchange Fund (IUEF), a Geneva-based body that paid scholarships for African students with money largely from Swedish donors, to make him deputy director in the late 1970s. The post gave him a way into the banned African National Congress (ANC). He diverted IUEF money to a covert South African operation called 'Long Reach' and used it to set up a news agency that recruited journalists for counter-intelligence. He was exposed in 1980. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission later gave him amnesty for bombings including the 1982 letter-bomb killing of Ruth First.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Craig Williamson' (TRC amnesty decisions 1999–2000)

n: Apartheid South Africa's secret fund bid for a US paper and senators' seats
rank: US Senate elections and a Washington newspaper
d: South Africa's Department of Information ran a secret propaganda programme, Project Annemarie, from the mid-1970s, paid from a slush fund hidden in the defence budget with the Bureau of State Security (BOSS) as banker; estimates put the cost at about $72 million or more. Using US publisher John P. McGoff as a front, it tried in 1974 to buy The Washington Star, and it contributed to the electoral defeats of US Senators John Tunney and Dick Clark, who opposed American involvement in Angola's war. South Africa's Erasmus Commission concluded in 1978–79 that Prime Minister John Vorster knew everything; Vorster and Information Minister Connie Mulder were forced out.
cite: Erasmus Commission reports, Dec 1978 and Jun 1979; Wikipedia, 'Information Scandal'

n: Foccart's Élysée Africa cell ran networks inside former French colonies
d: Jacques Foccart, secretary-general for African and Malagasy affairs to Presidents Charles de Gaulle and Georges Pompidou from 1960 to 1974, built personal networks (réseaux) tying French officials to the leaders of newly independent former colonies, such as Gabon's Omar Bongo and Côte d'Ivoire's Félix Houphouët-Boigny. He negotiated cooperation accords covering finance, education and the military, some defence agreements with secret clauses allowing French intervention, and was given charge of the secret services and of overseeing elections. With Houphouët-Boigny he encouraged French military interventions in Gabon in 1964 and Chad in 1969. Under this system, called Françafrique, the president's African cell, business networks and French intelligence made Africa decisions without parliamentary scrutiny.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jacques Foccart'; Wikipedia, 'Françafrique'

n: French mercenary Bob Denard commanded the Comoros presidential guard
who: Bob Denard and French secret services
d: Bob Denard, a French mercenary who worked for France's secret services, led the 1978 coup that returned Ahmed Abdallah to power in the Comoros and then commanded the islands' Presidential Guard for about eleven years, gaining business interests and Comorian citizenship. The islands also served as a base for getting round the embargo on apartheid South Africa. In 1989 Abdallah ordered the guard disarmed and was shot dead shortly afterwards; French paratroopers took Denard out of the country, and he was later acquitted over the killing for lack of evidence. In 1995 he led another coup, ended by French troops, and the court that later tried him recognised the secret services' role.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bob Denard'

n: Syria's spy chief Ghazi Kanaan picked Lebanon's candidates and officials
rank: Lebanese elections, security and judicial appointments
d: Ghazi Kanaan headed Syrian military intelligence in Lebanon for about twenty years from 1982, during Syria's 1976–2005 military presence there. He vetoed anti-Syrian candidates and pushed pro-Syrian ones onto electoral lists, drew the boundaries of fourteen electoral districts after the 1989 Taif Agreement, and shaped security and judicial appointments; the head of Lebanon's General Security agency reported directly to him. His deputy Rustum Ghazaleh succeeded him in 2002. After former prime minister Rafik Hariri was assassinated in February 2005 and the UN Security Council called for foreign forces to leave, Syria withdrew its troops by 30 April 2005. Kanaan died of a gunshot wound in October 2005.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ghazi Kanaan'; Wikipedia, 'Syrian occupation of Lebanon'; UN Security Council Resolution 1559, 2 Sep 2004

n: Iran hanged ex-deputy defence minister Alireza Akbari as an alleged MI6 spy
d: Iran convicted Alireza Akbari, who had been deputy defence minister under Ali Shamkhani and an adviser to the Iranian navy, of spying for Britain's foreign intelligence service, MI6. Iranian officials said he passed information on 178 Iranian figures, including the nuclear scientist Mohsen Fakhrizadeh. His death sentence was announced on 11 January 2023 and his execution by hanging on 14 January. Akbari and his family denied the charge; in a recording later released by the BBC he said he had been drugged, held in solitary confinement and tortured into confessing. Britain's foreign secretary called the allegations politically motivated and the execution barbaric.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Alireza Akbari'; BBC, Jan 2023

n: US intelligence used UN weapons inspectors' mission to eavesdrop on Iraq
d: US intelligence used eavesdropping gathered with the help of UNSCOM, the UN Special Commission set up to find and destroy Iraq's banned weapons, to listen to communications of the units guarding Saddam Hussein, The Washington Post and The Boston Globe reported in January 1999. The Post said UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan had convincing evidence of it. Sources said the monitoring was partly meant to help inspectors find weapons, but Annan reportedly believed Washington used it to penetrate Saddam's security. UNSCOM's chief, Richard Butler, denied that the US had used the commission, and US officials declined to comment.
cite: Reuters via Christian Science Monitor, 7 Jan 1999 (Washington Post, Boston Globe)

n: CIA-backed exile Ayad Allawi chosen as Iraq's interim prime minister
d: Ayad Allawi's exile group, the Iraqi National Accord, worked with the CIA from 1992 and received US covert aid reported at $5 million in 1995 and $6 million in 1996. The CIA backed its 1996 plan for Iraqi generals to move on Baghdad; Saddam's agents infiltrated the plot and many participants were executed. After the 2003 US invasion, Allawi sat on the US-appointed Iraqi Governing Council, and in December 2003 he met CIA officials at Langley to plan Iraq's new domestic intelligence service. On 28 May 2004 the Governing Council unanimously chose him as interim prime minister of the government that took over sovereignty from the US-led occupation in June 2004.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ayad Allawi' (citing Wurmser; Cockburn and Cockburn)

n: US-funded exile Ahmed Chalabi led Iraq's Governing Council
rank: President of the Iraqi Governing Council
d: Ahmed Chalabi's Iraqi National Congress (INC), an exile opposition group, ran on US government money for years: The Guardian estimated CIA funding in the 1990s at about $100 million, and the US Government Accountability Office found the State Department paid the INC nearly $33 million from March 2000 to September 2003. After the 2003 invasion, the US-run Coalition Provisional Authority gave Chalabi a seat on the Iraqi Governing Council, which he chaired in September 2003. On 19 May 2004 the US stopped its payments, and the next day Iraqi police backed by US soldiers raided his offices, amid reports, which he denied, that he had passed US secrets to Iran.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ahmed Chalabi' (citing The Guardian; GAO)

n: Chile's secret police chief Contreras was a CIA contact, paid in 1975
d: Manuel Contreras headed DINA, the secret police of General Augusto Pinochet's military government, from 1973 to 1977. A CIA report released on 19 September 2000 shows US policymakers authorised CIA contact with him from 1974 to 1977, and the agency made him a one-time payment in 1975, although US intelligence reports by then named him as the main obstacle to a better human rights policy in Pinochet's government. The CIA kept the relationship until 1977, despite reportedly holding intelligence that he ordered the 1976 killing of exiled Chilean diplomat Orlando Letelier in Washington. Chilean courts later convicted Contreras in many cases; at his death in 2015 his sentences totalled 529 years.
cite: CIA, 'CIA Activities in Chile' (Hinchey report), 19 Sep 2000; Wikipedia, 'Manuel Contreras'

n: CIA officer gave South Vietnam's coup generals $42,000 to topple Diệm
d: CIA officer Lucien Conein acted as the link between the US embassy and the South Vietnamese generals planning to overthrow President Ngô Đình Diệm, told them the US would not intervene to stop a coup, and gave them 3 million piastres, about $42,000, to reward units that joined. A State Department cable to Ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge had already said US policy was not to try to stop a coup and authorised the embassy to explore a change of leader. The generals moved on 1 November 1963 in Saigon; Diệm and his brother Ngô Đình Nhu were killed the next day after surrendering. A succession of military governments followed.
cite: Wikipedia, '1963 South Vietnamese coup' (Pentagon Papers; FRUS)

n: Greek junta leader Papadopoulos was Greek intelligence's link to the CIA
d: Georgios Papadopoulos, the army officer who led Greece's military coup on 21 April 1967 and became the junta's leader, had served from 1959 to 1964 in KYP, the Greek intelligence service, as its main contact with the CIA's top officer in Greece. Some sources describe him as on the CIA payroll from the 1950s. In 1973 The Observer accused the CIA of engineering the coup and reported that US military aid officials in Athens knew him as 'the first CIA agent to become Premier of a European country'. At his 1973 confirmation hearing, CIA director William Colby denied both claims but said the agency had 'worked with' him in his official role.
cite: The Observer, 1 Jul 1973; William Colby confirmation hearing, 1973; Wikipedia, 'Georgios Papadopoulos'

n: CIA cash briefcases for Chamoun's candidates in Lebanon's 1957 election
d: CIA money paid for selected candidates backed by President Camille Chamoun in Lebanon's June 1957 parliamentary election. CIA officer Wilbur Crane Eveland later wrote that he regularly drove to the presidential residence with 'a briefcase full of Lebanese pounds' to be spent on the campaign; American oil companies working in Lebanon also contributed. Independents, nearly all of them pro-Chamoun, won 51 of the 66 seats. The result left Chamoun's opponents with little representation in parliament, and the following year Lebanon fell into a political crisis in which US Marines landed near Beirut.
cite: Wilbur Crane Eveland, Ropes of Sand (1980); Wikipedia, '1957 Lebanese general election'

n: Suitcase of Venezuelan cash allegedly meant for Argentina's 2007 campaign
d: On 4 August 2007 Argentine police seized $790,550 in undeclared cash from Guido Alejandro Antonini Wilson, who arrived in Buenos Aires on a chartered plane that also carried representatives of Venezuela's state oil company, PDVSA. In December 2007 the FBI arrested men it accused of acting as Venezuelan government agents and trying to pay Antonini $2 million to stay silent. Two of them pleaded guilty in Miami and, with US prosecutors, said the money was meant for the presidential campaign of Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, who won that October. Both governments called for investigations; nothing was proven in Argentina, and the Argentine case was closed in 2015 under the statute of limitations.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Maletinazo' (US District Court, Miami, 2008)

n: CIA kept Castillo Armas on its payroll, then made him Guatemala's ruler
d: The CIA chose Carlos Castillo Armas, an exiled Guatemalan army officer, to lead its operation against President Jacobo Árbenz, whose land reform had expropriated land held by the US-based United Fruit Company. It planned to give him $225,000 for an abandoned 1952 plot, then kept him on its payroll at $3,000 a week. In June 1954 he led about 480 CIA-trained fighters into Guatemala; Árbenz resigned on 27 June, and after US-brokered talks Castillo Armas joined the ruling junta and took it over in July. The US recognised his government on 13 July 1954. He ruled until a presidential guard shot him dead on 26 July 1957.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Carlos Castillo Armas'; Wikipedia, '1954 Guatemalan coup d'état' (declassified CIA and State Department records)

n: CIA gave about $1 million to Indonesia's Masyumi party in the 1955 election
d: According to former CIA officer Joseph Smith's 1976 memoir, 'Portrait of a Cold Warrior', the CIA secretly gave about $1 million to Masyumi, a centrist Islamic party, during Indonesia's 1955 parliamentary election, the country's first, to reduce support for President Sukarno and the Communist Party of Indonesia. Masyumi won 57 seats, tying the Indonesian National Party (PNI) for the most, with 20.92% of the vote, a result below expectations. No party won a majority, and the PNI's Ali Sastroamidjojo formed a coalition government that included Masyumi. The amount rests on Smith's account and has not been independently confirmed.
cite: Joseph Burkholder Smith, Portrait of a Cold Warrior (1976), pp. 110–111; Wikipedia, '1955 Indonesian legislative election'

n: RAW joint secretary Rabinder Singh fled to the US as a suspected CIA mole
rank: Joint secretary, Research and Analysis Wing
d: Rabinder Singh, a former army major, rose in India's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), to joint secretary at its New Delhi headquarters, covering Southeast Asia. Counter-intelligence officers noticed him photocopying documents unrelated to his work, put him under surveillance and tapped his phones, suspecting he worked for the CIA. He disappeared in May 2004, reportedly via Nepal, and India dismissed him that year. A former RAW officer's book says he flew to the US from Kathmandu under a false identity; reports said the CIA arranged his US passports, which has not been officially confirmed. Interpol refused India's 2007 request for a red corner notice.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Rabinder Singh (intelligence officer)'

n: British officers and MI6 removed Oman's sultan and installed his son
d: Britain planned and carried out the 23 July 1970 palace coup in Salalah that removed Sultan Said bin Taimur of Oman and installed his son Qaboos. Oman's armed forces were under de facto British command: Brigadier John Graham, their overall commander, briefed the Arab officers of the Desert Regiment who carried out the coup, and British officials sent Qaboos, then under house arrest, cassette tapes setting out the plan. Accounts based on British records say MI6, the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence planned it and Prime Minister Edward Heath approved it. Britain denied involvement for forty years, saying its officers had acted on their own. An RAF plane flew the deposed sultan out.
cite: The Guardian (Ian Cobain), 2016; Mark Curtis, 'Britain's coup in Oman, 1970', 2016; Wikipedia, '1970 Omani coup d'état'

n: India's RAW allegedly helped unite Sri Lanka's opposition against Rajapaksa
d: India's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), was alleged to have helped bring Sri Lanka's divided opposition together against President Mahinda Rajapaksa before the January 2015 presidential election. Reports in The Sunday Times and other outlets said RAW's Colombo station chief helped coordinate opposition talks, persuaded Ranil Wickremesinghe not to stand so that a single candidate had a better chance, and kept in touch with former president Chandrika Kumaratunga, who helped convince Maithripala Sirisena to run. Sirisena won. The station chief was reportedly expelled before the vote. India's government and Sri Lanka's new foreign minister denied the claims. India was concerned about Chinese submarines docking in Sri Lanka in 2014.
cite: The Sunday Times and others, Jan 2015, as summarised in Wikipedia, '2015 Sri Lankan presidential election'

n: Japan accused of buying whaling-commission votes with aid
rank: Member-state votes at the International Whaling Commission
d: Japan was accused of using development aid to win votes at the International Whaling Commission (IWC), the body that regulates whaling worldwide, while it pressed to lift the ban on commercial whaling. It gave US$320 million in aid to Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Guinea, Morocco, Panama, St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines, St Kitts and Nevis, and Solomon Islands, and Caribbean members consistently voted with Japan from 2001. Antigua and Barbuda's prime minister Lester Bird acknowledged a 'quid pro quo', and Dominica's former fisheries minister Atherton Martin said Japan used money 'crudely to buy influence'. Japan denies vote-buying and notes that it also aids anti-whaling states.
cite: Wikipedia, 'International Whaling Commission' (citing Greenpeace, ABC and press statements by Lester Bird and Atherton Martin)

n: Bolivia's interior minister Antonio Arguedas said the CIA had recruited him
d: Antonio Arguedas, Bolivia's interior minister under President René Barrientos, said in 1968 that the CIA had recruited him in 1965, and gave details of CIA staff and their activities in Bolivia, a US State Department record shows. By his own account he had also smuggled a copy of the diary of Che Guevara, killed in Bolivia in October 1967, to Fidel Castro and then fled the country. US diplomats suspected Barrientos might have prompted his anti-CIA statements to shift blame for the diary leak onto the United States. Arguedas was brought back and tried for treason and espionage, survived three assassination attempts and took refuge in Mexico's embassy in 1969.
cite: US State Department, FRUS 1964–68, vol. XXXI, doc. 179; Time, 23 Feb 1970

n: Orellana network had the chiefs of Peru's property registry
rank: Head, registrar and IT chief of SUNARP
d: A criminal network run from the Lima law firm of Rodolfo Orellana got senior officials of Peru's national property registry, SUNARP, to work for it. Between 2009 and 2013 the firm changed the recorded owners of disputed land and sold 47 plots through front men, with the registry's former head Álvaro Delgado Scheelje, a registrar and its IT chief smoothing the paperwork. In February 2020 a Lima court convicted 19 people of criminal association and bribery: Orellana's sister Ludith got 10 years and the three registry officials 6 years and 8 months each. Orellana himself faces a separate laundering trial.
cite: Andina, 8 Feb 2020; LP Derecho, 11 Feb 2020

n: Traffickers bought early release from Peru's presidential pardons board
rank: Head of the presidential pardons commission
d: Convicted drug traffickers paid officials of the commission that advised President Alan García on pardons and sentence reductions, a case known in Peru as the 'narcoindultos' (narco-pardons). Between 2006 and 2011 more than 5,000 prisoners had sentences commuted or were pardoned, a disproportionate number of them traffickers. A congressional commission found the programme had been used to collect bribes from traffickers. In December 2015 a court sentenced the commission's head, Miguel Facundo Chinguel, García's former lawyer, to 13 years and 8 months for criminal conspiracy and taking bribes for the early release of at least three traffickers. Six lower commission officials were also convicted.
cite: Peru Reports, Dec 2015; InSight Crime, 'Can Peru Congress make narco-pardons case stick'

n: DEA probe of Fuerza Popular's secretary general over laundering
rank: Congressman and secretary general of Fuerza Popular
d: Reports in May 2016 said the US Drug Enforcement Administration was investigating Joaquín Ramírez, a congressman and secretary general of Fuerza Popular, Keiko Fujimori's party, for money laundering. A Peruvian pilot working as a DEA informant said he had given the agency a recording in which Ramírez said he had laundered $15 million for the 2011 Fujimori campaign through his petrol stations. Ojo Público reported that the DEA's main target was alleged trafficker Miguel 'Eteco' Arévalo. The DEA said Keiko Fujimori was not under investigation, and Ramírez called the claims a political attack. He resigned from the party post on 18 May 2016, during the presidential run-off campaign.
cite: Peru Reports, 18 May 2016; América TV, May 2016

n: Cocaine groups paid port security, dockers and customs contacts at Callao
rank: Port security chief, customs contacts, police
d: Cocaine trafficking groups paid people inside Callao, Peru's main seaport, to get drugs onto ships. An investigation by La República, reported by InSight Crime in 2015, quoted a former trafficker saying the port's security chief charged about $20,000 for entry and dockworkers took at least $10 per kilo. Corrupt workers loaded the cocaine after containers had cleared customs, and contacts inside customs warned traffickers hours ahead if a container was picked for a second check. Infiltration of the police and customs was given as one reason why less than 20% of the cocaine moving through Callao was detected. Peru's former anti-drug police chief said 80% of the country's cocaine left through Callao and Paita.
cite: InSight Crime, 22 May 2015, citing La República

n: Ex-head of Peru's anti-drug police investigated over traffickers' links
d: A secret police intelligence note sent to Peru's police commander in June 2023 linked General Deny Rodríguez Bardales, who had headed Dirandro, the national police's anti-drug directorate, in 2022, to anti-drug officers held for trafficking. The note said four officers and a sergeant under his command had ties to two sergeants who are jailed and on trial for drug trafficking in Loreto, the Amazon region bordering Colombia. Anti-drug prosecutors in Loreto and a team in Lima opened an investigation listing Rodríguez among those investigated, and he was retired at the end of December 2023. He said the police inspectorate had reviewed his case and found no responsibility.
cite: El Comercio, 2024

n: Paraguayan deputy Ulises Quintana accused of serving trafficker 'Cucho'
rank: Member of the Chamber of Deputies; prosecutors; police
d: Prosecutors say the cocaine network of Reinaldo 'Cucho' Cabaña had a member of Paraguay's Chamber of Deputies, three prosecutors and seven police officers working for it. In September 2018 anti-drug agents arrested Cabaña, seized 21 kg of cocaine and about $800,000, and charged the officials. Prosecutors allege that when Cabaña was arrested with $190,000, Colorado Party deputy Ulises Quintana intervened to get him released, that Cabaña financed Quintana's campaign, and that Quintana used the trafficker's assets. Quintana, who denies the charges, was stripped of immunity and jailed. In February 2026 a judge returned both men to Tacumbú prison in pre-trial detention ahead of trial in the case, called Operativo Berilo.
cite: EFE via El Venezolano, Sept 2018; Hoy (Paraguay), 27 Feb 2026

n: PCC paid Paraguayan prison staff as 75 inmates walked free
d: The Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), Brazil's largest prison gang, which also controls cocaine routes through Paraguay, got staff at the prison in Pedro Juan Caballero, on the Brazilian border, to help its members escape. In January 2020 at least 75 inmates, many of them PCC members, left over several days through a tunnel and, according to officials, the main gate. Interior Minister Euclides Acevedo said people working in the jail were complicit, and Justice Minister Cecilia Pérez said prisoners had reportedly offered staff $80,000 for help. Pérez ordered the entire prison staff fired. The escape showed how far the PCC had reached into Paraguay's prisons.
cite: OCCRP, 21 Jan 2020; AP, Jan 2020

n: Narco clan's mayor of Ypejhú ordered killing of journalist Pablo Medina
d: The Acosta family, a clan that ABC Color reporter Pablo Medina had linked to drug trafficking and killings, held the mayoralty of Ypejhú, a town on Paraguay's border with Brazil, through Vilmar 'Neneco' Acosta. Medina and his companion Antonia Almada were shot dead in 2014. Acosta fled to Brazil, where he was caught and later extradited. In December 2017 a Paraguayan court sentenced him to 29 years in prison plus 10 years of security measures as the intellectual author of the murders, finding that Medina's reporting on the clan's drug trafficking had put him on a hit list. The case became a reference point in Paraguay's debate about 'narcopolítica', drug money in local politics.
cite: ABC Color, 19 Dec 2017; La Nación (Paraguay), 20 Dec 2017

n: Paraguayan deputy Lalo Gomes charged with laundering drug money
rank: Member of the Chamber of Deputies
d: Paraguayan prosecutors charged Eulalio 'Lalo' Gomes, a Colorado Party member of the Chamber of Deputies from Pedro Juan Caballero, with laundering money from international drug trafficking. In July 2024 Brazilian media alleged he had helped Brazilian drug figures including Luiz Carlos da Rocha, alias 'Cabeça Branca'. On 19 August 2024, hours after the charges were filed against him, his son and three others, Gomes was shot dead when anti-drug police raided his home; officials said agents had been fired on. His family disputes that account. Prosecutors also charged an alleged front man and two officials of Zeta Banco.
cite: Ámbito / EFE, 19 Aug 2024; ABC Color, 19 Sept 2024

n: Gambling boss paid Rosario's chief prosecutor; senator charged as leader
rank: Regional chief prosecutor, Rosario; provincial senator
d: Leonardo Peiti, who financed illegal gambling in Santa Fe province, paid the prosecutors who were supposed to investigate him. In November 2025 a Rosario court sentenced Patricio Serjal, former head of Rosario's prosecutors, to nine years for taking bribes to leave Peiti alone; an office employee who passed the payments up got five years, and deputy prosecutor Gustavo Ponce Asahad had already been convicted. Peiti told the court he gave $200,000 to Peronist senator Armando Traferri for his campaign. Prosecutors charged Traferri as head of the network, but his fellow legislators kept his immunity in place for about four years. The court called him the central figure of the network's political side.
cite: La Política Online, 7 Nov 2025; La Capital (Rosario)

n: Alvarado clan had Rosario police chiefs and a prosecutor's employee
rank: Heads of police brigades and a police station; prosecutor's office employee
d: The criminal group of Esteban Alvarado, a Rosario drug and car-theft boss later sentenced to life, had senior officers of Santa Fe's police working for it. Between 2019 and 2021 courts convicted six officers, among them the head of the investigations police's operations brigade, the former head of the judicial division and a police station chief, of criminal association; each got three years and a six-year ban from office. They warned the gang of raids, passed it information from the unit investigating its rivals Los Monos, and steered murder inquiries toward rival gangs. An employee of a prosecutor's office who leaked a tapped phone to the group got one year.
cite: La Capital (Rosario), 21 Feb 2022

n: Mendoza federal judge Walter Bento sold rulings to detainees
d: People held on serious charges, including drug trafficking and smuggling, paid a network led by Walter Bento, the most powerful federal judge in Mendoza, Argentina, for house arrest or release. Federal judges in Argentina handle drug-trafficking cases. After a trial lasting two and a half years, Mendoza's Federal Oral Tribunal No. 1 found Bento and about twenty others guilty in February 2026 of illicit association, bribery, money laundering and illicit enrichment. Bento was sentenced to 18 years and fined 540 million pesos; his wife got six years and his son five. He had been detained since late 2023.
cite: Diario de Cuyo, 3 and 7 Feb 2026

n: Bagdad gang paid Panamanian police for checkpoints and escorts
rank: National Police sub-lieutenant and paid officers
d: Bagdad, a Panamanian gang federation, got officers of the National Police to work for it, according to prosecutors in Operation Neptuno. In April 2021 a police sub-lieutenant was charged as a key member: prosecutors said he shielded the group's cases, opened checkpoints, escorted vehicles carrying drugs and guarded its meetings in Chame and Playa Blanca. A notebook seized in the case allegedly listed police officers of various ranks and the sums they were paid for information. Nineteen members were charged with criminal association, money laundering and corruption of public officials. Bagdad has been linked to at least 27 killings in two years, including 13 inmates at La Joya prison.
cite: Panamá América, 11 Apr 2021

n: Two colonels arrested for tipping off trafficker 'César el Abusador'
rank: Two colonels and three other officers
d: The cocaine and laundering network of César Emilio Peralta, known as 'César el Abusador', had officers inside the Dominican security forces who warned it of action against it. In August 2019 Dominican authorities and the US DEA raided properties linked to the network, but Peralta escaped. About two weeks later, two colonels and three other officers were arrested on suspicion of leaking the arrest warrant and the planned raids to Peralta and his lieutenants, reportedly in return for a large payment in dollars. Investigators also looked at why an immigration alert was sent late. Peralta was later caught in Colombia in a joint operation with the United States.
cite: Dominican Today, Sept 2019; InSight Crime

n: Operation Falcón: cocaine network reached a Dominican state agency head
rank: Director of Comunidad Digna; a deputy
d: A Santiago-based cocaine and laundering network that authorities say moved more than $500 million had a serving government official and a congressman among its contacts. In September 2021 Dominican prosecutors, the drug agency DNCD and the US DEA carried out more than 80 raids. Those arrested included Juan Maldonado Castro, a four-term former deputy appointed in 2020 as director of the state programme Comunidad Digna; he was suspended by decree. Deputy Héctor Darío Féliz was accused of trying to move a man wanted for extradition so he could avoid arrest, but was not detained because of his parliamentary immunity. President Luis Abinader said the operation would continue 'whoever falls'.
cite: Diario Libre, 8 Sept 2021; El Caribe, Sept 2021

n: Cocaine trafficker sat in the Dominican Chamber of Deputies
rank: Member of the Chamber of Deputies
d: A man running a cocaine smuggling operation into the United States won a seat in the Dominican Republic's Chamber of Deputies. Miguel Andrés Gutiérrez Díaz was elected for Santiago in 2020 for the ruling Modern Revolutionary Party. While still a sitting deputy he was arrested in Miami on a US indictment for conspiracy to import cocaine. He pleaded guilty to drug trafficking and money laundering, admitting he sent cocaine to Florida in containers and boats between 2014 and 2020, about 5,000 kilograms according to his plea agreement. In April 2024 a federal court in Miami sentenced him to 16 years.
cite: El Día, 4 Apr 2024; Bloomberg/AP, 2021

n: Ex-army captain Quirino says drug money funded Fernández's campaign
rank: Presidential campaign and foundation of Leonel Fernández
d: Quirino Ernesto Paulino Castillo, a former Dominican army captain and drug trafficker, claims his drug money reached the campaign of Leonel Fernández, president from 2004 to 2012. Paulino was extradited to the United States on drug charges in 2005 and released in 2014. In a February 2015 television interview he said he funded Fernández's campaign from 2002 to 2004, gave more than $155,625 to Fernández's foundation FUNGLODE, and was owed about $500,000 used for the party nomination contest, and that Fernández knew the money was 'dirty'. He offered to take a polygraph test. His release after reported negotiations with US authorities raised questions about his credibility, and the claims have not been tested in court.
cite: Americas Quarterly, 10 Feb 2015; InSight Crime

n: Fugitive Figueroa Agosto held Dominican state ID and officers' help
rank: DNCD drug agency officers; intelligence directorate
d: José David Figueroa Agosto, a Puerto Rican drug trafficker on the run from US justice, lived in the Dominican Republic for about ten years under false names with help from inside its security agencies. When he was found he held a valid card from the national intelligence directorate, the DNI, and six gun permits issued by the interior ministry and the armed forces. After his girlfriend Sobeida Félix was arrested and $4.6 million seized in 2009, raids found a member of his group holding the original file of the DNCD drug agency's intelligence unit. A captain was accused of treason for reportedly taking $10,000. Figueroa was later sentenced to 209 years in prison in the United States.
cite: El Día, 4 Jan 2010; Acento

n: Costa Rica investigates 116 police over links to drug gangs
rank: 116 officers of the Ministry of Public Security
d: An internal intelligence report found that drug trafficking gangs had officers of Costa Rica's police working for them. On 5 August 2026 President Laura Fernández announced that 116 officers of the Ministry of Public Security were under investigation; Security Minister Gerald Campos said the report named 122 people and that the force had more than 38 active corruption cases. Officers were allegedly tied to drug trafficking, migrant smuggling and alcohol smuggling, some escorted criminals, and some coordinated clandestine landings of aircraft reportedly carrying drugs. The report had reached officials of the previous government in April, and Campos said no investigation was ordered then. The case goes to prosecutors.
cite: Revista EyN / AFP, 6 Aug 2026

n: Guanacaste police chief arrested for helping a drug-flight network
rank: Head of the Fuerza Pública delegation in Nandayure
d: A drug trafficking group in Guanacaste, Costa Rica, had the local police commander passing it information, according to the OIJ judicial police. In July 2024 the OIJ arrested the head of the Fuerza Pública delegation in Nandayure, a 19-year veteran, and another officer, together with ten other people, in the case known as Caso Coraza. Investigators say the group flew drugs abroad in small planes from clandestine airstrips, including one at a Guanacaste hotel, and laundered money by trading cattle for cash. The OIJ carried out 29 raids, including at two police delegations, and seized 15 vehicles and more than 600 head of cattle.
cite: Teletica, 1 July 2024; CRHoy, July 2024

n: Rotterdam customs officer waved cocaine containers through for 7.5%
rank: Customs officer selecting containers for inspection
d: Cocaine importers paid a Dutch customs officer at Rotterdam port, Gerrit G., to keep their containers out of inspection. He worked in the pre-arrival unit that chooses which containers are scanned, and removed his clients' shipments from that selection, taking 7.5% of the value of the drugs. He was arrested in April 2015 after police intercepted 400 kilos of cocaine; investigators found €1.1 million in cash at his flat and €1 million in bank accounts, and estimated he earned at least €3.5 million. In July 2017 the Rotterdam court sentenced him to 14 years, and the Hague appeals court upheld 14 years in May 2020. Two men were convicted of bribing him.
cite: DutchNews, 4 July 2017; Gerechtshof Den Haag, 18 May 2020

n: Criminals reported in management of Securitas's Rotterdam port guards
d: A cocaine network got its people inside Securitas, the security company guarding parts of Rotterdam port, according to the Algemeen Dagblad. Two Securitas guards were arrested in summer 2020, suspected of helping move cocaine, passing information to criminals and arranging logistics so that smuggling containers were not searched, in an inquiry covering 4,000 kilograms. A third suspect, believed to have directed them in dozens of transports, fled abroad. AD's sources said criminals held management positions at the firm and deliberately recruited corrupt guards. The evidence came from EncroChat, an encrypted phone service police had broken into. Securitas said the accusations went against its values and that staff are screened.
cite: NL Times / AD, 13 Jan 2021; NOS

n: Taghi network paid a senior Utrecht police officer for searches
d: The criminal organisation of Ridouan Taghi, then the Netherlands' most wanted drug trafficker, had a high-ranking Utrecht police officer searching police systems for it. According to the Algemeen Dagblad in July 2019, the officer was paid thousands of euros, several times, to look up people and photographs and pass the results to the gang. The allegation came from Nabil B., the crown witness against Taghi's network. The officer was dismissed and the Rijksrecherche, which investigates police misconduct, opened an inquiry.
cite: NL Times / AD, 10 July 2019

n: Prosecutors suspect underworld placed a trainee in Amsterdam police
d: Dutch prosecutors suspected that criminals had deliberately placed one of their contacts inside the Amsterdam police. Mehmet A., a 22-year-old trainee officer who had earlier worked as a guard at a detention centre, searched police systems from December 2017 for dozens of drug dealers, cash-machine bombers and motorcycle gang members, and sold the results at €250 a name. Buyers included two cannabis-trading brothers and the No Surrender motorcycle club. He was arrested in November 2018 after an anonymous tip. At his trial in March 2019 the prosecutor said an encrypted PGP phone given to him by a criminal pointed to his being 'positioned by the underworld', though there was no hard proof, and asked for 45 months.
cite: NL Times, 6 Mar 2019

n: Dutch police officer sold underworld 'subscriptions' to case files
d: Criminal suspects in the Netherlands paid a police officer, Mark M., for regular access to confidential police files about them. For about four years, until his arrest in September 2015, he used login details for the BlueView police information system to read criminal case files and passed them to contacts in the underworld, some of whom paid 'subscriptions'. He claimed he looked up the information as a hobby. In February 2018 the Den Bosch district court sentenced him to five years in prison, though it cleared him of bribery. Dutch police reported 18 officers suspended for leaking information in one year as the problem grew.
cite: DutchNews, 19 Feb 2018; DutchNews, May 2017

n: Amsterdam court desk worker sold personal data to a bombing suspect
rank: Information desk employee, Amsterdam district court
d: A man suspected of explosions and arson in The Hague and a shooting in Waalwijk got a worker inside the Amsterdam district court to supply him with confidential personal data. Sana C., who worked at the court's information desk with access to several systems holding personal details, was paid up to €700 per transaction. Police found her in 2024 during another investigation, with a court envelope holding six people's details and dozens of printouts. In May 2026 the court in Zwolle sentenced her to four years, one suspended, also for extorting almost €100,000 from a man, and banned her from public service for seven years. The buyer is thought to be hiding in Morocco.
cite: DutchNews, 28 May 2026

n: 'Airport broker' recruited Schiphol staff to move Suriname cocaine
rank: Logistics and transport staff at Schiphol firms
d: A cocaine network used an 'airport broker' to recruit staff of companies working at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, whose security passes let them move drugs past controls. In 2024 the Royal Marechaussee, the Dutch military police who guard the airport, arrested six men aged 32 to 51 in logistics, transport and parcel delivery jobs, suspected of smuggling cocaine hidden in pallets from Suriname. A former airport worker allegedly linked the broker with the others; police said several areas of work had to be involved to get the drugs out. €124,000 in cash and cryptocurrency was seized. About 60,000 people work at Schiphol, all screened.
cite: DutchNews, 31 May 2024

n: Antwerp drugs squad team leader arrested for leaking to gangs
rank: Chief inspector, Federal Judicial Police drugs department
d: Belgian investigators suspect that drug gangs had a source at the heart of Antwerp's fight against cocaine. In June 2023 a chief inspector and team leader in the drugs department of the Federal Judicial Police in Antwerp was arrested on suspicion of breaching professional secrecy by passing sensitive information to criminal gangs. Brussels investigators searched his home on the orders of an Antwerp judge, and he was released on conditions after questioning. He had been instrumental in dismantling the 'Mixers' gang, which had accused him of corruption. The Antwerp prosecutor's office said it was too early to draw conclusions.
cite: Brussels Times / De Standaard, 7 June 2023

n: Antwerp judge: gangs have inside staff in port, customs, police, courts
rank: Customs, police, municipal and prison staff
d: An Antwerp investigating judge wrote in October 2025 that cocaine networks had got people inside Belgium's state at many levels. In an open letter published on the website of Belgium's courts, the judge, one of 17 in Antwerp, said their investigations had led to the arrest of key port employees, customs officers, police officers, counter staff in several municipalities, and justice staff in prisons and in the courthouse. Moving one container could earn a port worker over €100,000. The judge, who had spent four months in a safe house after threats, warned that Belgium was turning into a 'narco-state'. Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden said she understood the concerns.
cite: Brussels Times, 27 Oct 2025; Maritime Executive, Oct 2025

n: Fake sick notes freed Guinea-Bissau's record cocaine traffickers
rank: Appeal Court judges; prison staff and doctors
d: Traffickers convicted over Guinea-Bissau's largest cocaine seizure, 1,869 kg found in 2019 in Operation Navara, got out of prison with help from inside the justice system, the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime reported. In April and May 2021 several were released on medical grounds that police later found were invented; officers said the Supreme Court's vice-president had authorised the release, and a judge ordered junior prison officials and doctors detained. In October 2020 the Court of Appeal had cut ringleader Braima Seidi Bá's 16-year sentence to six years in a ruling reportedly driven by bribes; one judge dissented. Seidi Bá was never detained.
cite: Global Initiative, West Africa Risk Bulletin 1, 2021

n: 'Cherif Cocaine' said to fund Niger's ruling party and enjoy protection
d: Cherif Ould Abidine, an Agadez transport businessman known locally as 'Cherif Cocaine', was reported to have financed Niger's ruling party and to have been protected by officials at the highest levels. A 2018 Global Initiative study by Peter Tinti, based on fieldwork in Agadez and Niamey, said it was an open secret that he enjoyed such protection and that he reportedly funded political campaigns, notably those of the PNDS party of President Mahamadou Issoufou. He reportedly also won a French government contract to carry military supplies to the Madama base near Libya. He died in 2016. The study said illicit money in Niger's electoral politics was almost certainly real but hard to document.
cite: Global Initiative, 'Drug trafficking in northern Niger', 18 June 2018

n: Senegal's police chief removed over report linking him to drug ring
d: A report by the head of Senegal's anti-drug police office accused his predecessor, Abdoulaye Niang, of being implicated in a Senegalese and Nigerian drug trafficking ring while he ran that office. By then Niang had become director-general of the national police. In July 2013 President Macky Sall relieved him of his duties so that he could defend himself. The report's author, Commissioner Cheikhna Keïta, had sent his findings to the authorities from February. A government inquiry said it found no evidence against Niang. The affair raised questions about whether traffickers had protection at the top of the police.
cite: AP via Star Tribune, 26 July 2013; Dakaractu

n: Fraudster Hushpuppi paid Nigerian 'supercop' Abba Kyari to jail a rival
rank: Deputy Commissioner of Police and team leader
d: Ramon Abbas, an internet fraudster known as Hushpuppi, used payments to Abba Kyari, a Nigerian deputy police commissioner who led a special investigation team under the Inspector-General of Police, to have a rival locked up. US court documents filed in 2021 said that after a co-fraudster, Vincent Chibuzo, tried to cheat Abbas over a scheme targeting Qatari businessmen, Kyari's team arrested Chibuzo, and Abbas sent Kyari about N8 million in two bank transfers. US prosecutors indicted Kyari and a court issued an arrest warrant. Nigeria's Police Service Commission suspended him from 31 July 2021. Kyari denied taking money.
cite: ICIR Nigeria, July 2021; TheCable, 1 Aug 2021

n: Kenya's security minister named five MPs and tycoons as drug suspects
d: In December 2010 Kenya's internal security minister, George Saitoti, told Parliament that sitting MPs were among people under investigation for drug trafficking. The list, drawn from a joint US–Kenyan inquiry, named MPs Hassan Joho, William Kabogo, Harun Mwau and Gideon Mbuvi, and Mombasa businessman Ali Punjani. A 2010 US embassy report alleged that Joho, later governor of Mombasa county, was involved in trafficking and that his brother was the clearing agent for containers holding a ton of cocaine in 2004. All denied the claims. Saitoti died in a 2012 helicopter crash and no one on the list was convicted; police said in 2015 they had found no evidence against Mwau.
cite: Correctiv, 'Kenya's drug barons', 16 Apr 2015

n: Kenyan troops in Somalia accused of sugar and charcoal deals with al-Shabaab
d: A November 2015 report by the rights group Journalists for Justice said Kenya Defence Forces units deployed in southern Somalia to fight al-Shabaab had become part of a sugar and charcoal smuggling cartel that included the militant group. The cartel was said to earn about $50 million a year, and the report argued that the trade helped keep al-Shabaab alive nearly four years after Kenya entered Somalia. Charcoal exports from Somalia were banned by the UN Security Council because they funded al-Shabaab. President Uhuru Kenyatta dismissed the report and the military denied the claims and asked for evidence.
cite: Business Daily, 12 Nov 2015; Citizen Digital, Nov 2015

n: Maputo kidnapping gangs had police and justice staff inside
d: Gangs that kidnap businesspeople and their families for ransom in Mozambique's capital have people inside the police and justice system. In January 2023 Nelson Rego, director-general of SERNIC, the national criminal investigation service, said publicly at its anniversary ceremony that employees of the bodies that administer justice were involved in kidnappings. Arrests followed: in May 2024 SERNIC detained two officers of Maputo's 23rd police precinct over the abduction of an eight-year-old girl from her primary school, for whom the kidnappers had demanded 200,000 meticais.
cite: AIM, 10 Jan 2023; AIM, 7 May 2024

n: Gold smuggling case reached Zimbabwe's spy agency and police
rank: CIO intelligence operatives; senior police officers
d: A gold smuggling syndicate had officers of Zimbabwe's Central Intelligence Organisation (CIO) and the police helping it move gold out through the main airport, according to police. In October 2020 Henrietta Rushwaya, president of the Zimbabwe Miners Federation, was stopped at Harare's Robert Mugabe International Airport with about 6 kg of gold worth $330,000 in her hand luggage, allegedly bound for Dubai. Six more people were arrested, among them two CIO operatives, a police superintendent and a detective chief inspector, as well as a businessman she said had supplied the gold. Rushwaya was remanded in custody while the case continued.
cite: VOA Zimbabwe, 29 Oct 2020; NewsDay

n: Thabo Bester bribed private prison staff to fake his death and escape
rank: G4S warders and CCTV contractor at Mangaung prison
d: Thabo Bester, a convicted rapist and murderer, paid staff at Mangaung Correctional Centre, a prison run for the South African state by the security company G4S, to help him escape in 2022 by faking his death in a cell fire with a corpse. Prosecutors say a G4S security supervisor and the technician who ran the prison's cameras were each promised R2.5 million and paid R40,000, and that other G4S employees were offered smaller sums. Bester and his partner, Dr Nandipha Magudumana, were arrested in Tanzania in April 2023. Several G4S staff were charged with corruption, arson and defeating the ends of justice.
cite: Sunday Times, 7 May 2023; TimesLIVE, 3 May 2023

n: Nafiz Modack convicted of paying a police brigadier to recover cars
d: Nafiz Modack, a Cape Town figure whom police describe as an underworld boss, paid a senior police officer to use his command for him. Between 2011 and 2013 Brigadier Kolindhren Govender of the South African Police Service received R146,000 from Modack and in return told officers under him to recover vehicles that belonged to Modack. Govender pleaded guilty to 51 corruption counts in December 2019. Modack was convicted of corruption in June 2025 and in September 2025 sentenced by the Cape Town Regional Court to 10 years, three suspended. He is separately on trial for the 2020 murder of anti-gang detective Charl Kinnear and is accused of paying an anti-gang unit sergeant for information.
cite: Daily Maverick, 21 Sept 2025; Daily Maverick, 18 June 2020

n: 28s gang boss Stanfield got gun licences through police registry staff
rank: Officers at the SAPS Central Firearm Registry
d: Ralph Stanfield, whom police describe as a leader of the Cape Town prison gang the 28s, obtained firearm licences for himself and his family with help from officers inside the police's Central Firearm Registry, the office that approves gun licences. Stanfield, his wife and his sister were arrested in June 2014 along with registry officers. The Supreme Court of Appeal ruled in December 2019 that the Stanfields had obtained their licences unlawfully. Their criminal case, with three former police officers and 18 others, was postponed repeatedly. The case was one of several showing gang figures getting guns and licences from inside the police, including a colonel who sold police-stored weapons to gangs.
cite: Daily Maverick, 18 June 2020; Daily Maverick, 2 Oct 2023

n: Reputed rosewood baron made vice-president of Madagascar's Senate
d: Madagascar's rosewood traffickers, who logged protected forests after the 2009 coup and exported the timber mainly to China, have had one of their reputed leaders placed in the national legislature. Sources of the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) named Erick Lambert Besoa as one of the top timber barons behind the logging. In 2021 President Andry Rajoelina nominated him to the Senate, and he became its vice-president. The EIA described him as a suspected trafficker accused of involvement in silencing environmental activists. He has not been charged. The EIA estimates up to 2.26 million rosewood logs are stockpiled in Madagascar, of which the government has declared about a tenth.
cite: African Arguments, Oct 2024; EIA, 'Convention Evasion', 3 Mar 2022

n: Saudi king's $100m 'gift' to Spain's King Juan Carlos
d: Saudi Arabia's King Abdullah transferred $100 million in 2008 to a Swiss bank account of a Panamanian foundation, Lucum, whose sole beneficiary was Spain's then head of state, King Juan Carlos I. Geneva prosecutor Yves Bertossa investigated whether the money was a commission linked to the Spanish-built high-speed railway between Mecca and Medina; Juan Carlos's former partner Corinna Larsen received €65 million of it. In December 2021 the Swiss closed the case, saying a link to the rail contracts could not be sufficiently established, and fined Mirabaud bank for failing to report the money. In March 2022 Spain's prosecutors also closed their inquiry, saying any crimes were covered by the immunity the constitution gives the head of state. Juan Carlos, who abdicated in 2014, had left Spain in 2020.
cite: Ara (2020); Catalan News (13 Dec 2021); Catalan News (2 Mar 2022)

n: UAE adviser George Nader funnelled $3.5m to buy access to US candidates
d: George Nader, an adviser to senior officials of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), used a US businessman, Ahmad 'Andy' Khawaja, to pass at least $3.5 million in illegal political contributions into the 2016 US election, the US Justice Department said. Nader's UAE company sent $4.9 million to Khawaja's company under a false software licensing agreement, and Khawaja made the donations in his own name to political committees, first around Hillary Clinton and then, after the election, $1 million to Donald Trump's inaugural committee. Prosecutors said the aim was access to and influence with a presidential candidate, and that Nader reported to a senior UAE official by encrypted message. The indictment was unsealed in December 2019; in July 2023 Nader was sentenced to a further one year and eight months.
cite: US Department of Justice press release (18 July 2023); Al Jazeera (6 Dec 2019)

n: UAE spy chief's firm secretly bought 49% of Trump family crypto company
rank: Largest outside shareholder and board seats, World Liberty Financial
d: An Abu Dhabi company backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE's national security adviser and brother of its president, secretly bought 49% of World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's cryptocurrency venture, the Wall Street Journal reported on 31 January 2026. Aryam Investment 1 agreed to pay $500 million, half upfront; Eric Trump signed four days before the January 2025 inauguration, and the deal was not disclosed. Executives of G42, the UAE artificial-intelligence firm Tahnoon chairs, helped manage Aryam and took seats on World Liberty's board. The report said $187 million went to Trump family entities. In November 2025 the US government approved sales of advanced Nvidia chips to G42. The White House and World Liberty said the deal did not influence policy.
cite: The Block, citing Wall Street Journal (1 Feb 2026)

n: North Korea chose UNDP's local staff and took their pay in hard currency
d: North Korea's government placed its own nominees in the Pyongyang office of the UN Development Programme (UNDP), the UN's main aid agency, and took the money paid for them. A 2008 report by the US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations found most local staff were North Koreans chosen by the government, against UNDP policy; their salaries went to the government in convertible currency with no check on what staff received. Officials had to be present at site visits, and in 2002 the government moved $2.72 million of its own funds abroad through a UNDP account. Four audits since 1999 had found problems but were kept from UNDP's own board. UNDP suspended its North Korea operations in March 2007 after the government refused new controls.
cite: US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations report (Jan 2008), via NK Economic Watch (24 Jan 2008)

n: Azerbaijan's oil company secretly paid for 10 US lawmakers' Baku trip
d: Azerbaijan's state oil company, SOCAR, secretly paid for ten members of the US Congress and 32 congressional staff to attend a 2013 conference in Baku, hiding the source through US non-profits. A confidential report by the House Office of Congressional Ethics, revealed by the Washington Post in May 2015, said SOCAR sent about $750,000 through the groups, which falsely told Congress they were the sponsors; guests received rugs, crystal tea sets and silk scarves worth $2,500 to $10,000. House rules bar foreign governments from paying for such trips. Kemal Oksuz, head of the Houston non-profit Turquoise Council, pleaded guilty on 10 December 2018 to hiding SOCAR's funding from the House Ethics Committee, after being extradited from Armenia.
cite: US Department of Justice press release (10 Dec 2018); Washington Post via Texas Tribune (13 May 2015)

n: UN Libya envoy León negotiated UAE job while leading Libya peace talks
d: While Spanish diplomat Bernardino León led the UN's Libya peace talks, the United Arab Emirates, which backed one side in Libya's civil war, offered him a highly paid job. Leaked emails reported by the Guardian in November 2015 showed that, months into his UN post, León wrote to the UAE foreign minister that his plan would 'completely delegitimise' the rival Tripoli parliament, that his moves had been 'consulted with' the UAE-backed side, and that 'I can help and control the process while I am there.' On 4 November 2015 the UAE named him first director-general of its state-backed Emirates Diplomatic Academy, and the UN replaced him with Martin Kobler. The Tripoli government said the hiring cast doubt on the talks; León said his emails were misrepresented.
cite: Al Jazeera (6 Nov 2015); The New Arab, citing the Guardian (5 Nov 2015)

n: Saudi 'Special Committee' kept 2,700 Yemeni leaders on its payroll
rank: Yemeni president, tribal, party and army leaders
d: Saudi Arabia ran its Yemen policy through the Special Committee, a body of its Council of Ministers that has paid Yemeni leaders since 1962. In June 2012 the Yemeni paper Al-Sharea printed part of a list of about 2,700 tribal, political and military figures it said received monthly Saudi payments totalling 56 million riyals, with ex-president Ali Abdullah Saleh, Sheikh Sadeq al-Ahmar and General Ali Mohsin reported at the top; the ruling party and the Islah party denied it, and MPs demanded an explanation. Saudi cables from 2010–2012 later published by Drop Site News show the committee authorising 50 million riyals for tribes fighting the Houthis and directing named sheikhs and a serving brigade commander.
cite: Global Voices (12 June 2012), citing Al-Sharea; Drop Site News, Saudi cables (2025)

n: Sudan's Bashir took $90m in cash from Saudi royals outside the budget
d: Saudi royals paid Sudan's president Omar al-Bashir $90 million in cash that he spent outside the state budget, an investigator told his corruption trial in Khartoum in August 2019. Brigadier Ahmed Ali testified that $25 million came from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and two earlier payments of $35 million and $30 million from the late King Abdullah. Bashir told investigators the money 'was not part of the state budget and I was the one who authorised its spending', and could not say how it was used. Bashir, who had ruled since a 1989 coup, was overthrown in April 2019. On 14 December 2019 the court convicted him of illegal possession of foreign currency and corruption and sent him to a reform centre for two years.
cite: Al Jazeera (19 Aug 2019); Al Jazeera (14 Dec 2019)

n: Ex-Al Jazeera reporter Fahad Yasin ran Somalia's spy agency for Qatar (alleged)
rank: Director, National Intelligence and Security Agency
d: Somali media and analysts allege that Qatar placed an ally at the head of Somalia's security apparatus. Fahad Yasin, a journalist for Qatar's state-funded Al Jazeera Arabic in Mogadishu from 2005 to 2011, became chief of staff to President Mohamed Abdullahi 'Farmaajo' in 2017, deputy head of the National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) in 2018 and its director from August 2019 to September 2021, then national security adviser. Commentators said he had channelled Qatari money into the 2012 presidential vote, and Garowe Online reported he coordinated sending Somali recruits to Eritrea who were told they would train in Qatar. Qatar denied funding Somalia through him. The prime minister suspended him in 2021 over the murder of NISA officer Ikran Tahlil, and he was replaced in May 2022.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Fahad Yasin Haji Dahir' (citing Reuters, BBC Somali, Garowe Online); Garowe Online, 'Qatar denies claims of funding Somalia through Fahad Yasin'

n: Azerbaijani Laundromat paid UNESCO chief's husband €345,000
rank: Spouse of UNESCO Director-General; later EBRD board
d: Shell companies in the Azerbaijani Laundromat, a $2.9 billion scheme that moved money from Azerbaijan's ruling circle, paid €345,000 between 2012 and 2014 to Kalin Mitrev, husband of UNESCO Director-General Irina Bokova, OCCRP reported in September 2017. One payment of €20,000 arrived on 25 October 2013, three days after UNESCO, the UN's cultural agency, hosted an exhibition requested by a foundation chaired by Mehriban Aliyeva, the Azerbaijani president's wife. Mitrev, by then Bulgaria's director on the board of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, said the money was for consultancy on a flood project and was declared. Bokova said she knew nothing of his business. Bulgaria's chief prosecutor and revenue agency opened checks.
cite: OCCRP, Azerbaijani Laundromat profile 'Kalin Mitrev' (Sept 2017); bne IntelliNews (Sept 2017)

n: Ex-MP Lintner convicted of bribing a Bundestag member for Azerbaijan
rank: Bundestag member and PACE delegate Karin Strenz
d: Azerbaijan used former German MP Eduard Lintner to pay a sitting member of the Bundestag, Germany's parliament, to promote its interests at the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), a human-rights body of national MPs. OCCRP's Laundromat records showed Lintner, a CSU deputy for 33 years and a PACE delegate until 2010, received €819,500 from Laundromat companies in 2012–2014. In July 2025 the Munich Higher Regional Court found he bribed public officials on Azerbaijan's behalf, the first such verdict against a German lawmaker, and gave him a nine-month suspended sentence; it found CDU MP Karin Strenz, who died in 2021, took money from his company and from Azerbaijani officials. Lintner called it legitimate lobbying and is appealing.
cite: OCCRP (30 July 2025); OCCRP, 'The Influence Machine' (2017); JAMnews (2025)

n: Pakistani intelligence recruited Indian diplomat Madhuri Gupta
rank: Second secretary, Indian High Commission in Islamabad
d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, recruited Madhuri Gupta, a second secretary at India's High Commission (embassy) in Islamabad, and she passed it information, an Indian court found. Indian police arrested her in 2010 after six months of surveillance. On 18 May 2018 a New Delhi court convicted her of spying and wrongful communication of information, saying she had passed 'categorically sensitive information, which could have been useful to the enemy country', and sentenced her to three years in prison. She had already spent about 21 months in custody. Gupta denied the charges, saying colleagues had falsely implicated her, and her lawyer said she would appeal.
cite: Al Jazeera (20 May 2018); Business Standard/PTI (18–19 May 2018)

n: Pakistani agent drew missile secrets from Indian defence lab director Kurulkar
d: A Pakistani intelligence operative posing as a woman online drew information from Pradeep Kurulkar, director of a laboratory of India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), the state body that designs its missiles and weapons, Indian investigators say. Kurulkar was arrested in Pune on 3 May 2023 after a complaint from DRDO's own vigilance department. On 30 June 2023 Maharashtra's Anti-Terrorism Squad filed a 1,837-page charge sheet under the Official Secrets Act, and reports of it said he discussed Indian missile systems with the operative. Kurulkar denies the charges and says he was the victim of a 'honey trap', a seduction set up to extract secrets. A Pune court refused him bail in December 2023.
cite: Wikipedia, 'DRDO espionage case'; Onmanorama (8 July 2023); Scroll.in (2023)

n: Pakistani handlers paid 11 Indian Navy sailors for naval secrets
d: Pakistani intelligence agencies paid serving Indian Navy personnel for information, through two Indian businessmen who sent money to the sailors' bank accounts on the handlers' instructions, India's National Investigation Agency (NIA) says. Fifteen people were arrested, 11 of them serving Navy personnel; the NIA took over the case from Andhra Pradesh police in December 2019 and charged 14 people in June 2020. The NIA said Mohammad Haroon Lakdawala and Imran Yakub Giteli, who had relatives in Pakistan, met intelligence operatives there and funded the payments from cross-border trade. In October 2025 a court sentenced the two to five and a half and six years, bringing convictions in the case to four. Related arrests continued into 2023.
cite: The News Minute (18 Oct 2025); The South First (2023)

n: Aide to Indian MP held for passing documents to Pakistan's High Commission
rank: Personal assistant to a Rajya Sabha MP
d: Pakistan's High Commission (embassy) in New Delhi paid an Indian MP's assistant for official documents, Delhi police said. In October 2016 police caught Mehmood Akhtar, a Pakistani in the High Commission's visa section, receiving military documents from two men; India ordered him to leave, and Pakistan expelled an Indian diplomat in return. Days later the Crime Branch detained Farhat, personal assistant to Munavvar Saleem, a Samajwadi Party member of the Rajya Sabha (India's upper house), saying he had handed official documents to Akhtar for money after making contact with the High Commission some years earlier. Saleem sacked him and said he regretted employing him.
cite: The News Minute (30 Oct 2016); Business Standard/IANS (29 Oct 2016)

n: Ex-ISI chief told Pakistan's top court the ISI funded Bangladesh's BNP
d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, paid money into the 1991 election campaign of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which won that vote and formed Bangladesh's government, a former ISI chief told Pakistan's Supreme Court. Asad Durrani, who headed the ISI in 1990–1992, made the admission in March 2012 during a hearing on the agency's mandate before a bench led by Chief Justice Iftikhar Chaudhry, Bangladesh's Daily Star reported. A UAE-based paper alleged the sum was Rs 50 crore to BNP leader Khaleda Zia, but this was not confirmed. The BNP denied receiving ISI money; Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina accused Khaleda Zia of serving Pakistan.
cite: The Daily Star (16 Mar 2012); Deccan Herald (Mar 2012)

n: Letter says North Korea paid Pakistan's army chief $3m for nuclear help
d: North Korea paid Pakistan's army chief and another senior general to approve passing nuclear-weapons technology to it, according to a 1998 letter that Pakistani scientist A.Q. Khan released and the Washington Post reported in July 2011. The letter, apparently signed by North Korean Workers' Party secretary Jon Byong-ho, said $3 million had gone to General Jehangir Karamat, then Chief of Army Staff, and $500,000 plus jewellery to Lieutenant-General Zulfiqar Khan. Western intelligence officials told the Post the letter was authentic. Pakistani officials called it a fake, and both generals denied it; Karamat said he 'was not in the loop'. Pakistan's centrifuge technology is known to have reached North Korea.
cite: Express Tribune/Reuters, citing Washington Post (8 July 2011)

n: A.Q. Khan took Urenco centrifuge designs from the Netherlands to Pakistan
d: Pakistani metallurgist A.Q. Khan, working inside the Dutch side of Urenco, the European uranium-enrichment consortium, took its centrifuge designs to Pakistan's nuclear programme. From 1972 he worked at FDO, a subcontractor to Urenco's Dutch partner, and visited the Almelo enrichment plant many times without official clearance. In late 1974 he was given the German G-1 and G-2 centrifuge designs to translate and had 16 days of unsupervised access. He left for Pakistan on 15 December 1975 with copied blueprints and contacts for nearly 100 suppliers, and in 1976 began centrifuge work there. A Dutch court convicted him in absentia of nuclear espionage in 1983; the verdict was overturned in 1985 for a faulty summons. The designs later reached Iran, Libya and North Korea.
cite: Carnegie Endowment, 'A.Q. Khan Nuclear Chronology' (Sept 2005)

n: North Korea's Ilsimhoe cell reached the Democratic Labor Party's leadership
rank: Deputy, Democratic Labor Party standing committee
d: A group called Ilsimhoe, taking orders from North Korea's ruling Workers' Party, had members inside South Korea's Democratic Labor Party (DLP), then a party with seats in the National Assembly, and passed the North information on the party's core membership. South Korea's National Intelligence Service arrested its founder Michael Jang and DLP central committee member Lee Jeong-hun on 24 October 2006. In April 2007 a Seoul court convicted five people of spying: Jang got nine years, Lee six, and Choi Gi-yeong, a former DLP vice secretary-general, four. The court rejected the charge that they formed a spy ring; the Supreme Court later upheld that they received the Workers' Party's orders. The case split the DLP.
cite: Daily NK, 'Michael Jang and the Ilsimhoe Scandal'; Joongang Ilbo via Free Korea (16 Apr 2007)

n: Wangjaesan ring passed South Korean political intelligence to the North
who: North Korean Workers' Party liaison department
d: A South Korean group called Wangjaesan, acting for North Korea's Workers' Party, gathered political intelligence in the South, and one member worked as secretary to a politician, a Seoul court heard. Prosecutors said its leader, a 49-year-old activist named Kim arrested in August 2011, met North Korean agents in China and Japan and in 2001 took orders from the Workers' Party's foreign liaison department to recruit more agents. In February 2012 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced Kim to nine years under the National Security Law and four others to two to seven years for leaking political information. The court rejected the charge that they had run an anti-state organisation for two decades.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily (23 Feb 2012)

n: North Korean-directed Chungbuk cell tried to recruit regional politicians
rank: Regional politicians and civic leaders (recruitment targets)
d: Three members of a group called Chungbuk Dongjihoe, acting on orders from North Korean agents, worked to recruit politicians and labour and civic figures in South Korea's North Chungcheong province, a court found. Prosecutors said the group swapped encrypted instructions and reports with the agents, collected local political information and received about $20,000 in operating funds. In February 2024 the Cheongju District Court sentenced the three, including chairman Son Mo, to 12 years each under the National Security Act. Their arrests in 2021 were among several cases in which South Korean prosecutors said North Korea tried to build networks reaching into parties and local politics.
cite: Asia Economy (16 Feb 2024); Korea JoongAng Daily (2021)

n: North Korean agent posing as a defector lectured at army bases
rank: South Korean army officers and bases
d: North Korea placed an agent, Won Jeong-hwa, inside South Korea's military circles by having her pose as a defector. Under that cover she gave 52 lectures at military bases, and prosecutors said she dated a South Korean army officer and used the relationship to make him work for her. She passed the North the locations of key military installations, lists of North Korean defectors and personal details of South Korean officers; business cards and photos of 23 officers were found among her belongings. She was arrested in July 2008, and in October 2008 the Suwon District Court sentenced her to five years in prison.
cite: NBC News/AP (15 Oct 2008); Korea Times (15 Oct 2008)

n: North Korean hacker paid a South Korean army captain in crypto
rank: Army captain; joint command system login
d: A North Korean agent known as 'Boris' used cryptocurrency to recruit a serving South Korean army captain, through a South Korean crypto-exchange operator, Lee. From 2021 Lee, following Boris's Telegram instructions, gave the captain a watch with a hidden camera and a hacking device called Poison Tap; the captain filmed secret material and handed over login details for the Korean Joint Command and Control System, the military's command network. The hacking attempt failed. The captain was paid about 48 million won and Lee about 700 million won in bitcoin. Both were arrested in April 2022. The captain, Kim, was sentenced to ten years, and in December 2025 the Supreme Court upheld Lee's four-year sentence.
cite: Korea Times (29 Apr 2022); Korea JoongAng Daily (28 Dec 2025)

n: Chongryon finance chief took ¥837m from Korean credit union in Tokyo
d: Chongryon, the association of pro-North Korean residents in Japan that serves as Pyongyang's de facto embassy, controlled a network of Korean credit unions called Chogin and drew money out of them. Kang Yong-gwan, former head of Chongryon's finance bureau, took 837 million yen from the Chogin Tokyo credit union in 13 transactions between 1994 and 1998. Chogin Tokyo collapsed in 1999. Police arrested Kang in November 2001 and searched Chongryon's headquarters; other Chogin chairmen were arrested in the following weeks over illicit loans. In March 2004 the Tokyo District Court sentenced Kang to six years in prison for embezzlement, and his appeal was rejected in October 2005.
cite: Japan Times (29 Nov 2001; 27 Mar 2004; 7 Oct 2005)

n: Oman says it broke up a UAE spy network in its government and army
d: Oman said in January 2011 that it had uncovered a spy network run for the United Arab Emirates that targeted 'Oman and the way its government and military work'. Its state news agency said several Omani nationals had been arrested about two months earlier, some of them government employees, and would be sent to court. The UAE denied any link and said it would cooperate with any transparent investigation. The case showed tension between two Gulf neighbours that are both members of the Gulf Cooperation Council.
cite: Al Jazeera (31 Jan 2011)

n: Afghan intelligence arrests officials and a general spying for Pakistan's ISI
rank: Foreign ministry diplomat; senior bureaucrats; an army general
d: Afghanistan's intelligence service, the National Directorate of Security (NDS), said in 2012 that Pakistan's spy agency, the ISI, and Iran had agents inside the Afghan government. In February 2012 it reported arresting four officials, including a senior diplomat in the Foreign Ministry's Asia section said to work for Pakistan's military intelligence. On 1 August 2012 NDS head Rahmatullah Nabil told parliament that 15 government employees, including senior bureaucrats and a military general, had been arrested for spying, and that some had confessed to working for the ISI or Iran. He also said insurgent infiltrators inside the security forces had been caught planning assassinations.
cite: RFE/RL (28 Feb 2012); RFE/RL (2 Aug 2012)

n: ISI chief in Kabul as the Taliban chose their prime minister
d: Pakistan's spy chief went to Kabul as the Taliban formed their government, and some analysts say he shaped who led it. Lieutenant-General Faiz Hameed, head of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), was in Kabul around 4 September 2021, three weeks after the Taliban took power. Pakistani analyst Ayesha Siddiqa said the visit helped decide that Mullah Hassan Akhund, not Abdul Ghani Baradar, would head the government; Akhund was named on 7 September. Pakistan and the Taliban denied any interference, and other experts said Taliban dependence on Pakistan had lessened. The Haqqani network, which the US calls an arm of the ISI, took the interior ministry.
cite: RFE/RL (Sept 2021)

n: Operation Midnight Jackal: ISI officers worked to topple Bhutto in parliament
d: Officers of Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), the military's spy agency, worked to bring down Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto by winning over her own party's members of the National Assembly before a no-confidence vote. Between 28 September and 6 October 1989, Brigadier Imtiaz Ahmed and Major Mohammed Amir met two PPP MNAs, Arif Awan and Rasheed Bhatti, at a Rawalpindi house to get them to defect to the opposition alliance. The civilian Intelligence Bureau had bugged the house and recorded the talks. Army chief General Mirza Aslam Beg retired both officers at Bhutto's request. The motion failed. In 1994 Bhutto's second government arrested Imtiaz and planned treason charges.
cite: The Herald (Aug 1994, republished by Dawn, 2018)

n: Qatar flew EU transport chief Hololei free while he negotiated its air deal
d: Qatar and its state airline paid for flights and holidays for Henrik Hololei, head of the European Commission's transport department, while he negotiated the EU–Qatar aviation agreement that opened Europe's skies to Qatar Airways. The trips, from 2015 to 2021, were revealed by Politico in 2023, and Hololei left the post in March 2023. An inquiry by OLAF, the EU anti-fraud office, concluded he shared confidential details of the deal with Qatar; a 2025 Commission disciplinary procedure found unauthorised gifts, conflicts of interest and breaches of confidentiality, and on 29 January 2026 the Commission terminated his contract. The European Public Prosecutor's Office opened a criminal corruption investigation in late 2024. The agreement, signed in 2019, remains in force.
cite: bne IntelliNews (Jan 2026); ERR News (2025); FDD (7 Nov 2024)

n: Saudi body paid sitting Italian senator and ex-PM Renzi up to $80,000 a year
d: A Saudi institute controlled by the royal family paid Matteo Renzi, Italy's former prime minister and a sitting senator, to sit on its advisory board. The Italian paper Domani reported in January 2021 that membership of the board of the FII Institute, which runs Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's 'Future Investment Initiative' conference, paid up to $80,000 a year. Renzi was in Riyadh at an FII event when Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte resigned, a government crisis Renzi's party had set off, and flew back overnight. At the event he praised the crown prince. The Democratic Party and others asked him to explain his ties to Riyadh after a US intelligence report linked the crown prince to Jamal Khashoggi's murder.
cite: Domani (26 Jan 2021); Fanpage.it (Feb 2021); Middle East Eye (2021)

n: Saudi cables: money to a Lebanese TV channel and party leader's plea
rank: Lebanese party leaders and MTV television
d: Saudi diplomatic cables published by WikiLeaks in June 2015 show Saudi Arabia being asked for, and in some cases paying, money to Lebanese parties, politicians and media in return for support. One cable says the Lebanese TV channel MTV asked for $20 million and received $5 million. Another quotes Samir Geagea, leader of the Lebanese Forces party, saying through an envoy that the party could not pay salaries and 'I'm ready to do what the kingdom demands.' MP Boutros Harb asked for Saudi money to found a party. A further list shows Saudi 'subscription' payments to about two dozen publications across the Arab world. Saudi Arabia told its citizens to ignore the leak.
cite: Global Voices (20 June 2015); Dawn (2015)
