n: Gülen followers won Turkey's judicial board, then picked top judges
rank: Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK); Court of Appeals
d: Followers of Fethullah Gülen, a Turkish preacher whose Hizmet movement placed members in state jobs, gained seats on the Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK), the body that appoints and moves Turkey's judges, in its 2010 election, and then used it to fill the top courts. Ahmet Hamsici, a former HSYK deputy chairman, said in a 31-page testimony after the 2016 coup attempt that Gülen wanted at least 140 Court of Appeals seats for his followers; the board agreed on 108, and about 107 of those named were appointed. The government, then allied with the movement, had bargained over the posts. In the 2014 HSYK election non-Gülenist candidates won and the government declared the movement's hold ended.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 18 Nov 2016 (Hamsici testimony); Daily Sabah, 13 Oct 2014

n: Leaked 2010 civil-service exam questions helped place Gülen followers
d: People working in the question-preparation unit of Turkey's state testing body leaked the 2010 Public Personnel Selection Exam (KPSS), the test about 808,000 people sat for civil-service jobs, and prosecutors say the questions went to followers of the Gülen movement so its members could be hired into the state. Prosecutors confirmed that general-culture, skills and education questions were seized at least 12 days before the test, and about 2,600 suspects were investigated. In 2019 an Ankara court sentenced 70 defendants, most of them wives of military officers linked to the movement, to between seven months and 14 years. A separate 2010 police promotion exam case led to 735 arrests.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 12 May 2016; Daily Sabah, 14 Feb 2019

n: Gülen-linked judges removed for cheating on Turkey's 2012 judge exam
d: Followers of the Gülen movement entered Turkey's courts as judges and prosecutors through a 2012 entrance exam whose questions had been leaked, according to the country's judicial board. After an opposition CHP deputy, Atilla Kart, complained that 20 named candidates had seen the questions, expert reports from prosecutors and the national testing centre (ÖSYM) found the candidates had marked the same questions wrong. In June 2015 the Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK) dismissed 37 judges and prosecutors on that evidence. The board linked the suspects to the movement, which was already accused over the 2010 civil-service exam leak. The case was used as evidence of a wider practice of placing members in state institutions.
cite: Daily Sabah, 11 Jun 2015

n: Gülen-linked prosecutor summoned Turkey's spy chief in 2012 'MİT crisis'
rank: Istanbul special prosecutor and police chiefs
d: Prosecutors and police chiefs that a Turkish court later tied to the Gülen movement used their posts to target the head of the national intelligence agency (MİT). On 12 February 2012 Istanbul prosecutor Sadrettin Sarıkaya, running a probe into the Kurdish KCK network, summoned MİT undersecretary Hakan Fidan over his talks with the PKK. Prime Minister Erdoğan ordered Fidan not to appear and passed a law requiring the prime minister's permission to prosecute intelligence officers. On 3 March 2021 the Istanbul 23rd High Criminal Court gave 10 of 18 defendants, including former police chiefs Yurt Atayün and Ali Fuat Yılmazer, aggravated life sentences for attempting to overthrow the government. Sarıkaya was jailed.
cite: Turkish Minute, 3 Mar 2021; Hürriyet Daily News (Sarıkaya arrest)

n: Gülen-linked gendarmes and prosecutors stopped Turkish spy-agency trucks
d: Gendarmerie officers and prosecutors whom Turkish courts tied to the Gülen movement used their posts in 2014 to stop and search trucks of the national intelligence agency (MİT) heading to Syria near the border, against government orders to let them pass. The government said the search was part of the movement's campaign from inside the state. On 28 June 2019 Ankara's 16th High Criminal Court convicted seven gendarmes and prosecutors of obtaining and disclosing confidential state documents. Former Adana chief prosecutor Süleyman Bağrıyanık received over 22 years, prosecutors Ahmet Karaca and Aziz Takcı 26 years each, and former brigadier general Hamza Celepoğlu about 20 years.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 29 Jun 2019

n: Court ties Istanbul police intelligence chiefs to Hrant Dink murder
rank: Istanbul police intelligence chief and deputy
d: An Istanbul court ruled in March 2021 that the 2007 killing of Hrant Dink, an Armenian-Turkish newspaper editor, was carried out in line with the aims of the Gülen movement, which it found had members inside the police and security services who let the plot go ahead. Of 76 defendants, former Istanbul police intelligence chief Ramazan Akyürek and his deputy Ali Fuat Yılmazer were given life sentences for premeditated murder, as were two former Istanbul interior-ministry officers. A former Trabzon commander, Ali Öz, got 28 years. The gunman, Ogün Samast, had been sentenced in 2011. Other defendants were convicted of membership of what Ankara calls 'FETÖ' and of destroying documents.
cite: Voice of America (AP), Mar 2021; Duvar English

n: Aide to Turkey's armed forces chief confessed to bugging for Gülenists
rank: Aide-de-camp to the Chief of General Staff
d: Lieutenant Colonel Levent Türkkan, aide-de-camp to Turkey's Chief of General Staff Hulusi Akar, told investigators after the July 2016 coup attempt that he had been a follower of the Gülen movement since school and had carried out its orders inside the military. He said movement members gave him the questions for his 1989 military academy entrance exam, and that he planted listening devices in the office of the previous chief, Necdet Özel, with a device supplied by a contact at Türk Telekom. State media published the confession as key proof of the movement's role. On 23 May 2017 he told an Ankara court the statement was false and given under torture; photos had shown him bruised.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 21 Jul 2016; Stockholm Center for Freedom, 24 May 2017

n: Turkey jailed Constitutional Court deputy chief as Gülen member
rank: Deputy President of the Constitutional Court
d: Turkish prosecutors said the Gülen movement had a member at the top of the Constitutional Court, the court that rules on whether laws and government acts are lawful. Alparslan Altan, the court's deputy president, was detained a day after the July 2016 coup attempt. In March 2019 a court sentenced him to 11 years and 3 months for membership of an armed terrorist organisation, the label Turkey uses for the movement. Altan denied the charge and said there was no concrete evidence. His case was part of a purge in which more than 150,000 people were removed from state jobs; the European Court of Human Rights later found his detention unlawful.
cite: Turkish Minute, 6 Mar 2019 (citing T24); Turkish Minute, 16 Apr 2019 (ECtHR)

n: Turkey convicted a UN war-crimes judge as a Gülen member
rank: Judge, UN Mechanism for International Criminal Tribunals
d: Turkey said the Gülen movement had a member sitting as a judge on a United Nations court. Aydın Sefa Akay, a Turkish judge at the UN Mechanism for International Criminal Tribunals, which handles remaining appeals from the Yugoslavia and Rwanda war-crimes tribunals, was detained in Turkey in September 2016 during the purge after the coup attempt. In June 2017 a Turkish court sentenced him to seven and a half years for membership of what Ankara calls 'FETÖ', then released him under a travel ban. The UN mechanism said Turkey's actions breached his protected status as a UN judge with diplomatic immunity. The European Court of Human Rights later faulted Turkey over his arrest.
cite: NBC News (AP), Jun 2017; Turkish Minute, 23 Apr 2024

n: Menzil Sufi order said to fill Turkish police posts vacated by Gülenists
rank: Police appointments; health and energy ministers
d: Menzil, a branch of the Naqshbandi Sufi order, moved its followers into Turkish state posts emptied by the purge of Gülen followers, according to journalists and the order's own leader. The book Metastaz by Barış Terkoğlu and Barış Pehlivan says that from 2014 new police recruits came largely from Naqshbandi and other sects, with Menzil dominant, and T24 reported police promotions made by reference to Menzil membership. Menzil chief Fevzeddin Erol told Sözcü that health minister Recep Akdağ and energy minister Taner Yıldız were members and that the order had 'men everywhere in the state'. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu denied it, and a court ordered T24's article removed.
cite: Foreign Policy, 15 Jan 2020

n: RSS economic ideologue Gurumurthy put on India's central bank board
rank: Reserve Bank of India central board
d: The government appointed Swaminathan Gurumurthy, co-convenor of the Swadeshi Jagran Manch, an economic body of the Hindu nationalist RSS, to the central board of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in August 2018, alongside Satish Marathe of Sahakar Bharati. At the board's nine-hour meeting on 19 November 2018, held amid a dispute between the government and the bank over its reserves, Gurumurthy was the most vocal member and won approval for restructuring bad small-business loans up to Rs 25 crore. Governor Urjit Patel agreed to a review of Rs 9.6 lakh crore in reserves and resigned on 10 December 2018. Gurumurthy said the resignation surprised him.
cite: Business Today, 8 Aug 2018 and 20 Nov 2018; The Week, 13 Dec 2018

n: RSS sends its own organiser to run the BJP as 'general secretary'
d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, places one of its full-time organisers, called pracharaks, inside India's ruling BJP as its general secretary (organisation), a post reserved by convention for senior RSS men. In July 2019 the RSS recalled Ram Lal after 13 years in the post and replaced him with B. L. Santhosh. The holder makes sure the BJP leadership carries out the RSS chief's instructions, reports to the RSS head and mobilises RSS workers at elections. In 2004 the then holder, Sanjay Joshi, drafted a resolution against party leader L. K. Advani over his praise of Jinnah, and Advani was forced to resign as party president.
cite: ThePrint, Jul 2019; Asian Age, 14 Jul 2019

n: Liberhan inquiry: RSS groups and UP government enabled Babri demolition
rank: Uttar Pradesh chief minister, bureaucracy and police
d: The Liberhan Commission, a 17-year official inquiry into the 1992 demolition of the Babri Mosque at Ayodhya, found that the RSS and its allied groups, together with Uttar Pradesh's BJP government, made it possible. Its report, given to the prime minister on 30 June 2009, named the RSS, VHP, Bajrang Dal, BJP and Shiv Sena, and called chief minister Kalyan Singh the 'pivotal figure'. It said his government transferred officers who opposed the plan, worked through handpicked bureaucrats, and that about 90% of the police sent to guard the mosque were sympathisers, the rest told not to use force. The demolition was followed by violence that killed hundreds.
cite: ThePrint, summary of Liberhan Commission report (2009)

n: VHP officials made public prosecutors in Gujarat 2002 riot trials
rank: Special public prosecutors in riot cases
d: Gujarat's government appointed lawyers from the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), a Hindu nationalist body in the RSS family, as public prosecutors in trials over the 2002 Gujarat riots, in which VHP members were among the accused. Citizens for Justice and Peace told the Supreme Court that Dilip Trivedi, general secretary of the VHP's Mehsana unit, prosecuted the Sardarpura massacre case and that Chetan Shah, a VHP supporter, handled the Gulbarga Society case. A Special Investigation Team report of 17 May 2010 said political affiliation appeared to have influenced the appointments. In 2021 Kapil Sibal told the court that 55 accused were bailed after Trivedi's appointment.
cite: Zee News (Supreme Court hearing, Oct 2003); LiveLaw, 11 Nov 2021

n: RSS history wing's leader made chair of India's history research council
rank: Chair, Indian Council of Historical Research
d: Y. Sudershan Rao, head of the Andhra Pradesh branch of the Akhil Bharatiya Itihas Sankalan Yojana (ABISY), a history body set up by the RSS, was made chair of the Indian Council of Historical Research (ICHR), the state body that funds and directs historical research, in July 2014. In March 2015 three ABISY-linked historians were nominated to the council on his recommendation. Critics, including historian Romila Thapar, said he had no peer-reviewed publications and saw the appointments as placing RSS-aligned people in state institutions. Rao said the Ramayana and Mahabharata were accurate history and announced a study of whether Adam's Bridge was man-made. He served until 2017.
cite: Wikipedia (Yellapragada Sudershan Rao, citing Indian press); Tribune, 27 Nov 2015

n: Gujarat made RSS school leader Batra's books part of state curriculum
d: Dinanath Batra, a full-time leader of Vidya Bharati, the RSS's school network, had his own books placed in Gujarat's state school curriculum. On 30 June 2014 the BJP government of Gujarat issued a circular listing six of his books, translated into Gujarati, as supplementary reading, and the state education minister said they were compulsory. In November 2014 Haryana's new BJP government named him to its committee of educationalists. Batra had earlier filed 70 objections to national NCERT textbooks and, in February 2014, made Penguin India withdraw and pulp Wendy Doniger's book on Hinduism after a lawsuit.
cite: Wikipedia (Dinanath Batra, citing Indian Express and others)

n: 62% of India's new military feeder schools went to Sangh and BJP figures
who: RSS, allied bodies and BJP politicians
d: Under a 2022 public-private scheme, India's Defence Ministry handed most new Sainik Schools, boarding schools that prepare cadets for the National Defence Academy, to bodies tied to the RSS and the ruling BJP. The Reporters' Collective found through RTI requests that of at least 40 agreements signed between May 2022 and December 2023, at least 62% went to such groups: 11 schools owned by BJP politicians or their trusts, 8 run by the RSS or allies and 6 tied to Hindutva or other Hindu religious groups. Vidya Bharati, the RSS school network, received seven affiliations. The ministry declined to share its selection process and said it does not check applicants' political leanings.
cite: The Reporters' Collective, 3 Apr 2024

n: VHP men took 9 of 11 key seats on the state-formed Ram temple trust
rank: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust
d: The Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), the Hindu nationalist body that led the campaign for a Ram temple at Ayodhya, took control of the trust India's government formed on the Supreme Court's orders to build it. In February 2020, nine of the 11 trustees with a decisive role were from the VHP or RSS, including its chairman Nritya Gopal Das, a member of the VHP's guidance council, and general secretary Champat Rai, a VHP vice-president. Former Modi aide Nripendra Misra chaired the construction committee, and four ex-officio members are senior government officers. Only two trustees had no RSS or VHP link.
cite: IANS via Lokmat Times, 21 Feb 2020; The Week, 19 Feb 2020

n: Gorakhnath Math's head monks held Gorakhpur's seat, then ran Uttar Pradesh
d: The Gorakhnath Math, a Hindu monastery in Gorakhpur, has sent its successive heads (mahants) into elected office for decades and its present head runs India's most populous state. Mahant Digvijay Nath, a national general secretary of the Hindu Mahasabha, won the Gorakhpur Lok Sabha seat in 1967; his successor Avaidyanath held it in 1970 and 1989 and for the BJP in 1991 and 1996; and Yogi Adityanath, Avaidyanath's disciple, won it five times from 1998 and founded his own youth group, the Hindu Yuva Vahini. Adityanath became mahant in 2014 and Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh on 19 March 2017, keeping both roles, and won a second term in 2022.
cite: Wikipedia (Gorakhnath Math; Yogi Adityanath); Deccan Herald, 2022

n: Tablighi Jamaat member Javed Nasir made head of Pakistan's ISI
d: Lieutenant General Javed Nasir, a member of Tablighi Jamaat, a worldwide Islamic missionary movement, was appointed Director-General of Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on 14 March 1992, over the army chief's objections and with little intelligence experience. During his 13 months in charge the ISI ran a covert programme to arm the Bosnian army against the UN arms embargo, including airlifting anti-tank missiles, and helped set up an Afghan mujahideen government. He was retired early on 13 May 1993, which commentators attributed to pressure from Arab states over his support for radical movements. He later became a Tablighi missionary.
cite: Wikipedia (Javed Nasir, citing Pakistani and international press)

n: Army officers and Harkat-ul-Jihad plotted Islamist coup in Pakistan, 1995
d: Serving Pakistani army officers working with Qari Saifullah Akhtar, chief of the militant group Harkat-ul-Jihad al-Islami, planned to seize power from inside the army in 1995. They intended to storm a corps commanders' meeting at army headquarters in Rawalpindi on 30 September, kill Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, the army chief and other leaders, and proclaim an Islamic caliphate with Major General Zahirul Islam Abbasi as its emir. Officers were detained on 26 September 1995 after Akhtar turned informer, and weapons and uniforms were seized. A court martial gave Abbasi seven years and Brigadier Mustansir Billah 14 years; two colonels were dismissed and jailed.
cite: Dawn (Supreme Court appeal coverage, Feb 2022); Wikipedia (Zahirul Islam Abbasi)

n: Haghani seminary graduates ran Iran's intelligence ministry and judiciary
d: Graduates and followers of the Haghani Circle, a hardline school of thought centred on a Qom seminary founded in 1964 by clerics including Mohammad Beheshti and Mohammad Taghi Mesbah Yazdi, have repeatedly headed Iran's Ministry of Intelligence, whose minister must by law be a qualified Islamic jurist. Ministers Mohammad Reyshahri, Ali Fallahian, Ali Younesi and Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei came from its circle. Mohseni-Ejei, a Haghani graduate, was intelligence minister from 2005 to 2009, prosecutor-general from 2009 to 2014, and became Chief Justice on 1 July 2021. The EU and US sanctioned him in 2011 for the detention and torture of protesters after the 2009 election.
cite: Wikipedia (Haghani Circle, citing Vali Nasr, The Shia Revival, 2006; Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i)

n: Ennahda leader Ghannouchi given life over 'secret apparatus' in Tunisia
d: Tunisian prosecutors accused Ennahda, the Islamist party that led the government after 2011, of running a 'secret apparatus' that infiltrated state institutions, spied, and was involved in the 2013 assassinations of leftist politicians Chokri Belaid and Mohamed Brahmi. Lawyers for the victims' families first presented documents in 2018 and named Mustapha Kheder as its head. In early June 2026 the Tunis Court of First Instance sentenced party leader Rached Ghannouchi to life plus 30 years for forming a terrorist alliance, gave eleven others life terms and thirteen more 10 to 48 years. Ennahda denied the charges as political, and rights groups called the trial part of a crackdown on opponents.
cite: Al Jazeera, 3 Jun 2026; Asharq Al-Awsat, Jul 2020

n: Saudi-inspired Madkhali Salafis entrenched in Libya's forces and mosques
rank: Special Deterrence Force; LNA brigades; religious endowments authority
d: Followers of Rabee al-Madkhali, a Saudi cleric whose ultra-conservative Salafi teaching demands obedience to rulers, built positions inside both of Libya's rival governments after 2011, the International Crisis Group reported in April 2019. In Tripoli they are strong in the Special Deterrence Force (Rada), nominally under the interior ministry and given a national remit by decree in May 2018. In the east they form units of Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army and dominate the eastern religious endowments authority, which runs mosques and issues fatwas. In late 2018 the Tripoli government named a Madkhali-sympathetic head of its endowments office; a former official estimated most Tripoli mosques were under Madkhali influence.
cite: International Crisis Group, Addressing the Rise of Libya's Madkhali-Salafis, 25 Apr 2019

n: Mali's High Islamic Council forced a rewrite of the national family code
d: Mali's High Islamic Council, the country's top Islamic body, had its demands written into the national family code after mass protests against an earlier version. The National Assembly adopted a new code on 3 August 2009 that expanded women's rights; after marches of up to 50,000 people, President Amadou Toumani Touré sent it back on 27 August. The amended text, endorsed by the council, was adopted on 2 December 2011. It recognises religious marriage, states that a wife must obey her husband and that the man is head of the family, sets marriage at 16 for girls with exceptions from 15, and altered the earlier gains in inheritance. FIDH said the council's demands were met.
cite: FIDH, 9 Dec 2011; Wikipedia (Malian Family Code)

n: Al-Shabaab agents inside Mogadishu's city hall, spy agency and chamber
d: Al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked Islamist insurgency, placed agents inside Somalia's institutions. On 24 July 2019 a blind woman using a false name, who worked as a disability coordinator in the office of Mogadishu mayor Abdirahman Omar Osman, blew herself up at a security meeting there, killing six officials; the mayor died of his wounds on 1 August. Al-Shabaab said the target was UN envoy James Swan. The National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) later paraded a government band singer it said was al-Shabaab's accountant, and the government dissolved the Chamber of Commerce board after finding the group had representatives on it.
cite: Daily Nation (Nairobi), Jan 2020; Al Jazeera, 25 Jul 2019

n: Hefazat-e-Islam's demands rewrote Bangladesh's school textbooks
d: Hefazat-e-Islam, a coalition of Qawmi madrasa teachers and clerics whose 2013 13-point charter demanded sharia law and a changed school curriculum, got its demands written into Bangladesh's state textbooks for 2017. Hefazat members said the government made the 29 changes they had asked for; its leader Shah Ahmad Shafi praised the authorities. Removed items included a poem by Humayun Azad, a Baul essay, a children's Ramayana excerpt and an excerpt from the novel Lalu, while essays on the Prophet and the early caliphs were added. The National Curriculum and Textbook Board's chairman denied Hefazat's influence. Critics said religious content was entering secular literature books.
cite: BenarNews, 17 Feb 2017; Wikipedia (2017 Bangladesh textbooks criticism)

n: Monks put on Sri Lanka's eastern land task force; no Tamils or Muslims
rank: Presidential Task Force for Archaeological Heritage, Eastern Province
d: In June 2020 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa placed senior Buddhist monks on a presidential task force to survey archaeological sites in Sri Lanka's Eastern Province and allocate land to them. Ellawala Medhananda Thera, Panamure Thilakawansha Thera and the chief prelate for the Northern and Eastern Provinces sat alongside the defence secretary, Major General Kamal Gunaratne, who chaired it, a police deputy inspector-general and the head of Derana TV. No Tamil or Muslim member was named, although those communities are over 70% of the province's people. The leader of the Tamil National Alliance wrote to the president objecting, and two minority members were later added.
cite: Daily FT, 4 Jun 2020

n: Buddhist monks' council met Sri Lanka's president monthly to steer policy
d: President Gotabaya Rajapaksa set up a Buddhist Advisory Council of senior monks from Sri Lanka's three monastic chapters in April 2020 to advise on carrying out government policy, and met it on the third Friday of each month at the Presidential Secretariat with ministry secretaries present. Its first meeting was on 24 April 2020. By September the monks had advised on archaeological sites, monastery land deeds, national security, the National Education Policy and placing Buddhist universities under the education ministry. The government reported acting on their proposals, appointing four state ministers to the education ministry and moving to amend the Antiquities Ordinance for temples built on archaeological sites.
cite: Daily FT, 21 Sep 2020

n: Santi Asoke sect's followers filled Palang Dharma party and Bangkok council
rank: Bangkok governor and city council; parliament
d: Santi Asoke, an ascetic Buddhist sect, placed its followers in Thai elected office through the Palang Dharma party. Chamlong Srimuang, a sect follower and former general, won the Bangkok governorship in 1985 and founded the party in 1988; sect members gathered the signatures needed to register it, and close to half its 1988 candidates were Santi Asoke followers. In 1990 the party won 49 of the 55 seats on Bangkok's city council, and in 1992 it won 41 and then 47 parliamentary seats and joined the coalition government. Chamlong led the May 1992 protests that forced military ruler Suchinda Kraprayoon out. Thaksin Shinawatra later led the party and served as a minister.
cite: Wikipedia (Palang Dharma Party; Chamlong Srimuang); McCargo, Southeast Asia Research, 1993

n: Unification Church money said to fund Nepal Family Party and its minister
d: The South Korean Unification Church is alleged to have funded Nepal's Nepal Family Party (Pariwar Dal), whose founder Ek Nath Dhakal served as cabinet minister for cooperatives and poverty alleviation from May 2012 and later as minister of peace and reconstruction under K. P. Sharma Oli. Leaked emails from 2017 to 2022, obtained by Newstapa and reported in Nepal in early 2026, show Dhakal asking the church's Asia president for at least $500,000 for the 2017 election and $20,000 a month for the party; the letters mention three former prime ministers. The church took 20 communist MPs abroad for 'principle education'. The church called the documents inauthentic, and the party denied foreign funding.
cite: Nepali Times, 2026; Wikipedia (Ek Nath Dhakal); Kantipur, 4 Feb 2026

n: Unification Church members signed up en masse to South Korea's ruling party
rank: People Power Party membership and leadership vote
d: A South Korean special counsel found that about 3,500 Unification Church followers joined the then-ruling People Power Party (PPP), about 3,100 of them between October 2022 and March 2023, ahead of the party convention that chose its leader. Prosecutors raided the firm holding the PPP membership list on 18 September 2025 and matched about 120,000 names against 1.2 million church records. They suspect the church first sought to help lawmaker Kweon Seong-dong and then backed Kim Gi-hyeon, who won the leadership. A former church official had texted a shaman about '11,101 new members'. Party figures said the overlap was statistically expected; the law requires proof members were coerced.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily, 26 Sep 2025

n: Ríos Montt's Verbo church elders became Guatemala's presidential secretaries
d: When General Efraín Ríos Montt took power in Guatemala in the coup of 23 March 1982, elders of his Pentecostal-style Church of the Word (Verbo), founded by the California mission Gospel Outreach, entered his government. Two Verbo elders, Francisco Bianchi and Álvaro Contreras, became his personal secretaries and key advisers, and he named Jorge Serrano Elías, a leader of the neo-Pentecostal Elim church, to head the new Council of State after dissolving Congress. Ríos Montt prayed with the elders before going to the palace. His 17-month rule saw the worst of the army's massacres of Maya villagers, and in 2013 a Guatemalan court convicted him of genocide; the verdict was later annulled.
cite: Pew Research Center, 5 Oct 2006; Christianity Today, 23 Apr 1982; Time, 21 Jun 1982

n: Ex-New Tribes missionary put in charge of Brazil's isolated-tribes unit
rank: Head of isolated and recently contacted peoples, FUNAI
d: In February 2020 Brazil's government named Ricardo Lopes Dias, an evangelical pastor who spent ten years as a missionary with New Tribes Mission (now Ethnos360), a US group with a history of contacting and converting isolated tribes, to head the department of FUNAI, the federal indigenous agency, that protects isolated peoples. The post gave him detailed information on more than 100 registered isolated groups. Federal prosecutors warned of possible genocide if missionaries gained that data, and in May 2020 appellate judge Antonio Souza Prudente annulled the appointment, citing a conflict of interest and risk to the no-contact policy. FUNAI called the ruling persecution of evangelicals.
cite: Mongabay, May 2020; Associated Press, 5 Feb 2020

n: Evangelical bloc gave pastor Feliciano Brazil's human-rights committee
rank: Chair, Chamber of Deputies Human Rights and Minorities Committee
d: Brazil's evangelical bloc in Congress used committee seat deals to take control of the Chamber of Deputies' Human Rights and Minorities Committee in 2013. Other parties gave up seats to the Social Christian Party (PSC), leaving the 18-member committee with five PSC members and six from the evangelical bloc, and on 7 March 2013 it elected pastor Marco Feliciano of the Assembly of God as chair despite his remarks against gay and Black people. Protests followed in several cities and a petition for his removal passed 442,000 signatures. In June 2013 the committee approved a bill to lift the Federal Psychology Council's 1999 ban on treating homosexuality as an illness.
cite: Global Voices, 19 Mar 2013; Associated Press via Star Tribune, 19 Jun 2013

n: Assembly of God pastor Everaldo allegedly steered Rio's health posts
rank: Rio de Janeiro State Health Secretariat; Cedae; Detran
d: Everaldo Pereira, an Assembly of God pastor and national president of the Social Christian Party (PSC), was arrested on 28 August 2020 in Operation Tris in Idem, a federal police inquiry into corruption in Rio de Janeiro state's health secretariat during the COVID-19 pandemic under PSC governor Wilson Witzel. Reports cited by Congresso em Foco said Everaldo, who held no government post, was the most powerful figure in Witzel's government and influenced appointments to the Health Secretariat, the state water company Cedae and the vehicle agency Detran. Witzel was suspended from office the same day and later removed. Everaldo had baptised Jair Bolsonaro in the Jordan River in 2016.
cite: Congresso em Foco, 28 Aug 2020 (citing O Dia); Channels TV/AFP, 28 Aug 2020

n: Opus Dei member Ollero sat on Spain's abortion appeal for seven years
d: Andrés Ollero, reported by Público to be a member of Opus Dei, the Catholic lay organisation, was a Popular Party deputy from 1986 to 2003 and then joined Spain's Constitutional Court, which rules on whether laws comply with the constitution. In 2014 he was made rapporteur on the Popular Party's appeal against the 2010 abortion law, responsible for drafting the ruling, but seven years later had brought no draft to the full court. He also sat on the bench that refused to hear a challenge to his former party colleague Jorge Fernández Díaz's award of a police medal to the Virgin Mary. In July 2021 the group Abogados Cristianos filed a criminal complaint against him over the delay.
cite: Público; InfoVaticana, 17 Jul 2021

n: Greek junta's officers in Cyprus's National Guard overthrew Makarios
d: Greece's military government used the Greek officers it had posted to Cyprus's army, the National Guard, to overthrow the Cypriot government. About 650 Greek officers were serving in the National Guard, and the junta also supplied, controlled and funded EOKA-B, an armed group that wanted Cyprus joined to Greece. On 2 July 1974 President Makarios wrote publicly to the Greek president demanding the officers' withdrawal and accusing the junta of plotting against him. On 15 July, on orders from junta leader Dimitrios Ioannidis, the National Guard attacked the presidential palace and installed Nikos Sampson. Turkey invaded on 20 July and came to hold 37 per cent of the island, which remains divided.
cite: Library of Congress Country Studies, 'Cyprus: The Greek Coup and the Turkish Invasion'; Wikipedia, '1974 Cypriot coup d'état'

n: Video shows Cyprus president's aides discussing cash for access
rank: Presidential chief of staff and circle
d: A secretly filmed video alleges that money from businessmen could buy access to Cyprus's President Nikos Christodoulides through people close to him. The eight-minute recording, posted online on 8 January 2026, shows his chief of staff Charalambos Charalambous, his brother-in-law and a former energy minister apparently discussing ways round the €1 million limit on campaign donations, cash for access to the presidency, and help for businessmen avoiding EU sanctions on Russia. Charalambous resigned, saying his words were taken out of context. The government did not deny the footage was real but called it a maliciously edited 'hybrid' attack, possibly by Russia. A former Supreme Court judge was appointed to investigate both its origin and those recorded.
cite: Irish Times (15 Jan 2026); Cyprus Mail (13 Jan 2026)

n: KGB 'home Russians' cultivated Finland's leaders, including Kekkonen
d: The Soviet KGB assigned its officers in Helsinki to individual Finnish politicians and officials, who each came to have a personal Soviet contact known as a 'kotiryssä', or 'home Russian'. Dozens of KGB officers worked under diplomatic cover at the Soviet embassy. Viktor Vladimirov, a KGB general posted there in 1955–60, 1970–71 and 1977–84, began the system and dealt with elite politicians, including President Urho Kekkonen. A former Soviet diplomat later said Vladimirov reported straight to the Soviet leadership and backed Ahti Karjalainen to succeed Kekkonen. The public learned of the system through a 1981 book. It is tied to 'Finlandization', the bending of Finnish policy to Moscow's wishes; Helsingin Sanomat reported in 2015 that the practice had almost ended.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kotiryssä' (citing Helsingin Sanomat 2003, 2009, 2015; Koivisto memoirs); Barents Observer (5 Nov 2012)

n: Samherji's ex-board chair became Iceland's fisheries minister
d: Kristján Þór Júlíusson, a former chairman of the board of Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, served as Iceland's Minister of Fisheries and Agriculture from November 2017 to November 2021, the post that regulates the industry. In November 2019 the 'Fishrot' leaks showed Samherji paying bribes in Namibia for fishing quotas. A whistleblower said that in 2014 Samherji's chief Þorsteinn Már Baldvinsson introduced Kristján, then health minister, to three Namibians later accused of taking those bribes as 'his man' in government. Kristján said he had not been involved with Samherji since leaving its board about 19 years earlier. About 4,000 people protested in Reykjavík calling for him to resign; he refused.
cite: Iceland Monitor / Morgunblaðið (13 Nov 2019); High North News (26 Nov 2019); Wikipedia, 'Kristján Þór Júlíusson'

n: TV figure 'Boki 13' bribed North Macedonia's special prosecutor
rank: Head of the Special Prosecution Office
d: Bojan Jovanovski, a television personality known as 'Boki 13', used his closeness to Katica Janeva, head of North Macedonia's Special Prosecution Office, to sell the country's richest man, Jordan Orce Kamčev, milder treatment in his criminal case. The Special Prosecution Office had been set up to pursue high-level crimes after a wiretapping scandal. Kamčev had been detained in November 2018 on extortion and money-laundering charges and was released in March 2019. In July 2019 Jovanovski and his security chief were arrested at the Greek border carrying €1.5 million. In June 2020 a court found he had bribed Janeva with €50,000 and jailed him for nine years; Janeva got seven years for misuse of office.
cite: OCCRP (22 Jun 2020); RFE/RL (2020)

n: Serbian intelligence officer gave instructions to a Macedonian MP
org_label: Serbian Security Information Agency (BIA) and Russian intelligence
d: Leaked files of Macedonia's own counter-intelligence service say a Serbian intelligence officer at Serbia's embassy in Skopje steered a pro-Russian Macedonian MP. The documents, prepared in 2017 for the service's director and published by OCCRP partners on 4 June 2017, say Goran Živaljević of Serbia's Security Information Agency (BIA) gave instructions to Ivan Stoilković, an MP who led the Democratic Party of Serbs in Macedonia, a partner in the ruling coalition, and that Stoilković was in contact with Russian diplomats. They also say three officers of Russia's foreign intelligence service (SVR) worked from the Russian embassy and tried to recruit current and former army and interior ministry staff. Stoilković declined to discuss the contacts; Serbia said Živaljević broke no rules.
cite: OCCRP / Spooks and Spin (4 Jun 2017)

n: Tycoon Savvidis paid Macedonian politicians to fight the name deal
d: Ivan Savvidis, a Russian-Greek billionaire and former member of Russia's parliament for the ruling United Russia party, paid at least €300,000 to opponents of the agreement that renamed Macedonia 'North Macedonia', a deal needed for it to join NATO. According to Macedonian interior ministry documents seen by OCCRP partner IRL, the money, some carried in cash across the Greek border, went to more than a dozen Macedonian politicians from several parties, to new nationalist groups and to football hooligans linked to the opposition VMRO-DPMNE party, ahead of protests in which a petrol bomb was thrown at parliament. Greece separately expelled two Russian diplomats for paying opponents of the deal. Savvidis denied funding the protests.
cite: OCCRP (16 Jul 2018); Eurasia Review (18 Jul 2018)

n: Mafia banker Michele Sindona became the Vatican's financial adviser
rank: Financial adviser to the Holy See
d: Michele Sindona, a Sicilian banker who laundered heroin money for Mafia families, was hired by the Holy See to manage its investments. After Italy ended the Vatican's tax exemption on Italian investment income in 1968, the Holy See took Sindona on as financial adviser, and his work with the Vatican Bank (the IOR) began in 1969; large sums moved from his banks through the Vatican to Swiss banks. He was also a member of the secret P2 Masonic lodge. When his Franklin National Bank in New York failed in 1974, the Vatican lost an estimated 35 billion lire. In 1986 an Italian court jailed Sindona for life for ordering the 1979 murder of Giorgio Ambrosoli, liquidator of his banks; he died of cyanide poisoning in prison days later.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Michele Sindona'; Wikipedia, 'Institute for the Works of Religion'

n: Polish communist secret police had an informant in the Vatican
d: Poland's communist Security Service (SB), the secret police, had an informant close to Pope John Paul II in Rome. In April 2005, weeks after the Pope's death, Poland's Institute of National Remembrance, the state body that holds communist-era police files, announced that about 700 pages showed Father Konrad Hejmo, a Dominican priest who ran pastoral care for Polish pilgrims at the Vatican, had been a secret collaborator under the code names 'Hejnal' and 'Dominik' during the 1980s. Hejmo's Dominican superior, who reviewed the files, called them convincing. It was not established how much secret information he passed on. The case was part of a wider picture of communist services trying to watch the Polish-born Pope.
cite: NBC News / Associated Press (Apr 2005); Mail & Guardian (28 Apr 2005)

n: Iranian agents worked alongside Bosnian Interior Ministry staff
rank: Interior Ministry and AID intelligence agency
d: Iran built a presence inside Bosnia's wartime security apparatus. On 15 February 1996 NATO-led troops raided a ski chalet at Fojnica that they called a terrorist training cell, arresting three Iranians and several Bosnians who worked for the Interior Ministry, and finding explosives, weapons and models of UN buildings. Western officials said the Bosnian intelligence agency AID, under former interior minister Bakir Alispahić, worked largely beyond government control and close to Iran, one of Bosnia's few wartime allies. The United States made ending Iran's military role a condition of a $400 million programme to train and equip the Bosnian army, and demanded that AID be shut down.
cite: Christian Science Monitor (12 Mar 1996)

n: MG Baltic bribed Lithuania's Liberal leader and parties for votes
rank: Liberal Movement leader and Labour Party MP
d: MG Baltic, one of Lithuania's largest business groups, paid politicians and their parties to get decisions it wanted in parliament. On 12 May 2016 anti-corruption officers searched Eligijus Masiulis, leader of the Liberal Movement, and detained MG Baltic vice-president Raimondas Kurlianskis; prosecutors said Masiulis had taken a bribe from Kurlianskis, and €242,000 was found in his possession. A lower court acquitted everyone in 2022, but the Court of Appeal convicted them in 2023 and the Supreme Court made it final on 24 October 2024. Masiulis got five and a half years in prison, Labour MP Vytautas Gapšys four years and three months, and Kurlianskis five and a half years. The Liberal Movement, the Labour Party and MG Group were fined as organisations.

n: Russia's GRU recruited a Lithuanian Air Force officer
d: Sergey Moiseyenko, an army surgeon at a military hospital in Šiauliai who worked for Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, recruited a Lithuanian Air Force officer in 2012. The officer, Sergej Pusin, served at Šiauliai airbase, which hosts NATO's Baltic air-policing mission, and was paid 500 to 1,000 euros at secret meetings in Moiseyenko's garage. Moiseyenko passed Russian intelligence copies of Lithuanian defence ministry documents and personal files of airbase officers, and sought details of NATO flights and training. He was detained in late 2014 and a Šiauliai court sentenced him to ten and a half years; appeals failed. Lithuania pardoned him in November 2019 as part of a spy swap with Russia.
cite: LRT (15 Nov 2019)

n: FSB officer tried to recruit Lithuania's presidential guards
d: Nikolai Filipchenko, an officer of the Kaliningrad branch of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) who used a false identity, tried to recruit officers of Lithuania's VIP Protection Department, the unit that guards the president, in order to plant listening devices in the office and home of President Dalia Grybauskaitė. Lithuanian authorities said the operation aimed at infiltrating state institutions, law enforcement and intelligence services. He was detained on 29 April 2015 on a train from Kaliningrad, the first FSB officer caught spying in Lithuania. A Vilnius court jailed him for ten years on 7 July 2017. He was pardoned in November 2019 in a prisoner swap with Russia.
cite: LRT (15 Nov 2019); RFE/RL (7 Jul 2017)

n: Insurer ICBL paid Barbados's industry minister for state contracts
d: Senior executives of the Insurance Corporation of Barbados Limited (ICBL) paid Barbados's Minister of Industry, Donville Inniss, to use his post to win the company government business. In 2015 and 2016 Inniss helped ICBL get two Barbadian government insurance contracts covering more than $100 million of state property, and took about $36,000 in bribes, routed through a US bank account in the name of a friend's dental company in New York. Because the money passed through the United States, US prosecutors charged him. A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted him of money laundering on 16 January 2020, and on 27 April 2021 he was sentenced to two years in prison.
cite: US Department of Justice (27 Apr 2021)

n: Contractors and Trinidad's finance minister rigged Piarco airport bids
d: Contractors building the new Piarco International Airport terminal in the late 1990s worked with Trinidad and Tobago's then finance minister, Brian Kuei Tung, to rig bids and charge inflated prices. Raul Gutierrez Jr, president of the Miami firm Calmaquip Engineering, and five co-defendants pleaded guilty in US courts in 2006; prosecutors said the group hid the scheme through offshore companies and bank accounts, and Gutierrez was jailed for six years in 2007. The government sued 52 people and firms in Miami in 2004. In March 2023 a jury found Gutierrez, Kuei Tung and businessman Steve Ferguson liable for racketeering and fraud, and in May 2023 a judge entered a final judgment of US$131.3 million for Trinidad and Tobago.
cite: Caribbean Today (May 2023); White & Case / Law360 (Mar 2023); FreightWaves (18 Jan 2007)

n: Trafigura paid $31m into a Jamaican ruling-party account
d: Trafigura, a Dutch-registered oil trading company that held an agreement to lift oil for the Jamaican government, paid $31 million into an account linked to the then governing People's National Party (PNP) in 2006. Three payments of just over $10 million each were wired on 6 and 12 September 2006 to an account named CCOC ('Colin Campbell Our Candidate'), and about $30 million then went to the party's campaign account. The PNP called it a donation, Trafigura called it a commercial payment, and the party said the money was returned. Dutch prosecutors investigated possible bribery of Jamaican officials; after the UK Privy Council ruled in April 2021 that five PNP figures, including former prime minister Portia Simpson Miller, must answer questions, Trafigura went on trial in the Netherlands.
cite: Jamaica Gleaner (11 Mar 2022); Stabroek News (20 Apr 2021)

n: Senior Bahamian police officers indicted for protecting cocaine flights
rank: Senior Royal Bahamas Police Force officers
d: A cocaine trafficking network got senior Bahamian police and military officials working for it, according to a US indictment filed on 27 November 2024. Prosecutors say that since at least May 2021 two high-ranking officers of the Royal Bahamas Police Force and a Bahamian military official helped cocaine arriving on charter flights from Colombia and Venezuela pass through Bahamian airports, and let boats carry it on to Florida, for bribes of $10,000 to $2 million. One officer allegedly demanded $2 million on behalf of an unnamed 'high-ranking Bahamian politician'. Others allegedly shared US Coast Guard information with traffickers and misled the DEA. Police Commissioner Clayton Fernander, who was not accused, resigned on 4 December 2024.
cite: InSight Crime (12 Dec 2024); WLRN (9 Dec 2024)

n: Businessmen hid $200,000 in donations to New Zealand's National Party
org_label: Yikun Zhang and the Zheng brothers
d: Three businessmen, Yikun Zhang and the brothers Colin and Joe Zheng, channelled $100,000 in 2017 and $100,050 in 2018 to New Zealand's National Party, splitting each sum into smaller gifts under other people's names so the true donors would not be publicly declared. The Serious Fraud Office prosecuted them, and in 2022 the High Court found them guilty of obtaining by deception, while clearing them over donations to the Labour Party; they were sentenced to community detention in November 2022. The Court of Appeal later overturned the National Party convictions, finding the men had deceived the Electoral Commission and the party but had not been shown to benefit personally, as the law requires.
cite: New Zealand Herald; RNZ (5 Oct 2022; 30 Nov 2022)

n: Plan to pay 40 Maldivian MPs with Indian money to impeach Muizzu
d: The Washington Post reported on 30 December 2024 that Maldivian opposition politicians had planned to bribe 40 members of parliament, including some from President Mohamed Muizzu's own People's National Congress, to vote to impeach him, using about $6 million to be sought from India. Muizzu had won office on a platform of reducing India's influence. The paper cited an internal document titled 'Democratic Renewal Initiative' and said an officer of India's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), explored ways to remove Muizzu through two intermediaries, who confirmed the plan existed. There is no report that money was paid; Muizzu's coalition won a parliamentary majority in April 2024. Former president Mohamed Nasheed denied any Indian role.
cite: ThePrint (30 Dec 2024), citing The Washington Post; Business Standard (31 Dec 2024)

n: ERHC may have paid São Tomé officials for oil rights, inquiry says
d: ERHC, a small Houston oil company controlled from 2001 by Nigerian businessman Emeka Offor, a major donor to Nigeria's ruling party, secured favourable oil rights from São Tomé and Príncipe, including the right to pick the best blocks without the usual one-time fee. A 1997 contract had already given ERHC exploration rights for 25 years for $5 million. In 2005 São Tomé's attorney general reported that bidding for blocks in the zone shared with Nigeria showed 'serious procedural deficiencies and political manipulation' and that ERHC 'may have made improper payments to government officials'. US federal authorities investigated whether ERHC bribed São Tomé officials, and the FBI raided its Houston offices in 2006. ERHC denied wrongdoing, and no charges were reported.
cite: CorpWatch / Washington Post (2007); Offshore Magazine

n: Russian intelligence agent worked inside a Danish energy firm
rank: Employee at an energy technology firm
d: A Russian intelligence service paid a Russian man who worked in Denmark to collect information from inside a Danish company and a university. A court in Aalborg found that over several years he gathered information, mainly on energy technology, from the Technical University of Denmark and from a business in north-west Denmark, and passed it to Russian intelligence for payment. The Danish fuel cell maker SerEnergy confirmed it had employed him. He was arrested in July 2020, and after a closed trial the court on 10 May 2021 sentenced him to three years in prison followed by permanent expulsion. Russia called the case a 'witch hunt'.
cite: Moscow Times / AFP (10 May 2021); The Local Denmark (9 Dec 2020)

n: Drug traffickers reached Fiji's narcotics police and customs
d: Drug trafficking networks moving methamphetamine through the Pacific got officers of Fiji's police and customs working for them. In May 2025 two officers of the police Counter Narcotics Bureau and a senior customs border manager were among seven people charged after more than 4 kg of methamphetamine was found in air cargo at Nadi airport; the bureau was later disbanded. In December 2025 Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu confirmed that seven senior officers, including Fisi Nasario, director of the serious organised crime and intelligence department, were under investigation after leaked chats appeared to show officers discussing drug shipments and payments with traffickers. Fiji's policing minister said 27 police officers were involved in 33 drug cases between January 2023 and October 2025.
cite: RNZ (27 May 2025); OCCRP (10 Dec 2025)

n: Angolan banker's charity card funded Mauritius president's spending
d: Álvaro Sobrinho, an Angolan banker, gained influence over Mauritius's president, Ameenah Gurib-Fakim, through his charity, the Planet Earth Institute (PEI). Gurib-Fakim was the charity's vice-chair and used a PEI credit card for private spending, and PEI paid for business trips that the government approved. Sobrinho was seeking a banking licence from Mauritius's Financial Services Commission, and Gurib-Fakim asked the regulator to issue it. After the newspaper L'Express published her card statements, she repaid the spending and resigned on 23 March 2018. Before leaving she named a judge to inquire into Sobrinho's activities without consulting the cabinet, and in June 2018 the government set up a commission of inquiry into her own conduct.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ameenah Gurib-Fakim' (citing L'Express, Le Mauricien)

n: BND report accused Liechtenstein officials of aiding launderers
d: A report by Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, said organised crime had reached inside Liechtenstein's institutions. Published by Der Spiegel on 8 November 1999, it accused unnamed Liechtenstein banks, politicians and judges of cooperating with the Russian mafia and drug cartels to launder money. Prime Minister Mario Frick called it dubious and unfair. In 2000 a member of parliament, Gabriel Marxer, lost his immunity and was arrested; he was acquitted in 2002. An investigator hired by the government, Kurt Spitzer, rejected the allegations but found weaknesses in legal cooperation. The Financial Action Task Force blacklisted Liechtenstein in June 2000, and the country ended anonymous accounts opened by trustees before being removed from the list in June 2001.
cite: Wikipedia, '1999–2001 Liechtenstein financial crisis'; Christian Science Monitor (3 Jul 2000)
